Motion & kinematics

Describing how things move, precisely.

Distance, displacement, and speed

Distance is the total path length traveled; displacement is the straight-line change in position, including direction. Speed is distance covered per unit time; velocity is displacement per unit time, so it includes direction too.

Acceleration

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes over time — speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction all count as acceleration.

The equations of motion

For constant acceleration, three simple equations connect everything: v = u + at (final velocity), s = ut + ½at² (distance), and v² = u² + 2as — where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, a is acceleration, t is time, and s is distance.

Final velocity calculator (v = u + at)

Initial velocity (m/s) · Acceleration (m/s²) · Time (s)

What's the difference between speed and velocity?

Speed is just how fast something moves; velocity also specifies which way it's moving.

What does a negative acceleration mean?

Negative acceleration (deceleration) means velocity is decreasing in the positive direction, or increasing in the negative direction.

Newton's laws of motion

The three rules that govern how forces cause motion.

Newton's first law

An object stays at rest, or keeps moving at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force — often called the law of inertia.

Newton's second law

The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma. A bigger force causes more acceleration; a bigger mass resists acceleration more.

Newton's third law

For every action force, there's an equal and opposite reaction force — when you push on a wall, it pushes back on you with the same force.

Force calculator (F = ma)

Mass (kg) · Acceleration (m/s²)

According to Newton's first law, what happens to a moving object with no net force acting on it?

Without a net force, there's nothing to change the object's velocity, so it just keeps going the same way.

What does Newton's third law say about forces?

Forces always occur in these equal, opposite pairs, acting on two different objects.

Work, energy & power

How force, motion, and time combine into work and power.

Work

Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of that force: Work = Force × Distance, measured in joules.

Kinetic and potential energy

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Gravitational potential energy is stored energy due to height: PE = mgh. Energy can convert between these forms, but the total stays constant in an isolated system.

Power

Power is how quickly work is done, or energy is transferred: Power = Work ÷ Time, measured in watts. The same amount of work done faster means more power.

Kinetic energy calculator (KE = ½mv²)

Mass (kg) · Velocity (m/s)

What happens to an object's kinetic energy if its velocity doubles?

Since KE depends on velocity squared, doubling velocity quadruples the kinetic energy.

What does power measure?

Power captures the rate of doing work — the same job done faster means more power.

Gravitation

The force that pulls every mass toward every other mass.

Newton's law of gravitation

Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass — the force gets stronger with more mass and weaker with more distance, following an inverse-square relationship.

Weight vs mass

Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays constant everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass (Weight = mg), so it changes depending on the local gravitational field strength.

Gravity on other worlds

Different planets and moons have different gravitational field strengths, so the same object weighs differently on each, even though its mass never changes.

Pick a location and see how a 70kg astronaut's weight compares

Why does an astronaut's weight change on the Moon, even though their mass doesn't?

Weight depends on local gravity (Weight = mg), so a weaker gravitational field means less weight for the same mass.

Waves & sound

How energy travels without carrying matter along with it.

What a wave is

A wave transfers energy from one place to another through a medium (or through empty space, for light) without the medium itself traveling along with it.

Wave properties

Wavelength is the distance between successive identical points on a wave; frequency is how many waves pass a point per second; amplitude is the wave's height, related to its energy. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

Sound as a wave

Sound is a longitudinal wave — a series of compressions and rarefactions traveling through a medium like air. It needs a medium to travel through, which is why sound can't travel through the vacuum of space.

Wave speed calculator (v = fλ)

Frequency (Hz) · Wavelength (m)

Why can't sound travel through the vacuum of space?

As a mechanical wave, sound needs particles to compress and expand — with no particles in a vacuum, sound simply can't propagate.

Light & optics

Reflection, refraction, and how lenses bend light.

Reflection

Light bounces off a surface following the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from a line perpendicular to the surface.

Refraction

Light bends when it passes between materials of different density (like air and water), because its speed changes — this bending is why a straw looks bent when it's placed in a glass of water.

Lenses

A convex lens converges light rays to a focus point, used to correct farsightedness and in magnifying glasses. A concave lens spreads light rays apart, used to correct nearsightedness.

Pick an optical phenomenon to explore

What causes light to bend when it passes from air into water?

That speed change at the boundary between two materials is exactly what causes refraction.

Electricity & circuits

Current, voltage, and resistance in a circuit.

Current, voltage, and resistance

Current is the flow rate of electric charge, measured in amperes. Voltage is the electrical push driving that flow, measured in volts. Resistance opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms.

Ohm's law

Ohm's law ties these together: Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = IR). Increase the resistance in a circuit and, for the same voltage, current drops.

Series vs parallel circuits

In a series circuit, components share a single path, so the same current flows through all of them. In a parallel circuit, components each have their own path, so voltage is the same across each branch while current can differ.

Ohm's law calculator (V = IR)

Current (A) · Resistance (Ω)

According to Ohm's law, what happens to current if resistance increases (at constant voltage)?

With the same voltage pushing charge through a bigger resistance, less current can flow.

Magnetism

Why magnets attract, repel, and how they relate to electricity.

Magnetic poles

Every magnet has a north and south pole. Like poles repel each other; unlike poles attract — the same basic rule as electric charges.

Magnetic fields

A magnet is surrounded by a magnetic field, a region where it can exert a force on other magnetic materials, visualized as field lines running from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

Electromagnetism

Moving electric charge creates a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field can induce an electric current — this deep link between electricity and magnetism is the basis of electric motors and generators.

Pick a pole combination and see what happens

What happens when two north poles are brought close together?

Like poles always repel — this is true for both norths and both souths.

Heat & thermodynamics

How heat moves, and the laws that govern energy.

Conduction, convection, radiation

Conduction transfers heat through direct contact between particles (like a metal spoon heating up in soup). Convection transfers heat through the movement of a fluid (like warm air rising). Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves, needing no medium at all (like sunlight warming your skin).

Specific heat capacity

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. Water has a very high specific heat capacity, which is why it heats up and cools down slowly compared to most materials.

The laws of thermodynamics

The first law says energy can't be created or destroyed, only converted between forms. The second law says heat naturally flows from hotter to colder objects, never spontaneously the other way, without additional energy input.

Heat energy calculator (Q = mcΔT)

Mass (kg) · Specific heat (J/kg°C) · Temperature change (°C)

Which heat transfer method needs no medium at all?

Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves, which is why sunlight can heat things across the vacuum of space.

Modern physics

Atoms, photons, and the edge of classical physics.

The photoelectric effect

Shining light on certain metals can knock electrons loose, but only if the light's frequency is high enough — brighter dim light below that frequency does nothing, which classical wave theory couldn't explain. Einstein explained it by treating light as discrete packets of energy called photons.

Wave-particle duality

Light (and even matter) can behave like both a wave and a particle depending on the experiment — a strange but well-confirmed feature of quantum physics that classical physics never anticipated.

Special relativity, briefly

Einstein's special relativity showed that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer, no matter how fast they're moving, which leads to strange but confirmed effects like time passing more slowly for objects moving close to light speed.

Pick a modern physics phenomenon to explore

What did the photoelectric effect reveal about light?

Only light above a minimum frequency could eject electrons, which only made sense if light's energy came in discrete photon packets.

Circular motion & centripetal force

Why moving in a circle always means accelerating.

Uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction keeps changing — and acceleration is any change in velocity, not just speed.

Centripetal force

The force that keeps an object moving in a circle always points toward the center of the circle, called centripetal force: F = mv²/r.

Everyday examples

A satellite orbiting Earth, a car turning a corner, and a ball on a string all rely on some force — gravity, friction, tension — supplying this center-pointing pull.

Centripetal force calculator (F = mv²/r)

Mass (kg) · Speed (m/s) · Radius (m)

Which direction does centripetal force always point?

That inward pull is exactly what continuously redirects the object's velocity to keep it moving in a circle.

Simple harmonic motion

The repeating back-and-forth motion of pendulums and springs.

What SHM is

Simple harmonic motion happens when a restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always points back toward it — producing smooth, repeating oscillation.

Pendulums

A simple pendulum's period (time for one full swing) depends only on its length and local gravity: T = 2π√(L/g) — notably, not on the mass of the bob or the swing's amplitude (for small swings).

Springs

A spring follows Hooke's law, F = -kx, where k is the spring constant and x is displacement from equilibrium — the negative sign shows the force always opposes the displacement.

Pendulum period calculator (T = 2π√(L/g))

Length (m) · Gravity (m/s²)

What happens to a pendulum's period if you make it longer?

A longer pendulum takes more time to complete each swing, since period grows with the square root of length.

Momentum & collisions

The quantity that's always conserved when things collide.

What momentum is

Momentum is mass times velocity (p = mv) — a measure of how hard it would be to stop something moving.

Conservation of momentum

In an isolated system with no external forces, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after — even though individual objects' velocities can change dramatically.

Elastic vs inelastic collisions

In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved along with momentum (like billiard balls). In an inelastic collision, momentum is still conserved but kinetic energy isn't — some converts to heat or deformation, as when two cars crash and stick together.

Momentum calculator (p = mv)

Mass (kg) · Velocity (m/s)

What's always conserved in a collision within an isolated system?

Momentum conservation holds for every collision type — kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions specifically.

Pressure & fluids

Force spread over area, and why things float.

What pressure is

Pressure is force spread over an area: P = F/A. The same force concentrated on a smaller area creates much higher pressure, which is why a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one.

Pascal's law

Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions — the principle behind hydraulic systems, where a small force on a small piston creates a large force on a bigger one.

Archimedes' principle

An object submerged in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces. If that buoyant force is greater than or equal to the object's weight, it floats.

Pressure calculator (P = F/A)

Force (N) · Area (m²)

According to Archimedes' principle, what determines the buoyant force on a submerged object?

That displaced fluid's weight is exactly what pushes back up on the object, however much it weighs itself.

Bernoulli's principle

Why faster-moving fluid has lower pressure.

The core idea

Bernoulli's principle states that within a flowing fluid, faster-moving regions have lower pressure, and slower-moving regions have higher pressure — a direct consequence of energy conservation along a streamline.

Airplane wings

A wing's curved upper surface makes air travel faster over the top than underneath, creating lower pressure above and higher pressure below — the resulting pressure difference contributes to lift.

Other examples

A perfume atomizer, a shower curtain that billows inward, and a chimney drawing smoke upward all rely on fast-moving air creating a region of lower pressure nearby.

Pick a Bernoulli's principle example to explore

According to Bernoulli's principle, what happens to pressure where fluid moves faster?

Faster flow trades some of the fluid's pressure energy for kinetic energy, lowering the pressure in that region.

Heat engines & entropy

Why no engine can be perfectly efficient.

What a heat engine does

A heat engine converts heat energy into mechanical work by moving heat from a hot reservoir to a cold one, extracting some useful work along the way — car engines and power plant turbines both work this way.

Why 100% efficiency is impossible

The second law of thermodynamics guarantees some heat is always wasted to the cold reservoir rather than converted to work, capping every heat engine's efficiency below 100%, no matter how well designed.

Entropy always increases

Entropy, a measure of disorder, always increases (or stays the same) in an isolated system over time — this one-way trend is why heat flows from hot to cold and not spontaneously the other way.

Pick a heat engine fact to explore

Why can't any real heat engine be 100% efficient?

No matter how well-engineered, some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir, capping efficiency below 100%.

Electromagnetic induction

How a changing magnetic field creates electric current.

Faraday's law

Faraday's law of induction says a changing magnetic field through a loop of wire induces an electromotive force (voltage) in that loop — the faster the change, the bigger the induced voltage.

Lenz's law

Lenz's law says the induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change that created it — a built-in resistance to change that's a direct consequence of energy conservation.

Generators

Electric generators spin a coil of wire within a magnetic field (or vice versa), continuously changing the magnetic flux through the coil and inducing a current — turning mechanical motion into electricity.

Pick a scenario and see the induced effect

What does Lenz's law say about the direction of an induced current?

This opposition is a direct consequence of energy conservation — otherwise you'd get energy for free.

AC vs DC current

Constant flow versus current that keeps reversing.

Direct current (DC)

In direct current, charge flows steadily in one direction — the kind of current produced by batteries and used in most small electronics.

Alternating current (AC)

In alternating current, the direction of flow reverses periodically (50 or 60 times per second in most household power) — the kind of current delivered by wall outlets.

Why AC is used for power transmission

AC voltage can be stepped up or down easily using transformers, letting power be transmitted at very high voltage (and low current) over long distances to minimize energy loss, then stepped back down for safe home use — something DC can't do nearly as efficiently.

Pick a current type and see its properties

Why is AC preferred for long-distance power transmission?

Stepping voltage up for transmission and back down for use dramatically cuts energy lost as heat in the wires.

Semiconductors & diodes

The materials at the heart of modern electronics.

What a semiconductor is

A semiconductor's electrical conductivity sits between that of a conductor and an insulator, and — unlike a metal — its conductivity can be finely controlled, most often by adding tiny amounts of other elements (doping).

p-type and n-type

Doping with an element that has extra electrons creates n-type material, with free negative charge carriers. Doping with an element that has fewer electrons creates p-type material, with positive 'holes' that act as charge carriers.

Diodes

A diode is made by joining p-type and n-type material together, creating a junction that lets current flow easily in one direction but blocks it in the other — the basis of countless electronic circuits.

Pick a doping type and see its charge carrier

What does a diode do?

That one-way behavior, from the p-n junction, is exactly what makes diodes useful in countless circuits.

Nuclear physics

Binding energy, fission, and fusion.

Binding energy

Binding energy is the energy that would be needed to completely separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons — it's also, by Einstein's E=mc², related to a tiny bit of 'missing mass' compared to the separated particles.

Nuclear fission

Fission splits a heavy, unstable nucleus (like uranium-235) into smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy — the process behind nuclear power plants and early nuclear weapons.

Nuclear fusion

Fusion combines light nuclei (like hydrogen) into a heavier one, releasing even more energy per reaction than fission — this is what powers the sun and other stars, and remains a major engineering challenge to sustain and harness on Earth.

Pick a nuclear process and see how it releases energy

Which nuclear process powers the sun?

The sun fuses hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing the energy that reaches us as sunlight.

The electromagnetic spectrum

From radio waves to gamma rays, all the same kind of wave.

One family of waves

Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays are all electromagnetic waves — differing only in wavelength and frequency, all traveling at the speed of light.

Energy and frequency

Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) electromagnetic waves carry more energy per photon — which is why gamma rays are dangerous to living tissue while radio waves are harmless.

Visible light is a tiny sliver

The narrow band of wavelengths our eyes can detect, visible light, is just a small slice of the full electromagnetic spectrum, sitting between infrared and ultraviolet.

Pick a region of the spectrum and see its use

Which type of electromagnetic wave carries the most energy per photon?

Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency in the spectrum, giving them the most energy per photon.

Static electricity & electric fields

Charges at rest, and the forces between them.

Charging by friction and induction

Rubbing two materials together can transfer electrons from one to the other, leaving both with a net static charge. Induction can also redistribute charge on a nearby conductor without any direct contact at all.

Electric fields

An electric field is the force per unit charge that a charged object would feel at any point in space near another charge — field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

Coulomb's law

Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: F = kq₁q₂/r², where the force grows with charge and shrinks rapidly with distance, following an inverse-square relationship.

Coulomb's law calculator (F = kq₁q₂/r², k=8.99×10⁹)

Charge 1 (μC) · Charge 2 (μC) · Distance (m)

What happens to the electric force between two charges if the distance between them doubles?

Since force follows an inverse-square relationship with distance, doubling distance cuts force to 1/4.

Capacitors

Storing electric charge and energy in a field.

What a capacitor does

A capacitor stores electric charge (and energy) in the electric field between two conductive plates separated by an insulator, charging up when connected to a voltage source and releasing that charge later.

Capacitance

Capacitance (C = Q/V) measures how much charge a capacitor can store per volt applied — larger plate area and smaller plate separation both increase capacitance.

Uses

Capacitors provide the quick burst of energy for a camera flash, smooth out fluctuations in power supply circuits, and help tune radio receivers to specific frequencies.

Capacitance calculator (C = Q/V)

Charge (μC) · Voltage (V)

What happens to a capacitor's capacitance if you increase its plate area?

More plate area allows more charge to be stored at the same voltage, which is exactly what capacitance measures.

Simple machines

Trading force for distance without creating energy.

What simple machines do

Simple machines — levers, pulleys, inclined planes, and wheels and axles — make a task easier by changing the size or direction of the force needed, not by reducing the total work required.

Mechanical advantage

Mechanical advantage is how much a machine multiplies an applied force — a mechanical advantage of 4 means the machine lets you apply 4 times less force, but you'll need to move your end 4 times farther.

Why total work stays the same (ideally)

In an ideal, frictionless machine, the work you put in equals the work you get out — trading a smaller force over a longer distance for a larger force over a shorter distance, or vice versa.

Pick a simple machine and see how it trades force for distance

Does a simple machine reduce the total work needed to do a task?

Ideally, a simple machine changes how the work is applied — smaller force over more distance, or vice versa — not the total amount.

Rotational motion & torque

The rotational version of force and motion.

Torque

Torque is the rotational equivalent of force — it depends on both the force applied and how far from the pivot point (the lever arm) it's applied: τ = F × r.

Moment of inertia

Moment of inertia is the rotational equivalent of mass — it measures how much an object resists changes to its rotational motion, depending on both mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation.

Angular momentum conservation

Angular momentum is conserved in the absence of external torque — this is why a spinning figure skater speeds up when pulling their arms in, reducing their moment of inertia.

Torque calculator (τ = F × r)

Force (N) · Lever arm length (m)

Why does a figure skater spin faster when they pull their arms in?

With no external torque, angular momentum stays constant — so reducing moment of inertia must increase rotational speed to compensate.

Projectile motion

Why thrown objects follow a curved path.

Independent horizontal and vertical motion

A projectile's horizontal motion (constant velocity, ignoring air resistance) and vertical motion (constant downward acceleration from gravity) happen completely independently of each other, even though they combine into one curved path.

The parabolic path

Because horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes steadily, a projectile traces out a parabola — symmetric on the way up and down.

Maximizing range

For a given launch speed, a projectile's horizontal range is maximized at a 45° launch angle — any steeper or shallower angle covers less horizontal distance.

Projectile range calculator (R = v²sin(2θ)/g)

Launch speed (m/s) · Launch angle (degrees)

At what launch angle is a projectile's range maximized (ignoring air resistance)?

45° gives the best balance between how long the projectile stays airborne and how fast it moves horizontally.

Fluid dynamics

How viscosity and speed shape the way fluids flow.

Viscosity

Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow — honey has high viscosity and flows slowly, while water has low viscosity and flows easily.

Laminar vs turbulent flow

Laminar flow moves in smooth, orderly layers with no mixing between them. Turbulent flow is chaotic and swirling, with mixing and eddies — which flow type occurs depends on speed, viscosity, and the size of the flow path.

Drag

Drag is the resistive force a fluid exerts on an object moving through it, which generally increases with speed — this is why fuel efficiency drops so much at higher driving speeds, as air drag rises sharply.

Pick a fluid dynamics scenario to explore

What generally happens to drag force as an object's speed through a fluid increases?

Faster motion through a fluid generally means more resistive drag force pushing back against it.

Doppler effect

Why a siren's pitch changes as it passes you.

What the Doppler effect is

The Doppler effect is the apparent change in a wave's frequency due to relative motion between the source and the observer — the wave itself doesn't actually change, just how it's perceived.

Approaching vs receding sources

As a sound source approaches, sound waves bunch up in front of it, raising the perceived frequency (higher pitch). As it moves away, waves stretch out behind it, lowering the perceived frequency (lower pitch) — this is why a passing ambulance siren changes pitch.

Astronomical redshift

The same effect applies to light: galaxies moving away from us stretch their light to longer (redder) wavelengths, called redshift — this is key evidence that the universe is expanding.

Pick a Doppler effect scenario to explore

Why does an ambulance siren sound higher-pitched as it approaches you?

The source's own motion compresses the waves ahead of it, raising the frequency an observer perceives.

Quantum mechanics basics

Where certainty breaks down at the smallest scales.

The uncertainty principle

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that you can never simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle — the more precisely you know one, the less precisely you can know the other. This isn't a measurement flaw; it's a fundamental limit of nature.

The wave function

A particle's behavior is described by a wave function, which doesn't give an exact location but rather the probability of finding the particle at any given place — a fundamentally probabilistic description of reality.

Quantization

Many quantities in quantum mechanics, like an electron's energy in an atom, can only take specific, discrete values rather than any value at all — this quantization is where the field gets its name.

Pick a quantum concept to explore

What does the uncertainty principle say about position and momentum?

This is a fundamental feature of quantum nature, not a limitation of measuring instruments.

Astrophysics & cosmology

Stars, black holes, and the origin of the universe.

How stars shine

Stars generate energy through nuclear fusion, mostly fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, releasing the light and heat that eventually reaches us across space.

The Big Bang

The Big Bang theory describes the universe expanding from an extremely hot, dense state roughly 13.8 billion years ago — supported by evidence like the cosmic microwave background radiation and the observed redshift of distant galaxies.

Black holes

A black hole forms when enough mass collapses into a small enough space that its gravity becomes so strong not even light can escape past a boundary called the event horizon.

Pick a topic and see the key evidence or idea

What is often cited as key evidence for the Big Bang theory?

This faint background radiation, detected uniformly across the sky, is strong evidence of the universe's hot, dense early state.

Units & measurement

The SI system and how precision is tracked.

SI base units

Science relies on seven SI base units: the meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), and candela (light intensity) — every other unit is built from these.

Significant figures

Significant figures indicate how precisely a measurement is known. A calculated answer can never be more precise than the least precise measurement that went into it.

Dimensional analysis

Dimensional analysis checks whether an equation makes physical sense by tracking units through a calculation — if the units on both sides of an equation don't match, something's wrong.

Pick a quantity and see its SI unit

Why can't a calculated answer be more precise than the measurements used to find it?

A chain of calculations is only as precise as its weakest link — the least precise input measurement.

Vectors & scalars

Quantities with direction, and quantities without.

Scalars vs vectors

A scalar quantity has only magnitude (like mass or temperature); a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction (like velocity or force).

Adding vectors

Vectors add head-to-tail: the resultant vector runs from the start of the first vector to the end of the last. For perpendicular vectors, the resultant's size follows the Pythagorean theorem.

Vector components

Any vector can be broken into perpendicular components (usually horizontal and vertical), which is often easier to work with than the vector as a whole — especially in problems like projectile motion.

Resultant of two perpendicular vectors (R = √(a²+b²))

Vector A (units) · Vector B (units)

What's the key difference between a scalar and a vector?

Direction is exactly what a vector adds on top of a plain magnitude.

Free fall & terminal velocity

Falling under gravity alone, and what stops the acceleration.

Free fall

In free fall, gravity is the only force acting on an object, giving it constant downward acceleration (about 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface) — every falling object accelerates at the same rate, regardless of mass, if air resistance is ignored.

Why a feather and a hammer fall together in a vacuum

Without air resistance, mass doesn't affect an object's acceleration due to gravity — famously demonstrated on the Moon, where an astronaut dropped a feather and a hammer and they hit the ground at the same instant.

Terminal velocity

In real air, resistance grows with speed until it exactly balances gravity — at that point, acceleration stops and the object falls at a constant terminal velocity. A skydiver's spread-out body position increases air resistance and lowers terminal velocity.

Free fall calculator (v = gt)

Gravity (m/s²) · Time falling (s)

Why did the feather and hammer hit the ground at the same time on the Moon?

With no atmosphere on the Moon, both objects experienced pure gravitational acceleration, unaffected by their different masses.

Hooke's law & elasticity

How materials stretch, and when they don't spring back.

Hooke's law

Hooke's law states that the force needed to stretch or compress a spring is proportional to the displacement: F = kx, where k is the spring constant — a stiffer spring has a larger k.

Elastic vs plastic deformation

Within the elastic limit, a material returns to its original shape once the force is removed. Stretch it past that limit, and the deformation becomes plastic — permanent, even after the force is removed.

Energy stored in a stretched spring

A stretched or compressed spring stores elastic potential energy, equal to ½kx² — this is the energy released when a spring is allowed to snap back.

Elastic potential energy calculator (½kx²)

Spring constant (N/m) · Extension (m)

What happens if a spring is stretched past its elastic limit?

Beyond the elastic limit, the material's internal structure is permanently altered, so it can't fully spring back.

Center of mass & equilibrium

The balance point of an object, and what makes it stable.

What center of mass is

An object's center of mass is the single point where its entire weight can be considered to act — for a symmetric, uniform object, that's simply its geometric center.

Types of equilibrium

An object is in stable equilibrium if, when disturbed, it returns to its original position (like a ball in a bowl); unstable equilibrium if it moves further away once disturbed (like a ball balanced on a hill); and neutral equilibrium if it stays in its new position (like a ball on a flat surface).

Why a low, wide base is more stable

An object is harder to tip over when its center of mass sits low and its base is wide, since it takes a much bigger tilt before the center of mass moves outside the base and gravity starts pulling it over.

Pick an object shape and see its stability

Why is a wide, low base more stable than a tall, narrow one?

A wide, low base gives a lot of room for the center of mass to shift before gravity can pull the object over.

Work-energy theorem

Connecting the work done on an object to its change in motion.

The work-energy theorem

The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy — pushing something harder or farther increases its kinetic energy by exactly that amount of work.

Conservation of mechanical energy

In the absence of friction or other resistive forces, the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) of a system stays constant — energy just converts between the two forms, like a pendulum swinging between height and speed.

Where 'lost' energy actually goes

When friction is present, mechanical energy isn't destroyed — it converts into heat (and sometimes sound), which is why a sliding object eventually stops and everything around it warms up very slightly.

Work-energy calculator: change in KE from work done

Work done (J)

According to the work-energy theorem, what does net work done on an object equal?

Work put into an object goes directly into changing how much kinetic energy it has.

Efficiency of machines

Why no real machine gets 100% of its energy out as useful work.

What efficiency measures

Efficiency compares useful energy output to total energy input: Efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%. A perfectly efficient machine would return 100% of the energy put into it as useful work.

Why real machines fall short

Friction, air resistance, and heat losses in real machines always waste some input energy, converting it to heat instead of useful work — which is why every real machine's efficiency is below 100%.

Improving efficiency

Lubrication reduces friction, streamlining reduces air resistance, and insulation reduces heat loss — all common ways engineers push a machine's efficiency closer to (but never quite reaching) 100%.

Efficiency calculator

Useful energy output (J) · Total energy input (J)

Why can't any real machine reach 100% efficiency?

Some energy always escapes as heat or sound due to friction and resistance, which is unavoidable in any real system.

Thermal expansion

Why materials grow when heated.

Why materials expand when heated

Heating a substance makes its particles vibrate and move more vigorously, on average pushing each other slightly farther apart — which shows up as a small increase in the material's overall size.

Why engineers plan for it

Bridges, railway tracks, and pipelines all include small expansion gaps or flexible joints, since a solid material that can't expand freely when heated will buckle or crack under the internal stress.

Water's unusual behavior

Unlike most substances, water actually expands as it cools from 4°C down to freezing, and expands further when it freezes solid — which is exactly why ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.

Pick a scenario and see the thermal expansion effect

Why do bridges include expansion joints?

Without room to expand, a heated material would build up internal stress and eventually crack or buckle.

Specific latent heat

Why temperature holds steady during a change of state.

What latent heat is

Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state — melting, freezing, boiling, or condensing — without any change in temperature.

Why temperature doesn't rise during a phase change

All the energy added during melting or boiling goes into breaking the forces holding particles in a fixed structure (or pulling them apart entirely), rather than speeding the particles up — so temperature holds steady until the change is complete.

Latent heat of fusion vs vaporization

The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to melt a unit mass of a solid into liquid; the specific latent heat of vaporization is the energy needed to boil a unit mass of liquid into gas — vaporization almost always takes much more energy than fusion.

Latent heat calculator (Q = mL)

Mass (kg) · Specific latent heat (J/kg)

Why does the temperature of melting ice stay at 0°C until it's fully melted?

That energy is used entirely to change the ice's state, not to raise its temperature, until the phase change finishes.

Electric power & household electricity

How power, energy, and electricity bills connect.

Electric power

Electric power is the rate energy is transferred by a current: P = VI (voltage times current), also expressible as P = I²R or P = V²/R using Ohm's law.

The kilowatt-hour

Electricity bills are measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) — the energy used by a 1000-watt appliance running for one hour — rather than joules, simply because it's a more convenient everyday unit.

Fuses and circuit breakers

Fuses and circuit breakers protect a circuit from dangerously high current by breaking the circuit automatically if current exceeds a safe limit, preventing overheating and potential fires.

Electric power calculator (P = VI)

Voltage (V) · Current (A)

What does a kilowatt-hour actually measure?

It's the energy a 1000-watt device would use running for one hour — a practical unit for household billing.

Transformers

Changing AC voltage up or down using magnetic induction.

How a transformer works

A transformer has two coils of wire wound around a shared iron core. Alternating current in the primary coil creates a constantly changing magnetic field, which induces a voltage in the secondary coil purely through electromagnetic induction — no direct electrical connection needed.

Step-up and step-down

The ratio of turns between the coils sets the voltage change: more turns on the secondary coil steps voltage up, fewer turns steps it down. The relationship is Vp/Vs = Np/Ns.

Why transformers only work with AC

Since transformers rely on a constantly changing magnetic field to induce voltage, they don't work with steady DC current, which produces no changing field once it settles at a constant value.

Transformer calculator (Vp/Vs = Np/Ns)

Primary voltage (V) · Primary turns · Secondary turns

Why don't transformers work with direct current (DC)?

Induction requires a changing magnetic field, and steady DC current stops producing one once it reaches a constant value.

Motors & generators

Turning electricity into motion, and motion back into electricity.

Electric motors

An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical motion: current flowing through a coil in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is used to spin the coil continuously.

Generators

A generator does the reverse: spinning a coil within a magnetic field (by any mechanical means — steam turbines, wind, flowing water) induces a current, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy.

Two sides of the same principle

A motor and a generator are built almost identically — the difference is just which energy conversion direction is being used, electrical-to-mechanical or mechanical-to-electrical.

Pick a device and see its energy conversion

What's the key difference between a motor and a generator?

They're built on the same basic principle, just running the energy conversion in opposite directions.

Nuclear reactors

Harnessing controlled fission to generate electricity.

Controlled chain reaction

A nuclear reactor sustains a controlled fission chain reaction, where neutrons released from splitting one uranium nucleus go on to split others — carefully controlled so the reaction continues steadily rather than escalating.

Moderators and control rods

A moderator (often water or graphite) slows down neutrons to the speed most likely to trigger further fission. Control rods, made of neutron-absorbing material, can be inserted or withdrawn to speed up, slow down, or stop the reaction.

From heat to electricity

The heat released by fission boils water into steam, which spins a turbine connected to a generator — a nuclear power plant essentially uses fission just as another, more powerful way to boil water for a steam turbine.

Pick a reactor component and see its role

What is the purpose of control rods in a nuclear reactor?

By absorbing more or fewer neutrons, control rods let operators speed up, slow down, or halt the fission chain reaction.

Radiation & safety

Managing exposure to ionizing radiation.

Measuring radiation dose

Radiation dose — the biological impact of radiation exposure — is measured in sieverts (Sv). Different types of radiation and different tissues respond differently, which is why dose isn't just about the raw amount of radiation.

The ALARA principle

ALARA stands for 'As Low As Reasonably Achievable' — the guiding principle in radiation safety that exposure should always be minimized as much as practically possible, even when a dose is technically within a safe limit.

Reducing exposure: time, distance, shielding

Three practical tools reduce radiation exposure: spending less time near a source, increasing distance from it (radiation intensity falls off sharply with distance), and using shielding material like lead or concrete to absorb it.

Pick a radiation safety measure and see why it works

What does the ALARA principle recommend?

Even doses within an accepted safe range should still be minimized wherever practically possible.

Mass-energy equivalence

Einstein's E=mc² and why tiny masses hide huge energy.

What E=mc² means

Einstein's famous equation shows that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, interchangeable under the right conditions — a certain amount of mass is equivalent to a specific, calculable amount of energy.

Why the effect is so huge

Since the speed of light, c, is an enormous number, and the equation squares it, even a tiny amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy — which is why nuclear reactions release so much more energy than chemical ones for the same mass of fuel.

Where this shows up

Nuclear fission and fusion both convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy, matching E=mc² almost exactly — one of the most thoroughly tested equations in all of physics.

Mass-energy calculator (E = mc², c=3×10⁸ m/s)

Mass converted (kg)

Why does converting even a tiny amount of mass release such a huge amount of energy?

Since E=mc² multiplies mass by the speed of light squared — a huge number — even a small mass corresponds to enormous energy.

General relativity basics

Gravity reimagined as the curvature of spacetime.

Gravity as curvature, not force

Einstein's general relativity reimagines gravity not as a force pulling objects together, but as the curvature of spacetime itself caused by mass and energy — objects simply follow the straightest possible path through that curved spacetime.

Evidence supporting it

Starlight bending as it passes near the sun, first confirmed during a 1919 solar eclipse, matched general relativity's predictions rather than Newton's. GPS satellites also need tiny relativistic time corrections to stay accurate, since time passes slightly differently for them than on Earth's surface.

Black holes as extreme curvature

A black hole represents an extreme case of this curvature — so much mass concentrated in so little space that spacetime folds in on itself, trapping anything, even light, that crosses its event horizon.

Pick a piece of evidence and see what it confirms

According to general relativity, what is gravity actually caused by?

Einstein's insight replaced the idea of a gravitational 'pull' with objects following curved paths through warped spacetime.

Fundamental particles

The building blocks of everything, and the forces between them.

Quarks and leptons

Protons and neutrons are themselves made of even smaller particles called quarks, held together by the strong force. Electrons belong to a different family called leptons, which aren't made of anything smaller as far as we know.

The fundamental forces

Four fundamental forces govern all known interactions: the strong force (binding quarks and nuclei), the weak force (responsible for some radioactive decay), electromagnetism (governing charged particles and light), and gravity (the weakest, but dominant at large scales).

The Higgs boson

The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012, is linked to the Higgs field, which is what gives many fundamental particles their mass in the first place — without it, particles like electrons would have no mass at all.

Pick a particle or force and see its role

What are protons and neutrons made of?

Quarks, held together by the strong force, are the smaller particles that make up both protons and neutrons.

Frontiers of physics

The biggest open questions physicists are still chasing.

Dark matter

Galaxies rotate faster than the visible matter within them should allow under normal gravity — this mismatch is strong evidence for dark matter, an invisible substance that seems to add extra gravitational pull but has never been directly detected.

Dark energy

The universe's expansion isn't just continuing — it's accelerating, a discovery that led to the concept of dark energy, a mysterious force pushing space apart, which makes up most of the universe's total energy content.

Searching for a unified theory

Quantum mechanics describes the very small extremely well, and general relativity describes gravity and the very large extremely well — but the two don't fit together smoothly, and finding a single theory (like string theory) that unifies them remains one of physics' biggest unsolved challenges.

Pick a mystery and see the key evidence for it

What evidence suggests dark matter exists?

That extra rotational speed implies far more gravitational pull — and therefore more mass — than we can actually see.

Physics of sound: music & harmonics

Why instruments sound the way they do.

Pitch and frequency

Pitch is our perception of a sound's frequency — higher frequency vibrations are heard as higher pitch. A note one octave higher has exactly double the frequency.

Timbre and harmonics

Two instruments playing the same note still sound different because of timbre — caused by the different mix of overtones (harmonics) each instrument produces on top of the main frequency, giving each its distinctive tonal color.

Resonance

Resonance happens when an object vibrates especially strongly at its natural frequency. Instrument bodies — a guitar's hollow body, a violin's f-holes — are shaped specifically to resonate with and amplify certain frequencies, projecting sound much louder than the vibrating string alone could.

Pick a musical physics concept to explore

What makes two instruments playing the same note sound different from each other?

That unique blend of overtones on top of the fundamental frequency is exactly what gives each instrument its own character.

Renewable energy physics

The physics behind solar cells and wind turbines.

Solar cells

A solar (photovoltaic) cell generates electricity through the photovoltaic effect: photons of light striking a semiconductor material knock electrons loose, and the cell's internal structure directs that flow of electrons into a usable current.

Wind turbines

A wind turbine converts the kinetic energy of moving air into mechanical rotation of its blades, which spins a generator to produce electricity — essentially the same generator principle used in traditional power plants, just driven by wind instead of steam.

Efficiency and intermittency challenges

Both solar and wind power face real physical limits: solar cells can only convert a fraction of incoming light into electricity, and both sources are intermittent — dependent on sunlight or wind being available — which is why energy storage remains a major engineering focus.

Pick a renewable energy source and see how it generates electricity

What effect lets a solar cell generate electricity directly from sunlight?

Photons striking the semiconductor material knock electrons loose, and the cell's structure channels them into a usable electric current.

Orbital mechanics & Kepler's laws

Why planets sweep out equal areas in equal times.

Kepler's first law

Planets orbit the sun in ellipses, not perfect circles, with the sun at one focus of the ellipse rather than the center.

Kepler's second law

A line from the sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times — meaning a planet moves faster when closer to the sun and slower when farther away.

Kepler's third law

The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the sun — a mathematical link that let scientists predict orbits long before Newton explained why it worked.

Pick a Kepler's law and see what it says

According to Kepler's second law, when does a planet move fastest in its orbit?

Sweeping equal areas in equal time means the planet must move faster when it's closer in, where the arc is more tightly curved.

Escape velocity

How fast you'd need to go to leave a planet's gravity behind forever.

What escape velocity is

Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object needs to permanently break free of a planet's gravitational pull, without any further propulsion.

What it depends on

Escape velocity increases with the planet's mass and decreases with its radius — a more massive, more compact body is harder to escape from.

Earth vs other worlds

Earth's escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s. The Moon's much weaker gravity gives it an escape velocity of only about 2.4 km/s, which is part of why it was far easier to launch rockets home from the Moon than from Earth.

Pick a body and see its approximate escape velocity

What two properties of a planet determine its escape velocity?

More mass packed into a smaller radius both increase the gravitational pull that has to be overcome.

Angular velocity & angular acceleration

Measuring rotation the way we measure straight-line motion.

Angular velocity

Angular velocity measures how fast something rotates, in radians per second, rather than how fast it moves in a straight line — it's the rotational equivalent of ordinary velocity.

Angular acceleration

Angular acceleration measures how quickly angular velocity itself changes over time, just as ordinary acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes.

Connecting angular and linear motion

A point on a rotating object has a linear speed equal to its angular velocity times its distance from the axis of rotation — which is why the outer edge of a spinning disk moves faster than a point closer to its center, even though both share the same angular velocity.

Linear speed from angular velocity (v = ωr)

Angular velocity (rad/s) · Radius (m)

Why does the outer edge of a spinning disk move faster than a point near its center?

Linear speed equals angular velocity times radius, so a larger radius means a higher linear speed at the same rotation rate.

Moment of inertia

Why some shapes are harder to spin up than others.

What moment of inertia measures

Moment of inertia measures how resistant an object is to changes in its rotational motion — the rotational equivalent of mass in Newton's second law.

Why mass distribution matters

Unlike ordinary mass, moment of inertia depends heavily on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation — mass farther from the axis contributes much more to moment of inertia than the same mass close to the axis.

Real-world consequences

A hollow cylinder has a larger moment of inertia than a solid cylinder of the same mass and radius, since more of its mass sits farther from the axis — which is why a solid ball rolls down a ramp faster than a hollow one of the same size and mass.

Pick a shape and see its rotational behavior

Why does a solid ball roll down a ramp faster than a hollow ball of the same mass and size?

With its mass concentrated closer to the center, the solid ball resists rotational acceleration less.

Conservation of angular momentum

Why spinning objects resist changes to their rotation axis.

The conservation law

In the absence of external torque, a system's total angular momentum stays constant — a rotational parallel to the conservation of linear momentum.

Changing shape changes speed

Since angular momentum is moment of inertia times angular velocity, if a spinning object's moment of inertia decreases (like a skater pulling in their arms), its angular velocity must increase to keep angular momentum constant.

Gyroscopic stability

A rapidly spinning object, like a gyroscope or a bicycle wheel, strongly resists changes to its rotation axis — this stubborn stability is why bicycles are so much easier to balance while moving than standing still.

Pick a scenario and see the angular momentum effect

Why does a spinning skater speed up when they pull their arms in?

With angular momentum held constant, a smaller moment of inertia requires a correspondingly larger angular velocity.

Collisions in two dimensions

Momentum conservation when objects don't collide head-on.

Momentum as a vector

Momentum is a vector quantity, so in a two-dimensional collision, momentum must be conserved separately along each perpendicular direction (usually x and y), not just as a single overall total.

Glancing collisions

When two objects collide at an angle rather than head-on, they typically scatter off in different directions afterward — but the vector sum of their momenta before and after the collision must still match exactly.

Why this matters in practice

Physicists use two-dimensional momentum conservation to reconstruct particle collisions in accelerators, analyze billiard shots, and model car crashes that happen at an angle rather than straight on.

Pick a fact about 2D collisions to explore

In a two-dimensional collision, how must momentum be conserved?

Since momentum is a vector, both its x- and y-components must independently balance before and after the collision.

Impulse & impulse-momentum theorem

How force and time together change an object's momentum.

What impulse is

Impulse is the product of force and the time it acts: Impulse = FΔt — a way of capturing how a force applied over some duration changes an object's motion.

The impulse-momentum theorem

The impulse-momentum theorem states that impulse equals the change in momentum: FΔt = Δ(mv) — the same net effect can come from a large force over a short time, or a smaller force over a longer time.

Why airbags and padding work

Airbags and padded surfaces extend the time over which a collision's force acts, which — for the same change in momentum — reduces the peak force experienced, lowering the risk of injury.

Impulse calculator (Impulse = FΔt)

Force (N) · Time (s)

Why do airbags reduce injury in a crash?

Stretching out the time over which momentum changes lowers the force needed to produce that same change.

Friction

The resistive force that opposes sliding.

Static vs kinetic friction

Static friction resists the start of motion between two surfaces in contact; kinetic friction resists motion that's already happening. Static friction is usually slightly stronger than kinetic friction for the same surfaces.

The coefficient of friction

The coefficient of friction (μ) is a number describing how much two particular surfaces resist sliding against each other — rougher surface pairings generally have higher coefficients.

The friction force formula

Friction force is approximately proportional to the normal force pressing the two surfaces together: F = μN — notably, it doesn't depend much on the surface area in contact.

Friction force calculator (F = μN)

Coefficient of friction · Normal force (N)

Which is usually stronger for the same two surfaces: static or kinetic friction?

It typically takes slightly more force to get something moving from rest than to keep it moving once it's already sliding.

Terminal velocity & the drag equation

A closer look at how air resistance caps falling speed.

Drag force

Drag force from air resistance increases with speed — roughly with the square of speed at typical falling speeds — which is why it eventually catches up to and balances the constant pull of gravity.

Reaching terminal velocity

As a falling object speeds up, drag grows until it exactly equals the object's weight; at that point, net force is zero, acceleration stops, and the object falls at a constant terminal velocity.

What changes terminal velocity

A larger surface area facing the airflow increases drag at a given speed, lowering terminal velocity — which is exactly why a skydiver falls much slower spread-eagle than in a head-first dive.

Pick a scenario and see the effect on terminal velocity

Why does a skydiver fall slower spread-eagle than head-first?

More exposed surface area facing the airflow increases air resistance, which balances gravity at a lower speed.

Pendulums: simple vs physical

Not every swinging object behaves like a textbook pendulum.

The simple pendulum

A simple pendulum assumes all the mass is concentrated in a single point (the bob) at the end of a massless string — its period depends only on length and gravity, not on the mass of the bob.

The physical pendulum

A physical pendulum is any rigid object swinging about a pivot, where mass is distributed throughout its shape rather than concentrated at one point — its period depends on its moment of inertia and where its center of mass sits relative to the pivot.

Why the distinction matters

Real swinging objects, like a swinging door or a metronome's arm, behave as physical pendulums, and analyzing them accurately requires accounting for their full mass distribution, not just treating them as a simple pendulum.

Pick a pendulum type and see what determines its period

What determines the period of an ideal simple pendulum?

For small swings, a simple pendulum's period depends purely on length and gravitational acceleration, not the mass of the bob.

Resonance & natural frequency

Why pushing at just the right rhythm can build huge oscillations.

Natural frequency

Every physical system that can oscillate has a natural frequency it 'prefers' to vibrate at, determined by its own physical properties, like stiffness and mass.

Resonance

Resonance occurs when a system is driven by a periodic force at (or very near) its natural frequency, causing the amplitude of oscillation to build up dramatically, far beyond what the same force could achieve at other frequencies.

The Tacoma Narrows Bridge

The dramatic 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge is a famous, if debated, real-world illustration of the danger of resonance — wind-driven oscillations built up to catastrophic amplitude, ultimately tearing the bridge apart.

Pick a resonance example and see what happens

What happens when a system is driven at its natural frequency?

Driving a system at its own natural frequency lets energy add up efficiently with each cycle, producing resonance.

Standing waves

Waves that seem to stay in place instead of traveling.

How standing waves form

A standing wave forms when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and interfere — often a wave and its own reflection — creating a pattern that appears to oscillate in place rather than travel.

Nodes and antinodes

Nodes are points on a standing wave that never move at all; antinodes are points that oscillate with maximum amplitude, halfway between adjacent nodes.

Standing waves in instruments

A guitar string or an organ pipe produces sound through standing waves — the specific pattern of nodes and antinodes that fits the string or pipe's length determines which frequencies (notes) it can naturally produce.

Pick a term and see what it means

What is a node in a standing wave?

Nodes are fixed points of zero displacement, staying still while the rest of the wave oscillates around them.

Wave interference

What happens when two waves overlap.

Constructive interference

When two waves overlap in phase — crest meeting crest — their displacements add together, producing a wave with larger amplitude than either wave alone.

Destructive interference

When two waves overlap out of phase — crest meeting trough — their displacements partially or fully cancel, producing a smaller or even zero amplitude at that point.

Noise-canceling headphones

Noise-canceling headphones exploit destructive interference deliberately: a microphone detects incoming ambient sound, and the headphones generate an inverted sound wave that cancels much of it out before it reaches your ear.

Pick an interference type and see the result

How do noise-canceling headphones reduce ambient sound?

By producing a wave that's out of phase with the incoming noise, the two largely cancel each other out.

Diffraction

How waves bend around obstacles and through openings.

What diffraction is

Diffraction is the bending and spreading of waves as they pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle — a behavior unique to waves, not seen with simple particles.

When diffraction is most noticeable

Diffraction is most pronounced when the size of the opening or obstacle is comparable to the wave's wavelength — which is why sound (with long wavelengths) diffracts noticeably around corners, while visible light (with much shorter wavelengths) diffracts far less obviously in everyday situations.

Diffraction gratings

A diffraction grating uses many closely spaced slits to diffract light into distinct patterns based on wavelength, letting scientists precisely measure and separate different colors (or wavelengths) of light — a key tool in spectroscopy.

Pick a diffraction example to explore

When is diffraction most noticeable?

That close match between wavelength and gap size is what makes the bending and spreading effect most apparent.

Polarization of light

Why some sunglasses cut glare so effectively.

What polarization is

Light is a transverse wave, meaning it can vibrate in many directions perpendicular to its direction of travel. Polarized light has its vibrations restricted to just one direction.

Polarizing filters

A polarizing filter only lets through light vibrating in one specific direction, blocking the rest — stacking two polarizing filters at 90° to each other blocks essentially all light.

Why polarized sunglasses reduce glare

Light reflecting off a flat surface like water or a road tends to become partially polarized in one direction. Polarized sunglasses are designed to block that specific direction, cutting down reflected glare much more than ordinary sunglasses.

Pick a polarization scenario to explore

Why do polarized sunglasses reduce glare from water or roads so effectively?

Reflected light tends to polarize in a specific direction, which these lenses are designed to filter out.

Total internal reflection & fiber optics

How light gets trapped inside a thin glass fiber.

Total internal reflection

When light traveling in a denser medium hits a boundary with a less dense medium at a steep enough angle (beyond the critical angle), it reflects entirely back into the denser medium instead of refracting out — total internal reflection.

How optical fibers use this

An optical fiber's core is surrounded by a cladding layer with a lower refractive index, so light entering the core at a suitable angle keeps reflecting internally over and over, traveling enormous distances along the fiber with very little loss.

Why fiber optics matter

Optical fibers carry data as pulses of light rather than electricity, enabling the enormous bandwidth and long-distance, low-loss transmission that underlies most of the modern internet's backbone infrastructure.

Pick a fact about fiber optics to explore

What keeps light traveling along the inside of an optical fiber?

Total internal reflection bounces the light repeatedly along the fiber's length instead of letting it escape.

Lenses & image formation

Reading a ray diagram to predict where an image forms.

Converging and diverging lenses

A converging (convex) lens bends parallel light rays inward to a focus point; a diverging (concave) lens spreads parallel rays outward, as if they came from a focus point in front of the lens.

Real vs virtual images

A real image forms where light rays actually converge and can be projected onto a screen (like on a camera sensor). A virtual image forms where rays only appear to come from, and can't be projected onto anything — like the enlarged image seen through a magnifying glass.

Magnification

Magnification compares an image's size to the original object's size — a lens can magnify (image larger than object), reduce (image smaller), or leave the size unchanged, depending on the object's distance from the lens.

Pick a lens scenario and see the image type

What's the key difference between a real image and a virtual image?

Real images form where light rays actually converge; virtual images only appear to come from a point where rays don't truly meet.

Mirrors & image formation

How curved mirrors bend reflections into different images.

Concave mirrors

A concave mirror curves inward and converges reflected light, capable of forming either a real, inverted image (for objects beyond its focal point) or a magnified, upright virtual image (for objects closer than the focal point) — the same basic behavior used in makeup mirrors and telescopes.

Convex mirrors

A convex mirror curves outward and always produces a smaller, upright virtual image, regardless of object distance — its wider field of view is exactly why convex mirrors are used for car side mirrors and store security mirrors.

Plane mirrors

An ordinary flat (plane) mirror always produces an upright, same-size virtual image that appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

Pick a mirror type and see its typical image

Why are convex mirrors used for car side mirrors?

That wide field of view helps drivers see more of what's behind and beside them, even though objects appear smaller.

The human eye as an optical instrument

How your eye focuses light, and why glasses correct it.

How the eye focuses light

The eye's cornea and lens work together to focus light onto the retina at the back of the eye, where light-sensitive cells convert it into signals sent to the brain. The lens changes shape to focus on objects at different distances, a process called accommodation.

Nearsightedness and farsightedness

In nearsightedness (myopia), the eye focuses images in front of the retina, making distant objects blurry — corrected with a diverging lens. In farsightedness (hyperopia), images focus behind the retina, making close objects blurry — corrected with a converging lens.

Why corrective lenses work

Glasses and contact lenses add just enough extra converging or diverging power to shift where light focuses, moving the image precisely back onto the retina.

Pick a vision condition and see its correction

Why does a nearsighted eye need a diverging lens to correct vision?

A diverging lens spreads the incoming light slightly, pushing the focus point back exactly onto the retina.

Color & the visible spectrum

Why objects appear the colors they do.

White light is a mixture

Ordinary white light, like sunlight, is actually a mixture of all the visible wavelengths — a prism or raindrop can separate it into the familiar rainbow of colors by refracting each wavelength slightly differently.

Why objects have color

An object appears a particular color because it absorbs most wavelengths of light striking it and reflects (or transmits) the rest — a red apple looks red because it reflects mostly red wavelengths and absorbs the others.

Additive vs subtractive color mixing

Mixing colored light (like on a screen) is additive — combining all colors of light makes white. Mixing colored pigments (like paint) is subtractive — each pigment absorbs more wavelengths, so combining many tends toward black or brown.

Pick a color scenario and see the physics behind it

Why does a red apple appear red?

An object's apparent color comes from which wavelengths of light it reflects back to your eye rather than absorbing.

Electric potential & potential difference

The energy landscape that drives current through a circuit.

Electric potential energy

A charge placed in an electric field has electric potential energy, related to its position within that field, similar to how a mass has gravitational potential energy based on height.

Potential difference (voltage)

Potential difference, or voltage, is the energy transferred per unit charge moving between two points — it's what actually drives current to flow through a circuit, from higher to lower potential.

Why voltage matters in circuits

A battery's voltage represents the energy it can give to each unit of charge passing through it — a higher voltage battery can push more energy into the same current, which is why voltage and current together determine a circuit's total power.

Pick a term and see what it means

What does voltage (potential difference) actually represent?

Voltage measures how much energy each unit of charge gains or loses moving between two points in a circuit.

Series & parallel resistor circuits

How resistors combine differently depending on how they're wired.

Resistors in series

Resistors in series share the same current, and their resistances simply add together: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ... — adding more resistors in series always increases total resistance.

Resistors in parallel

Resistors in parallel share the same voltage across each branch, but current splits between them. Total resistance follows 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... — adding more resistors in parallel always decreases total resistance.

Why the distinction matters

Household wiring uses parallel circuits so that each appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched independently — if they were wired in series, turning off one appliance would cut off power to all the others.

Two resistors in series calculator (R = R1 + R2)

Resistor 1 (Ω) · Resistor 2 (Ω)

Why is household wiring set up in parallel rather than in series?

In a series circuit, switching off one device would cut the whole circuit — parallel wiring keeps each device independent.

Kirchhoff's laws

The two rules that govern any electric circuit, however complex.

Kirchhoff's current law

Kirchhoff's current law states that the total current flowing into a junction in a circuit must equal the total current flowing out — charge can't pile up or vanish at a junction.

Kirchhoff's voltage law

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the sum of all voltage changes around any closed loop in a circuit must equal zero — energy gained from a battery must exactly equal energy lost across all the resistances in that loop.

Why these laws matter

Kirchhoff's laws let engineers analyze circuits far too complex for simple series/parallel resistor rules alone, forming the mathematical backbone of circuit analysis in electronics.

Pick a Kirchhoff's law and see what it says

What does Kirchhoff's current law say about a circuit junction?

This reflects that electric charge is conserved — it can't simply build up or vanish at a junction point.

Electric field lines & equipotential surfaces

Visualizing invisible fields with lines and surfaces.

Electric field lines

Electric field lines are a visual tool showing the direction a positive test charge would be pushed at any point — lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and denser lines mean a stronger field.

Equipotential surfaces

An equipotential surface connects all points at the same electric potential — no work is needed to move a charge along one, since there's no potential difference between any two points on it.

Field lines and equipotentials are perpendicular

Electric field lines always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, since a field always points in the direction potential changes fastest, which is necessarily perpendicular to a surface of constant potential.

Pick a term and see what it describes

At what angle do electric field lines cross equipotential surfaces?

Since the field points in the direction of fastest potential change, it must be perpendicular to surfaces of constant potential.

Magnetic force on a moving charge

Why a charged particle curves inside a magnetic field.

The magnetic force formula

A charged particle moving through a magnetic field feels a force F = qvB sin θ, where q is its charge, v is its velocity, B is the magnetic field strength, and θ is the angle between velocity and field.

The force is always perpendicular

This magnetic force always acts perpendicular to both the particle's velocity and the magnetic field — which means it changes the particle's direction but never its speed, curving its path into a circle (or helix) rather than speeding it up or slowing it down.

Applications

This principle underlies mass spectrometers (sorting particles by how much their paths curve) and particle accelerators, which use magnetic fields to steer and focus beams of charged particles.

Magnetic force calculator (F = qvB, charge in μC)

Charge (μC) · Velocity (m/s) · Field strength (T)

Why does a magnetic force change a charged particle's direction but never its speed?

A perpendicular force can only redirect motion, never add or remove energy along the direction of travel.

The motor effect

How a current-carrying wire feels a push inside a magnetic field.

What the motor effect is

When a current-carrying wire sits inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force — called the motor effect — as long as the current isn't running exactly parallel to the field.

Finding the direction

The direction of this force is always perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field, commonly found using the right-hand (or left-hand, in some conventions) rule.

From force to rotation

In an electric motor, this force acts on a current-carrying coil positioned in a magnetic field. Since the force pushes opposite sides of the coil in opposite directions, it creates a torque that spins the coil continuously.

Pick a fact about the motor effect to explore

What is the motor effect?

This force between current and magnetic field is exactly what electric motors are built around.

Cyclotrons & particle accelerators

Using electric and magnetic fields to push particles to extreme speeds.

How a cyclotron works

A cyclotron accelerates charged particles by repeatedly applying an electric field as they spiral outward, while a magnetic field bends their path into an ever-widening circle — each pass through the electric field adds a little more speed.

Why magnetic fields are used for steering

Since a magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity, magnetic fields are ideal for bending a particle's path without changing its speed, letting accelerators guide particles around curved paths.

Modern particle accelerators

Massive modern accelerators, like the Large Hadron Collider, use the same basic principles at enormous scale — accelerating particles to nearly the speed of light and colliding them to study the fundamental building blocks of matter.

Pick a fact about particle accelerators to explore

Why are magnetic fields, rather than electric fields, used to steer particles in a circular path?

That perpendicular force is exactly what's needed to curve a path continuously without ever slowing the particle down.

Superconductivity

Materials that carry current with zero resistance.

What superconductivity is

Below a certain critical temperature, some materials lose all electrical resistance entirely, becoming superconductors — current can flow through them indefinitely without losing any energy to heat.

Why it's hard to use widely

Most known superconductors only work at extremely low temperatures, often near absolute zero, requiring expensive cooling — the search for materials that superconduct at higher, more practical temperatures remains an active research area.

Applications

Superconducting magnets, cooled to very low temperatures, are used in MRI machines and particle accelerators, where their ability to carry huge currents without energy loss creates extremely strong, stable magnetic fields.

Pick a fact about superconductivity to explore

What defines a material as a superconductor?

That complete loss of resistance below a critical temperature is the defining feature of superconductivity.

Thermal conductivity

Why some materials feel colder to the touch than others.

What thermal conductivity measures

Thermal conductivity measures how easily a material conducts heat — metals generally have high thermal conductivity, while materials like wood, plastic, and air have much lower conductivity.

Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature

Metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood does, even if both are at the same room temperature — that faster heat loss is what makes metal feel colder to the touch.

Insulation

Good insulating materials have very low thermal conductivity, often relying on trapped air pockets (as in fiberglass insulation or a winter coat's fill) to slow heat transfer, since still air itself conducts heat quite poorly.

Pick a material and see its thermal conductivity

Why does metal feel colder than wood, even at the same room temperature?

That faster heat transfer away from your skin is what makes metal feel noticeably colder, even without a real temperature difference.

The ideal gas law

Connecting pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas.

The ideal gas law

The ideal gas law combines the individual gas laws into one equation: PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the amount of gas (in moles), R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature.

What 'ideal' means here
