An ideal gas is a simplified model assuming gas particles have no volume of their own and no attractive forces between them — a good approximation for real gases under normal conditions, though it breaks down at very high pressure or low temperature.

Using the law

The ideal gas law lets you calculate any one of pressure, volume, temperature, or amount of gas, given the other three — a fundamental tool across physics, chemistry, and engineering.

Ideal gas law calculator (P = nRT/V, R=8.314)

Amount of gas (mol) · Temperature (K) · Volume (m³)

What does the 'n' represent in the ideal gas law PV = nRT?

n is the quantity of gas present, measured in moles, directly tied to how many particles are in the sample.

Heat capacity & calorimetry

Measuring how much energy it takes to change a temperature.

Specific heat capacity

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree — substances with high specific heat capacity, like water, resist temperature change more than those with low specific heat capacity, like metals.

The calorimetry equation

Calorimetry uses Q = mcΔT to relate heat energy (Q) to mass (m), specific heat capacity (c), and temperature change (ΔT) — measuring any three of these lets you calculate the fourth.

Calorimeters

A calorimeter is a device designed to measure heat changes in a chemical or physical process by carefully tracking the resulting temperature change of a known mass of surrounding water or another medium.

Calorimetry calculator (Q = mcΔT)

Mass (kg) · Specific heat (J/kg°C) · Temperature change (°C)

Why does water resist temperature change more than most metals?

A higher specific heat capacity means more energy is needed to change water's temperature by the same amount.

Absolute zero & the third law of thermodynamics

The coldest temperature theoretically possible.

What absolute zero is

Absolute zero, 0 kelvin (about -273.15°C), is the theoretical temperature at which particles have the minimum possible thermal motion — it's the natural zero point of the Kelvin temperature scale.

Why it can't actually be reached

The third law of thermodynamics states that absolute zero can be approached arbitrarily closely but never actually reached in any finite number of physical processes — scientists have gotten extraordinarily close in laboratories, but never all the way there.

Why absolute zero matters

Using an absolute temperature scale (kelvin, rather than Celsius or Fahrenheit) is essential for many physics equations, including the ideal gas law, since those relationships only work correctly when temperature is measured from true zero motion.

Pick a fact about absolute zero to explore

According to the third law of thermodynamics, can absolute zero actually be reached?

No finite physical process can bring a system exactly to absolute zero, only ever closer and closer to it.

Refrigerators & heat pumps

Moving heat 'uphill' from cold to hot.

Moving heat against its natural direction

Heat naturally flows from hot to cold on its own — a refrigerator or heat pump does the opposite, moving heat from a cooler space to a warmer one, which requires work input rather than happening spontaneously.

How a refrigerator works

A refrigerator uses a refrigerant fluid that absorbs heat from inside the fridge as it evaporates, then releases that heat outside the fridge as it's compressed back into a liquid — completing a repeating cycle.

Heat pumps for heating buildings

A heat pump uses the same basic cycle to move heat from outside air (even cold outside air) into a building, which can be a far more energy-efficient way to heat a space than generating heat directly through resistive heating.

Pick a fact about refrigeration to explore

Why does running a refrigerator require energy input?

Moving heat against its natural direction — from cold to hot — always requires outside work, as the second law of thermodynamics demands.

Blackbody radiation

Why hot objects glow, and what color they glow.

What a blackbody is

A blackbody is an idealized object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and re-emits energy based purely on its temperature, in a well-defined spectrum — a useful model for real glowing objects like stars and heated metal.

Wien's displacement law

Wien's law states that hotter objects emit their peak radiation at shorter wavelengths — this is why a metal bar glows dull red when moderately hot, but shifts toward white-hot as it gets even hotter, its peak emission shifting to shorter wavelengths.

Blackbody radiation and star color

A star's color reveals its surface temperature through this same principle — cooler red stars, medium-temperature yellow stars like our sun, and hot blue stars all follow the same blackbody radiation curve, just at different peak temperatures.

Pick a temperature and see the resulting glow color

According to Wien's law, what happens to an object's peak emitted wavelength as it gets hotter?

Hotter objects concentrate their emitted radiation at shorter, higher-energy wavelengths, shifting the glow color from red toward blue.

The Stefan-Boltzmann law

How much energy a hot object radiates, and how fast that grows.

The law itself

The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total energy radiated by an object per unit area is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: P/A = σT⁴, where σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

Why the fourth power matters so much

Because temperature is raised to the fourth power, even a modest increase in temperature causes a huge increase in radiated energy — doubling an object's absolute temperature increases its radiated power by a factor of 16.

Why this matters for stars and planets

This steep relationship is central to understanding how much energy stars radiate, and helps explain how a planet's temperature settles into balance between the energy it absorbs from its star and the energy it radiates back into space.

Stefan-Boltzmann calculator (P/A = σT⁴, σ=5.67×10⁻⁸)

Temperature (K)

If an object's absolute temperature doubles, what happens to the energy it radiates per unit area?

Since radiated power depends on temperature to the fourth power, doubling temperature means 2⁴ = 16 times more radiated energy.

Photon energy & Planck's constant

Why light comes in indivisible packets of energy.

Light as photons

Light doesn't deliver energy continuously — it comes in discrete packets called photons, each carrying a specific amount of energy depending on the light's frequency.

The photon energy equation

A photon's energy is given by E = hf, where h is Planck's constant (an extremely small fixed number) and f is the light's frequency — higher frequency light means higher energy photons.

Why this matters

This quantized nature of light explains phenomena classical wave theory couldn't, like the photoelectric effect, and is foundational to essentially all of quantum mechanics.

Photon energy calculator (E = hf, h=6.63×10⁻³⁴)

Frequency (Hz)

What determines the energy of a single photon?

Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency, following E = hf — higher frequency means higher energy per photon.

The Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

An early, simple picture that got quantum jumps right.

Electrons in fixed orbits

Niels Bohr proposed that a hydrogen atom's electron can only occupy specific, fixed circular orbits at set distances from the nucleus, each corresponding to a specific, quantized energy level.

Quantum jumps

An electron can jump between these fixed energy levels by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy exactly equal to the difference between the two levels — it can't exist in between them at all.

Why the model mattered (and where it fell short)

The Bohr model successfully explained hydrogen's observed spectral lines for the first time, a major breakthrough — but it fails to accurately describe atoms with more than one electron, and was later superseded by the full quantum mechanical model.

Pick a Bohr model concept to explore

What happens when an electron in the Bohr model absorbs a photon with the right amount of energy?

The photon's energy must precisely match the gap between two allowed energy levels for the jump to occur.

Atomic spectra & spectral lines

How every element leaves its own fingerprint in light.

Emission spectra

When atoms of a specific element are excited (heated or electrically charged), they emit light only at specific wavelengths, producing a pattern of bright lines called an emission spectrum — unique to each element.

Absorption spectra

When white light passes through a cooler gas, the gas absorbs light at those same specific wavelengths, producing dark lines in an otherwise continuous spectrum — the reverse pattern of emission.

Reading the fingerprint

Since each element's spectral lines are unique, spectroscopy lets scientists identify which elements are present in something as distant as a star, just by analyzing the specific wavelengths of light it emits or absorbs.

Pick a spectrum type and see how it forms

How can scientists determine which elements are present in a distant star?

Each element leaves a unique fingerprint of spectral lines, which spectroscopy can identify from light alone.

X-rays: production & diffraction

Generating and using one of the highest-energy forms of light.

Producing X-rays

X-rays are commonly produced by firing high-speed electrons at a metal target — the sudden deceleration of the electrons as they strike the metal releases their energy as high-frequency X-ray photons.

X-ray diffraction

Since X-rays have wavelengths comparable to the spacing between atoms in a crystal, they diffract distinctly off a crystal's regular atomic structure, producing a pattern that reveals the crystal's atomic arrangement.

Applications

Medical X-ray imaging exploits how different tissues absorb X-rays differently (bone absorbs much more than soft tissue), while X-ray diffraction in research famously helped reveal the structure of DNA.

Pick an X-ray fact to explore

Why are X-rays useful for studying the atomic structure of crystals?

That close match in scale lets X-rays diffract in a pattern that reveals the crystal's atomic arrangement.

Radioactive decay law & half-life math

The exponential math behind a decaying sample.

The decay law

Radioactive decay follows an exponential law: N = N₀e^(-λt), where N₀ is the initial amount, λ is the decay constant (unique to each isotope), and t is time — describing how the remaining amount shrinks continuously rather than in sudden steps.

Half-life and the decay constant

Half-life and the decay constant are directly related: t½ = ln(2)/λ — a larger decay constant means faster decay and a shorter half-life.

Why decay is random but predictable

Any single radioactive atom decays at a completely random, unpredictable moment — but with enough atoms in a sample, the overall decay rate becomes remarkably predictable, following the same exponential curve every time.

Remaining amount calculator (N = N₀ × 0.5^(t/half-life))

Initial amount (g) · Time elapsed (years) · Half-life (years)

Why is radioactive decay of a large sample so predictable, even though each individual atom decays randomly?

Statistics smooths out the unpredictability of any one atom once you're dealing with the enormous number of atoms in a real sample.

Nuclear binding energy curve

Why some nuclei are more stable than others.

What the binding energy curve shows

Plotting binding energy per nucleon against atomic mass produces a curve that peaks around iron and nickel — nuclei near this peak are the most stable, tightly bound nuclei that exist.

Why fission releases energy

Very heavy nuclei, like uranium, sit below the peak of the curve — splitting them into medium-sized nuclei closer to the peak releases energy, since the resulting nuclei are more tightly bound overall.

Why fusion releases energy

Very light nuclei, like hydrogen, also sit below the peak — combining them into heavier nuclei closer to the peak (like helium) also releases energy, for the same underlying reason: moving toward the most stable, tightly bound configuration.

Pick a nucleus type and see why nuclear reactions release energy

Why do both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy?

Whether splitting heavy nuclei or combining light ones, both shift toward nuclei with a higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing the difference as energy.

Cosmic rays

High-energy particles raining down from space.

What cosmic rays are

Cosmic rays are extremely high-energy particles — mostly protons — arriving from space, some originating from the sun and others from far more distant and energetic sources like supernova explosions.

What happens when they hit the atmosphere

When a cosmic ray strikes Earth's upper atmosphere, it collides with air molecules and triggers a cascading shower of secondary particles, most of which never reach the ground directly.

Why cosmic rays matter

Cosmic rays contribute a small but real background dose of radiation, are a hazard that must be shielded against for astronauts on long space missions, and even occasionally cause tiny errors in sensitive electronics.

Pick a fact about cosmic rays to explore

What happens when a cosmic ray strikes Earth's upper atmosphere?

That collision cascade spreads the original particle's energy among many secondary particles, most of which don't reach the surface.

The physics of flight

The four forces that keep an airplane in the air.

The four forces of flight

Flight balances four forces: lift (upward, from the wings), weight (downward, from gravity), thrust (forward, from engines), and drag (backward, from air resistance) — steady, level flight requires lift to balance weight and thrust to balance drag.

How wings generate lift

A wing's shape and angle push air downward as it passes, and by Newton's third law, the air pushes back up on the wing — this reaction force, combined with pressure differences from the wing's curved shape, together generate lift.

Why angle of attack matters

Tilting a wing to increase its angle relative to the airflow (angle of attack) increases lift, up to a point — push the angle too far, and airflow separates from the wing's surface, causing a sudden, dangerous loss of lift called a stall.

Pick a force of flight and see its role

What happens if a wing's angle of attack becomes too steep?

Beyond a critical angle, smooth airflow over the wing breaks down, causing lift to collapse suddenly — a stall.

The physics of sports: the Magnus effect

Why a spinning ball curves through the air.

What the Magnus effect is

The Magnus effect is the curved path a spinning object takes as it moves through a fluid (like air), caused by the interaction between the object's spin and the surrounding airflow.

Why spin causes curving

A spinning ball drags air around with it slightly, creating faster airflow (and lower pressure) on one side and slower airflow (and higher pressure) on the other — this pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, curving its path.

Where you see it in sports

A soccer player's curling free kick, a baseball pitcher's curveball, and a golf ball's backspin-driven lift all rely on the Magnus effect, deliberately using spin to bend a ball's trajectory in ways that are hard for opponents to predict.

Pick a sports example and see the Magnus effect in action

What causes the Magnus effect on a spinning ball?

The spin drags air around the ball unevenly, creating a pressure imbalance that pushes the ball sideways.

Biomechanics: levers in the body

How your bones and muscles work as simple machines.

The body as a system of levers

Many parts of the human body function as levers, with bones acting as rigid arms, joints acting as pivots, and muscles providing the force — understanding this helps explain both human movement and common injuries.

Classes of levers in the body

A first-class lever, like the head balancing on the neck, has the pivot between the force and the load. A second-class lever, like standing on tiptoes, has the load between the pivot and the force. A third-class lever, like the forearm lifting a weight, has the force applied between the pivot and the load — the most common type in the human body.

Why muscles need so much force

Because most body levers are third-class, with the muscle's force applied closer to the joint than the load, muscles must generate far more force than the weight being lifted — a biomechanical trade-off for greater range of motion and speed.

Pick a body lever example and see its class

Why do muscles often need to generate much more force than the weight they're lifting?

That lever arrangement trades extra muscular force for a greater range of motion and speed at the end of the limb.

Physics of the ear & hearing

How sound waves become the sensation of hearing.

From sound wave to eardrum

Sound waves traveling through air cause the eardrum to vibrate — the eardrum's vibration pattern precisely matches the pressure variations of the incoming sound wave.

Amplification in the middle ear

Three tiny bones in the middle ear (the ossicles) mechanically amplify the eardrum's vibrations before passing them to the fluid-filled inner ear, since sound energy would otherwise be mostly reflected at the boundary between air and the denser inner ear fluid.

The cochlea and frequency detection

The spiral-shaped cochlea in the inner ear is lined with tiny hair cells that respond to different frequencies at different points along its length, converting specific frequencies of vibration into distinct nerve signals your brain interprets as pitch.

Pick a part of the ear and see its role

Why does the middle ear need to mechanically amplify sound before it reaches the inner ear?

Without that boost, most sound energy would simply bounce off the boundary between air and the inner ear's fluid instead of passing through.

Seismology: earthquake waves

How P-waves and S-waves reveal Earth's hidden structure.

P-waves and S-waves

Earthquakes generate two main types of body waves: P-waves (primary waves), which compress and stretch material as they travel and can pass through solids, liquids, and gases; and S-waves (secondary waves), which move material side to side and can only travel through solids.

Why P-waves arrive first

P-waves travel significantly faster than S-waves through the same material, which is why seismographs always detect the P-wave arriving before the S-wave from the same earthquake — the time gap between them helps calculate distance to the earthquake's source.

Mapping Earth's interior

Since S-waves can't travel through liquid, the discovery that they don't pass through Earth's outer core was key evidence that this layer is liquid — seismic waves have been one of the primary tools for mapping Earth's internal structure without ever drilling that deep.

Pick a seismic wave type and see its properties

How did scientists determine that Earth's outer core is liquid?

The absence of S-waves passing through that layer was strong indirect evidence that it must be liquid.

Why the sky is blue

Rayleigh scattering and the color of daylight.

Rayleigh scattering

Sunlight entering the atmosphere collides with tiny gas molecules, which scatter shorter wavelengths of light (blue and violet) much more strongly than longer wavelengths (red and orange) — a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering.

Why the sky looks blue, not violet

Although violet light scatters even more than blue, sunlight contains less violet to begin with, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue — together, this is why we perceive the sky as blue rather than violet.

Why sunsets are red and orange

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere to reach your eyes, scattering away almost all the blue light along the way and leaving mostly the longer, redder wavelengths to reach you directly.

Pick a sky-color scenario to explore

Why does the sky appear blue rather than violet, even though violet scatters even more strongly?

A combination of sunlight's spectrum and human eye sensitivity is what tips the color we perceive toward blue rather than violet.

Superfluidity

A liquid with zero viscosity — no resistance to flow at all.

What superfluidity is

Below an extremely low critical temperature, certain liquids (most famously helium-4) become superfluids — flowing with absolutely zero viscosity, meaning no internal resistance to flow whatsoever.

Strange behaviors

A superfluid can flow up and over the walls of its container in a thin film, seemingly defying gravity, and once set circulating in a loop, it can keep flowing indefinitely without ever slowing down.

Why it happens

Superfluidity is a macroscopic quantum phenomenon — at low enough temperatures, a huge number of helium atoms settle into the exact same lowest-energy quantum state, behaving collectively as a single coordinated entity rather than as ordinary, independent particles.

Pick a superfluid behavior to explore

What makes a superfluid different from an ordinary liquid?

That complete absence of internal friction is exactly what allows a superfluid's strange, seemingly gravity-defying behaviors.

Time dilation & the twin paradox

Why a traveling twin ages more slowly than one who stays home.

Time dilation

Special relativity shows that time passes more slowly for an object moving at high speed relative to an observer — the faster the relative speed, the more pronounced this time dilation becomes, though it's only noticeable at speeds approaching the speed of light.

The twin paradox

In the famous thought experiment, one twin stays on Earth while the other travels on a high-speed round trip through space — when the traveling twin returns, they've aged less than the twin who stayed behind, since they spent their journey moving at relativistic speed.

Why it's not really a paradox

It seems paradoxical because each twin could argue the other one was 'moving.' But the traveling twin must accelerate to turn around and come back, breaking the symmetry between the two perspectives — this is what resolves the apparent contradiction and confirms which twin actually ages less.

Pick a fact about the twin paradox to explore

In the twin paradox, why is the situation not actually symmetric between the two twins?

That acceleration during the turnaround breaks the symmetry, which is exactly why one twin genuinely ages less than the other.

Algebra basics

Solving for the unknown.

What algebra does

Algebra uses letters (variables) to stand in for unknown numbers, letting you write general rules and solve for a specific value that makes an equation true.

Balancing an equation

Solving an equation means doing the same operation to both sides until the variable is isolated — whatever you add, subtract, multiply, or divide on one side, you must do to the other to keep the equation balanced.

Linear equations

A linear equation, like ax + b = c, has a variable raised only to the first power, and always has a single straight-line solution when graphed — solving it just takes a couple of balancing steps.

Linear equation solver (ax + b = c, solve for x)

a · b · c

What does 'solving an equation' mean?

A solution is the specific value that, substituted back in, makes both sides of the equation equal.

Quadratic equations

Equations with a squared variable, and how to crack them.

What makes an equation quadratic

A quadratic equation has its variable raised to the second power, in the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 — its graph is always a curved parabola, not a straight line.

The quadratic formula

Any quadratic equation can be solved with the quadratic formula: x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac)) / 2a — this works even when factoring the equation isn't straightforward.

The discriminant

The part under the square root, b²-4ac, is called the discriminant. If it's positive, there are two real solutions; if zero, exactly one; if negative, no real solutions at all (only complex ones).

Quadratic formula calculator (finds the positive root)

a · b · c

What does a negative discriminant tell you about a quadratic equation?

A negative number under the square root means there's no real number solution — only complex ones.

Functions & graphs

Mapping inputs to outputs, and what their shapes reveal.

What a function is

A function takes an input and produces exactly one output for it — written as f(x), where x is the input and f(x) is the resulting output.

Reading a graph

A function's graph plots every input-output pair as a point, letting you see at a glance how the output changes as the input changes — rising, falling, curving, or repeating.

Common function shapes

A linear function graphs as a straight line, a quadratic function graphs as a parabola, and an exponential function graphs as a curve that grows (or shrinks) increasingly quickly rather than at a constant rate.

Pick a function type and see its graph shape

What defines a function?

That one-output-per-input rule is exactly what separates a function from any other kind of relationship.

Trigonometry basics

Relating a right triangle's angles to its side lengths.

The three main ratios

In a right triangle, sine, cosine, and tangent each relate an angle to a ratio of two sides: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent — often remembered with SOH-CAH-TOA.

Using trig to find missing sides or angles

Knowing one angle (other than the right angle) and one side length lets you calculate every other side and angle in the triangle using these ratios.

Beyond triangles

Sine and cosine also describe smooth, repeating wave patterns, which is why trigonometry shows up constantly in physics — describing sound waves, alternating current, and oscillating motion.

Right triangle solver: find the opposite side (opposite = hypotenuse × sin(angle))

Hypotenuse · Angle (degrees)

In SOH-CAH-TOA, what does the 'CAH' part remind you of?

CAH stands for Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse, one of the three core trig ratios.

Geometry: angles & shapes

The rules that govern angles inside polygons.

Angles in a triangle

The three interior angles of any triangle always add up to exactly 180 degrees, no matter the triangle's shape or size.

Angles in a polygon

The sum of interior angles in any polygon with n sides is (n-2) × 180° — a triangle (3 sides) gives 180°, a quadrilateral (4 sides) gives 360°, and so on.

Types of angles

An acute angle is less than 90°, a right angle is exactly 90°, an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°, and a reflex angle is greater than 180°.

Polygon interior angle sum calculator ((n-2)×180°)

Number of sides

What is the sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral (4-sided shape)?

Using (n-2)×180° with n=4 gives 2×180° = 360°, true for any four-sided polygon.

Circles

Area, circumference, and the constant that ties them together.

Circumference

A circle's circumference (the distance around it) is found with C = 2πr, where r is the radius and π (pi) is approximately 3.14159 — the same ratio for every circle, regardless of size.

Area

A circle's area is found with A = πr² — since radius is squared, doubling a circle's radius actually quadruples its area, not just doubles it.

What makes π special

Pi is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, and it's the same fixed, irrational number for every circle that has ever existed or ever will — one of mathematics' most famous constants.

Circle calculator (Area = πr², Circumference = 2πr)

Radius

If you double a circle's radius, what happens to its area?

Since area depends on radius squared, doubling the radius multiplies the area by 2² = 4.

Statistics: mean, median & mode

Three different ways to describe a 'typical' value.

Mean

The mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by how many values there are — it's sensitive to extreme outliers, which can pull it away from where most of the data actually sits.

Median

The median is the middle value when data is sorted from smallest to largest — for an even number of values, it's the average of the two middle ones. It resists the influence of outliers much better than the mean.

Mode

The mode is the value that appears most often in a data set — useful for categorical data where mean and median don't even make sense, like the most common shoe size sold.

Enter a comma-separated list of numbers

Why is the median often more useful than the mean for data with extreme outliers?

Since the median only depends on the middle position of sorted data, one extreme value barely affects it — unlike the mean.

Probability

Measuring how likely an event is to happen.

What probability measures

Probability measures how likely an event is, as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain) — often written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage.

Calculating simple probability

For equally likely outcomes, probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes — like a 1-in-6 chance of rolling a specific number on a fair die.

Independent events

Two events are independent if one doesn't affect the other's probability — the probability of both independent events happening is found by multiplying their individual probabilities together.

Pick an event and see its probability

How do you find the combined probability of two independent events both happening?

For independent events, multiplying their individual probabilities gives the probability of both occurring together.

Calculus: derivatives

Measuring how fast something is changing, instantaneously.

What a derivative measures

A derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function at a specific point — for a position function, its derivative is velocity; for a velocity function, its derivative is acceleration.

The power rule

One of the simplest and most useful differentiation shortcuts, the power rule, says the derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹ — bring the exponent down as a multiplier, then reduce the exponent by one.

Derivatives as slopes

Geometrically, a function's derivative at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at exactly that point — a straight line just briefly touching the curve there.

Power rule calculator: derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹

Exponent n

What does a function's derivative represent geometrically?

The derivative captures exactly how steeply the function is rising or falling at that specific point.

Calculus: integrals

Adding up infinitely many infinitesimal pieces.

What integration does

Integration is, in a sense, the reverse of differentiation — it finds a function whose derivative matches the one you started with, often used to calculate the area under a curve.

The power rule for integration

The integral of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C — raise the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent, always adding a constant C, since any constant's derivative is zero.

Definite vs indefinite integrals

An indefinite integral gives a general antiderivative function (plus an unknown constant C); a definite integral, evaluated between two specific limits, gives an exact numerical value — typically the area under the curve between those two points.

Power rule calculator: integral of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)

Exponent n

Why does an indefinite integral always include a '+ C'?

Since a constant term vanishes when you differentiate, integration can't tell you what that original constant was — so +C accounts for every possibility.

Number systems

Natural numbers, integers, rationals, and beyond.

The building blocks

Natural numbers (1,2,3...) are the counting numbers. Adding zero and negatives gives integers. Adding fractions gives rational numbers — any number expressible as one integer divided by another.

Irrational numbers

Irrational numbers, like π and √2, can't be written as a simple fraction — their decimal expansions go on forever without repeating.

Real numbers

Together, rational and irrational numbers make up the real numbers — every point on the number line corresponds to exactly one real number.

Pick a number and see its classification

What makes a number irrational?

Irrational numbers have non-terminating, non-repeating decimal expansions, unlike rational numbers.

Fractions, decimals & percentages

Three ways of writing the same value.

Converting between forms

Any fraction can be converted to a decimal by dividing, and any decimal can be written as a percentage by multiplying by 100 — all three describe the exact same underlying quantity.

Why percentages are useful

Percentages express a quantity as a portion out of 100, making it easy to compare proportions across very different totals — 50 out of 200 and 25 out of 100 are both just 25%.

Common conversions

Recognizing that 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, and 1/3 ≈ 0.333 = 33.3% by heart makes quick mental estimates much easier.

Fraction to percentage converter

Numerator · Denominator

What does 3/4 equal as a percentage?

Dividing 3 by 4 gives 0.75, which is 75% when multiplied by 100.

Ratio & proportion

Comparing quantities and scaling them together.

What a ratio is

A ratio compares two quantities by division, written as a:b — a recipe calling for flour and sugar in a 3:1 ratio means three parts flour for every one part sugar.

Simplifying ratios

Like fractions, ratios can be simplified by dividing both sides by their greatest common factor — 8:12 simplifies to 2:3.

Proportion

A proportion states that two ratios are equal, like a/b = c/d — solving a proportion for an unknown value is a common way to scale a recipe, map, or blueprint up or down.

Proportion solver (a/b = c/x, solve for x)

a · b · c

If a map has a scale of 1:50000, what does 1 unit on the map represent in reality?

A 1:50000 ratio means every 1 unit of distance on the map corresponds to 50,000 of that same unit in real life.

Exponents & powers

Repeated multiplication, and the rules that simplify it.

What an exponent means

An exponent tells you how many times to multiply a base number by itself — 2⁴ means 2×2×2×2 = 16.

The exponent rules

Multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents (xᵃ·xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ); dividing subtracts them (xᵃ/xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ); raising a power to a power multiplies them ((xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ).

Zero and negative exponents

Any nonzero number raised to the power of zero equals 1. A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ.

Power calculator (xⁿ)

Base · Exponent

What does any nonzero number raised to the power of 0 equal?

By definition and by the pattern of the exponent rules, x⁰ = 1 for any nonzero x.

Roots & radicals

Undoing exponents to find the original base.

Square roots

The square root of a number is the value that, multiplied by itself, gives that number — √16 = 4, since 4×4 = 16.

Higher-order roots

A cube root asks what number, cubed, gives the target value — the cube root of 27 is 3, since 3³ = 27. Any root can be written as a fractional exponent: the nth root of x is x^(1/n).

Simplifying radicals

A radical is simplified by pulling out any perfect square (or cube, etc.) factors — √50 simplifies to 5√2, since 50 = 25×2 and √25 = 5.

Root calculator (nth root of x)

Number · Root (e.g. 2 for square root)

How can the nth root of a number be written using exponents?

A fractional exponent of 1/n is mathematically identical to taking the nth root.

Scientific notation

Writing very large or very small numbers compactly.

The format

Scientific notation writes a number as a value between 1 and 10, multiplied by a power of 10 — 6,500,000 becomes 6.5 × 10⁶.

Why it's useful

It makes extremely large numbers (like distances between stars) or extremely small numbers (like the size of an atom) far easier to read, write, and compare at a glance.

Multiplying and dividing in scientific notation

Multiply the decimal parts together and add the exponents when multiplying two numbers in scientific notation; divide the decimal parts and subtract the exponents when dividing.

Scientific notation exponent finder (number = m × 10^exponent)

Number

How is 0.00042 written in scientific notation?

Moving the decimal point four places to the right gives 4.2, matched by a 10⁻⁴ exponent.

Prime numbers & factors

The indivisible building blocks of every whole number.

What a prime number is

A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Numbers with more than two factors are called composite — 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 are the first few primes.

Prime factorization

Every whole number greater than 1 can be broken down into a unique product of prime numbers — 60 = 2×2×3×5, and no other combination of primes multiplies to 60.

Why primes matter

Prime numbers are foundational throughout mathematics, and their unpredictable distribution among larger numbers is exactly what modern cryptography relies on to keep encrypted data secure.

Pick a number and see its prime factorization

What defines a prime number?

That exact count of two factors is the defining property — 2 is prime and even, showing primes aren't always odd.

GCD & LCM

The biggest shared factor, and the smallest shared multiple.

Greatest common divisor

The greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers is the largest number that divides evenly into both — useful for simplifying fractions to their lowest terms.

Least common multiple

The least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers is the smallest number that both divide evenly into — essential for adding fractions with different denominators.

How GCD and LCM relate

For any two numbers, their GCD times their LCM equals the product of the two numbers themselves — a handy shortcut once you've found one of the two.

GCD calculator (Euclidean algorithm)

First number · Second number

Why is the least common multiple useful when adding fractions?

Converting both fractions to have the LCM as their denominator is exactly what lets you add them directly.

Arithmetic sequences & series

Numbers that change by the same amount each step.

What makes a sequence arithmetic

An arithmetic sequence adds (or subtracts) the same fixed amount, called the common difference, to get from one term to the next — like 3, 7, 11, 15, each step adding 4.

The nth term formula

Any term in an arithmetic sequence can be found directly with aₙ = a₁ + (n-1)d, where a₁ is the first term and d is the common difference — no need to list out every term before it.

Summing an arithmetic series

The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence is Sₙ = n/2 × (a₁ + aₙ) — pairing the first and last terms (and all the pairs in between) always gives the same sum.

Arithmetic sequence calculator (nth term)

First term · Common difference · Term number

What defines an arithmetic sequence?

That constant common difference between consecutive terms is exactly what makes a sequence arithmetic.

Geometric sequences & series

Numbers that change by the same multiple each step.

What makes a sequence geometric

A geometric sequence multiplies by the same fixed ratio, called the common ratio, to get from one term to the next — like 2, 6, 18, 54, each step multiplying by 3.

The nth term formula

Any term in a geometric sequence can be found with aₙ = a₁ × r^(n-1), where a₁ is the first term and r is the common ratio.

Summing a geometric series

The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = a₁(1-rⁿ)/(1-r) for r ≠ 1 — and if |r| < 1, an infinite geometric series actually converges to a finite total sum as n grows forever.

Geometric sequence calculator (nth term)

First term · Common ratio · Term number

What happens to an infinite geometric series if the common ratio's absolute value is less than 1?

With each term shrinking, the running total settles toward a fixed finite value rather than growing forever.

Polynomials

Expressions built from added terms of whole-number powers.

What a polynomial is

A polynomial is an expression made of terms added together, each a coefficient times a variable raised to a whole-number power — like 3x² + 5x - 2. The highest power present is called the degree.

Adding and subtracting polynomials

Combine polynomials by adding or subtracting matching terms — terms with the exact same variable and exponent, called like terms.

Multiplying polynomials

Multiplying polynomials means distributing every term in the first over every term in the second, then combining any resulting like terms — this is exactly what the FOIL method does for two two-term expressions.

Evaluate a quadratic polynomial (ax² + bx + c) at a value of x

a · b · c · x value

What determines a polynomial's degree?

Degree is defined purely by the largest exponent appearing on the variable, regardless of how many terms there are.

Factoring polynomials

Breaking an expression back down into multiplied pieces.

Why factor

Factoring rewrites a polynomial as a product of simpler expressions — the reverse of multiplying them out — which is essential for solving equations and simplifying expressions.

Factoring out a common term

The simplest factoring step pulls out the greatest common factor shared by every term — 6x² + 9x factors to 3x(2x + 3).

Factoring quadratics

A quadratic like x² + 5x + 6 factors into two binomials, (x+2)(x+3), by finding two numbers that multiply to the constant term and add to the middle coefficient.

Pick a quadratic and see its factored form

When factoring x² + bx + c into two binomials, what must the two numbers you find do?

Finding a pair that multiplies to the constant term and adds to the middle coefficient is the core trick of factoring a simple quadratic.

Rational expressions

Fractions with polynomials in the numerator and denominator.

What a rational expression is

A rational expression is a fraction where the numerator, denominator, or both, are polynomials — like (x+2)/(x-3).

Simplifying

Just like a numeric fraction, a rational expression can be simplified by factoring both the top and bottom and canceling any common factors.

Restrictions on the variable

Since division by zero is undefined, any value of the variable that would make the denominator zero must be excluded from the expression's domain.

Pick a rational expression fact to explore

Why must certain values be excluded from a rational expression's domain?

Division by zero has no defined value, so any value causing that must be excluded from where the expression is valid.

Systems of linear equations

Solving for two unknowns using two equations at once.

What a system of equations is

A system of linear equations is a set of two or more equations sharing the same variables — a solution is a set of values that satisfies every equation in the system simultaneously.

Solving by substitution

Substitution solves one equation for one variable, then plugs that expression into the other equation, reducing the system to a single equation in one unknown.

Solving by elimination

Elimination adds or subtracts the equations (after scaling if needed) to cancel out one variable entirely, again leaving a single equation in one unknown to solve directly.

2×2 system solver (ax+by=e, cx+dy=f)

a · b · e · c · d · f

What does a 'solution' to a system of two equations represent?

A true solution must work in every equation of the system simultaneously, not just one of them.

Inequalities

Comparing expressions that aren't necessarily equal.

What an inequality shows

An inequality compares two expressions using <, >, ≤, or ≥ instead of an equals sign, describing a range of possible values rather than one exact answer.

Solving inequalities

Inequalities are solved much like equations — the same operations apply to both sides — with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the direction of the inequality sign.

Graphing on a number line

A solution to an inequality is often shown as a shaded region on a number line, with an open circle for < or > (excluding the endpoint) and a closed circle for ≤ or ≥ (including it).

Pick an inequality operation and see its effect

What happens to an inequality's direction when you multiply both sides by a negative number?

Multiplying by a negative number reverses the relative order of the two sides, so the inequality sign must flip to stay true.

Absolute value equations

Solving for a distance from zero, in either direction.

What absolute value means

Absolute value measures a number's distance from zero on the number line, always giving a non-negative result — |5| = 5 and |-5| = 5 as well.

Solving absolute value equations

Since a quantity inside absolute value bars could have been positive or negative before, an equation like |x| = 5 has two solutions: x = 5 and x = -5.

Absolute value inequalities

An inequality like |x| < 5 describes every value within 5 units of zero (between -5 and 5), while |x| > 5 describes values farther than 5 units away in either direction.

Pick an absolute value equation and see its solutions

Why does |x| = 5 have two solutions instead of one?

Since absolute value discards sign information, both the positive and negative version of the same distance satisfy the equation.

Exponential equations & logarithms

Solving for an unknown exponent.

What a logarithm is

A logarithm answers the question 'to what power must this base be raised to get this number?' — log₂(8) = 3, since 2³ = 8. Logarithms are the inverse operation of exponentiation.

Solving exponential equations

When a variable appears in an exponent, like 2ˣ = 16, taking the logarithm of both sides (or recognizing 16 as 2⁴) lets you solve directly for that exponent.

Common and natural logarithms

Log base 10 is called the common logarithm (written log); log base e (approximately 2.718) is called the natural logarithm (written ln) — both show up constantly throughout science and engineering.

Logarithm calculator (log base b of x)

x · base

What question does a logarithm answer?

A logarithm is defined precisely as the inverse of exponentiation — finding the exponent that produces a given result.

Logarithm rules

The shortcuts that make working with logs manageable.

The product rule

The logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms: log(ab) = log(a) + log(b) — turning multiplication inside a log into addition outside it.

The quotient rule

The logarithm of a quotient equals the difference of the logarithms: log(a/b) = log(a) - log(b).

The power rule

The logarithm of a power pulls the exponent out front as a multiplier: log(aⁿ) = n·log(a) — extremely useful for solving equations where the variable sits in an exponent.

Pick a logarithm rule and see what it says

According to the power rule, how does log(x⁵) simplify?

The power rule pulls the exponent 5 out front as a multiplying coefficient.

Complex numbers

Numbers that let you take the square root of a negative.

The imaginary unit

Since no real number squared gives a negative result, mathematicians defined i as the square root of -1 — this 'imaginary unit' lets equations that have no real solution get a meaningful answer.

What a complex number is

A complex number combines a real part and an imaginary part, written as a + bi — real numbers are simply complex numbers where b = 0.

Where complex numbers are used

Far from being purely abstract, complex numbers are essential tools in electrical engineering (describing AC circuits), quantum mechanics, and signal processing.

Pick a complex number fact to explore

What is the defining property of the imaginary unit i?

i is defined precisely so that squaring it gives -1, something no real number can do.

Matrices basics

Organizing numbers into a rectangular grid you can compute with.

What a matrix is

A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers, organized into rows and columns — described by its dimensions, like a 2×3 matrix having 2 rows and 3 columns.

Adding and subtracting matrices

Two matrices of the same dimensions can be added or subtracted by combining their corresponding entries, position by position.

Why matrices matter

Matrices compactly represent systems of equations, transformations in geometry (like rotations and scaling), and are foundational to computer graphics, machine learning, and much of modern applied mathematics.

Pick a matrix fact to explore

What's required for two matrices to be added together?

Addition combines corresponding entries, which only makes sense if both matrices have exactly matching rows and columns.

Triangles: types & properties

Classifying the simplest possible polygon.

Classifying by sides

An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal; an isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides; a scalene triangle has all three sides different lengths.

Classifying by angles

An acute triangle has all angles less than 90°; a right triangle has exactly one 90° angle; an obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90°.

The triangle inequality

The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle must always be greater than the length of the third side — otherwise, the three sides simply can't form a closed triangle at all.

Pick a triangle description and see its classification

What does the triangle inequality say about a triangle's three side lengths?

If two sides summed together were too short, they couldn't reach around to close the triangle at all.

Congruence & similarity

When shapes are identical, and when they're just scaled versions.

Congruent shapes

Two shapes are congruent if they're exactly the same size and shape — one could be placed perfectly on top of the other after some combination of moving, rotating, or flipping.

Similar shapes

Two shapes are similar if they have the same shape but possibly different sizes — all corresponding angles are equal, and all corresponding sides are in the same fixed ratio.

Proving triangles congruent or similar

Triangles can be proven congruent using rules like SSS (all three sides match) or SAS (two sides and the included angle match), and proven similar using AA (two matching angles guarantee the third matches too).

Pick a scenario and see if it's congruence or similarity

What's the key difference between congruent and similar shapes?

Congruence requires an exact size match; similarity only requires proportional scaling with matching angles.

The Pythagorean theorem

The famous relationship between a right triangle's three sides.

The theorem itself

In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c².

Using it to find a missing side

Knowing any two sides of a right triangle lets you solve for the third directly using the theorem — a cornerstone calculation across geometry, construction, and navigation.

The converse is also true

If a triangle's three sides satisfy a² + b² = c², the triangle must be a right triangle — this converse is a quick, reliable way to test whether a given triangle has a right angle.

Pythagorean theorem calculator (find the hypotenuse)

Side a · Side b

In a right triangle with legs of 3 and 4, what is the length of the hypotenuse?

Since 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5, the hypotenuse measures 5.

Polygons: perimeter & area

Measuring the boundary and the space inside a shape.

Perimeter

Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape — found by simply adding up the lengths of all its sides.

Area of common shapes

A rectangle's area is length times width; a triangle's area is half its base times its height; a trapezoid's area is the average of its two parallel sides times its height.

Regular vs irregular polygons

A regular polygon has all sides and angles equal, making its area easy to calculate with a single formula; an irregular polygon usually needs to be broken into simpler shapes (like triangles) to find its total area.

Triangle area calculator (½ × base × height)

Base · Height

How is the area of a trapezoid calculated?

Averaging the two parallel sides accounts for the trapezoid's tapering shape before multiplying by its height.

3D shapes: volume & surface area

Measuring the space inside, and the skin around, a solid.

Volume

Volume measures how much three-dimensional space a solid occupies — a rectangular box's volume is simply length × width × height.

Surface area

Surface area measures the total area of every face covering a solid's outside — found by adding up the areas of each individual face (or using a direct formula for shapes like spheres and cylinders).

Common 3D formulas

A cylinder's volume is πr²h; a sphere's volume is (4/3)πr³; a cone's volume is exactly one-third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

Cylinder volume calculator (V = πr²h)

Radius · Height

How does a cone's volume compare to a cylinder with the same base and height?

A cone tapers to a point, and this geometric relationship works out to exactly one-third of the equivalent cylinder's volume.

Coordinate geometry: distance & midpoint

Measuring straight-line distance and finding the exact middle.

The distance formula

The distance between two points (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is found with d = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²) — essentially the Pythagorean theorem applied directly to coordinates.

The midpoint formula

The midpoint between two points is simply the average of their x-coordinates and the average of their y-coordinates: ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Why these formulas matter

Distance and midpoint calculations underlie everything from finding the length of a line segment on a graph to computing distances between real-world GPS coordinates.

Distance formula calculator

x1 · y1 · x2 · y2

What is the midpoint's y-coordinate calculated from?

Midpoint simply averages each coordinate separately — x with x, and y with y.

Coordinate geometry: equation of a line

Describing every point on a straight line with one equation.

Slope-intercept form

A line's equation is often written y = mx + b, where m is the slope (how steeply the line rises or falls) and b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).

Calculating slope

Slope is calculated as 'rise over run' between any two points on the line: m = (y₂-y₁)/(x₂-x₁) — the same value no matter which two points on the line you pick.

Parallel and perpendicular lines

Parallel lines always have the exact same slope. Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other — if one line has slope 2, a perpendicular line has slope -1/2.

Slope calculator (m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1))

x1 · y1 · x2 · y2

If one line has a slope of 3, what slope must a line perpendicular to it have?

Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, so 3 pairs with -1/3.

Transformations

Moving, turning, and flipping shapes without changing them.

Translation

A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction — the shape's size, orientation, and angles never change, only its position.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point by a certain angle — again preserving size and shape, just changing orientation.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape over a line (the line of reflection), producing a mirror image — every point ends up the same distance from the line, just on the opposite side.

Pick a transformation and see what it does

What stays the same in all three basic transformations — translation, rotation, and reflection?

These are all 'rigid' transformations — they preserve size and shape, changing only position or orientation.

Vectors in geometry

Quantities with both size and direction, used to describe movement.

What a vector represents

A vector represents a movement with both magnitude (length) and direction, often drawn as an arrow — unlike a point, which only marks a location.

Adding vectors

Vectors add head-to-tail: placing the tail of the second vector at the head of the first, the resultant vector runs from the very start to the very end.

Vectors in coordinates

A vector can be written as coordinate components, like (3,4), meaning 3 units across and 4 units up — its magnitude is then found with the Pythagorean theorem: √(3²+4²) = 5.

Vector magnitude calculator

x-component · y-component

What two properties does a vector have that a simple point doesn't?

A vector describes a movement — both how far and which way — unlike a point, which only marks a fixed location.

Circle theorems

Special angle relationships hidden inside every circle.

The angle at the center

The angle formed at a circle's center by two radii is always exactly twice the angle formed at the circle's edge by the same two endpoints — a foundational circle theorem.

Angles in a semicircle

Any angle inscribed in a semicircle (formed using the diameter as one side) is always exactly 90° — a direct and useful special case of the previous theorem.

Tangent lines

A tangent line touches a circle at exactly one point, and it's always perpendicular to the radius drawn to that exact point of contact.

Pick a circle theorem and see what it states

What is true about any angle inscribed in a semicircle?

This holds true for every semicircle regardless of size, a direct consequence of the center-angle circle theorem.

The unit circle

A circle of radius 1 that reveals every trig value at once.

What the unit circle is

The unit circle is a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin — for any angle measured from the positive x-axis, the coordinates of the point on the circle are exactly (cos θ, sin θ).

Why it's so useful

The unit circle extends sine and cosine beyond just right-triangle angles (0° to 90°) to any angle at all, including negative angles and angles beyond 360°.

Key angles to know

Certain angles — 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, and their multiples around the circle — have clean, memorable sine and cosine values that show up constantly throughout trigonometry.

Pick an angle and see its unit circle coordinates

On the unit circle, what do the coordinates of a point at angle θ represent?

This is exactly how sine and cosine are defined for any angle using the unit circle.

Trig identities

Equations that are always true, for any angle.

The Pythagorean identity

The most fundamental trig identity, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, holds true for every possible angle θ — it comes directly from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit circle.

Reciprocal identities

Three trig functions are simply reciprocals of the main ones: cosecant is 1/sine, secant is 1/cosine, and cotangent is 1/tangent.

Why identities matter

Trig identities let you rewrite complicated trigonometric expressions into simpler, equivalent forms — an essential skill for solving trig equations and simplifying calculus problems involving trig functions.

Pick a trig identity and see what it says

What does the Pythagorean identity state?

This identity holds for every angle and is one of the most frequently used relationships in trigonometry.

Graphs of sine, cosine & tangent

The repeating wave shapes behind the three main trig functions.

The sine and cosine waves

Both sine and cosine produce smooth, repeating wave patterns oscillating between -1 and 1, completing one full cycle every 360° — cosine is just sine shifted by 90°.

Amplitude and period

Amplitude is the wave's height from its center to its peak; period is the horizontal distance for one complete cycle — both can be stretched or compressed by adjusting the function's equation.

The tangent graph

Unlike sine and cosine, tangent's graph has vertical asymptotes (points it approaches but never reaches) wherever cosine equals zero, and it repeats every 180° instead of 360°.

Pick a trig function and see its graph behavior

Why does the tangent graph have vertical asymptotes?

Since tangent equals sine divided by cosine, it becomes undefined at every angle where cosine hits zero.

Inverse trig functions

Working backward from a ratio to find the angle.

What inverse trig functions do

While sine, cosine, and tangent take an angle and give a ratio, their inverses — arcsin, arccos, and arctan — take a ratio and give back the angle that produced it.

Restricted ranges

Since multiple angles can share the same sine (or cosine, or tangent) value, inverse trig functions are defined to return only one specific angle within a restricted range, avoiding ambiguity.

A practical use

If you know two sides of a right triangle, an inverse trig function lets you calculate the actual angle directly — essential for real-world problems in navigation, construction, and physics.

Inverse sine calculator (arcsin, in degrees)

Ratio (between -1 and 1)

What do inverse trig functions like arcsin calculate?

They reverse the usual direction — starting from a ratio and solving back for the angle that would produce it.

The law of sines

Solving triangles that aren't right triangles.

What the law of sines states

For any triangle, the ratio of a side's length to the sine of its opposite angle is the same for all three sides: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C).

When to use it

The law of sines is the go-to tool when you know two angles and one side, or two sides and a non-included angle — situations where basic right-triangle trig doesn't directly apply.

Beyond right triangles

Unlike SOH-CAH-TOA, the law of sines works on any triangle at all, not just right triangles, making it a far more general tool for solving unknown sides and angles.

Law of sines calculator (find side b, given a, angle A, angle B)

Side a · Angle A (degrees) · Angle B (degrees)

When is the law of sines especially useful?

It extends triangle-solving beyond right triangles, especially handy with two known angles and one known side.

The law of cosines

A Pythagorean theorem that works for any triangle.

What the law of cosines states

The law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to any triangle: c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C), where C is the angle opposite side c.

When to use it

This law is the right tool when you know all three sides (and want an angle) or two sides and the included angle (and want the third side) — situations the law of sines can't directly handle.

Connection to the Pythagorean theorem

When the angle C is exactly 90°, cos(90°) = 0, and the law of cosines collapses exactly into the familiar Pythagorean theorem, a² + b² = c².

Law of cosines calculator (find side c)

Side a · Side b · Angle C (degrees)

What does the law of cosines become when the included angle is exactly 90°?

Since cos(90°) = 0, the extra term vanishes, leaving exactly a² + b² = c².

Trigonometric equations

Solving for an angle that satisfies a trig equation.

What makes trig equations tricky

Because trig functions repeat periodically, a single trig equation like sin(x) = 0.5 usually has infinitely many solutions, not just one — requiring extra care to describe them all.

Finding the general solution

After finding one solution using inverse trig functions, the periodic nature of sine and cosine (repeating every 360°) or tangent (repeating every 180°) lets you generate every other valid solution by adding multiples of that period.

Restricting to one cycle

Most problems restrict solutions to a single interval, like 0° to 360°, which keeps the answer to a small, specific, finite set of values instead of an infinite family.

Pick a trig equation fact to explore

Why does sin(x) = 0.5 have two solutions between 0° and 360°?

The sine wave's shape means two different angles in that range can share the exact same sine value.

Radians vs degrees

Two different ways to measure the same angle.

What a radian is

A radian measures an angle based on arc length: one radian is the angle created when the arc length equals the circle's radius — a full circle measures exactly 2π radians.

Converting between the two

Since 360° equals 2π radians, converting between them uses the ratio π radians = 180° — multiply degrees by π/180 to get radians, or multiply radians by 180/π to get degrees.

Why radians matter in higher maths

Calculus and many advanced formulas involving trig functions only work cleanly when angles are measured in radians, since radians directly connect angle measure to arc length and circular motion.

Degrees to radians converter

Degrees

How many radians are in a full circle?

A full circle's arc length equals its circumference, 2πr, which corresponds to exactly 2π radians.

Limits

What a function approaches, even where it can't quite arrive.

What a limit is

A limit describes the value a function gets closer and closer to as its input approaches some specific number — even if the function isn't actually defined at that exact point.

Why limits matter

Limits are the foundation of all calculus — both derivatives and integrals are defined precisely as limits of simpler calculations.

Evaluating simple limits

For many well-behaved functions, you can find a limit by simply substituting the input value directly; when that gives an undefined result like 0/0, algebra (like factoring and canceling) is often needed first.

Limit of (x²-1)/(x-1) as x approaches a value (evaluated near x)

x value (approach, e.g. 1)

What does a limit describe?

A limit is about approach, not arrival — the function need not even be defined at the point itself.

Continuity

Functions you can draw without lifting your pencil.

What continuity means

A function is continuous at a point if its graph has no break, jump, or hole there — informally, you could trace it through that point without lifting your pencil.

The formal test

A function is continuous at a point if three things hold: the function is defined there, its limit exists there, and the limit equals the function's actual value at that point.

Types of discontinuities

A removable discontinuity is a single missing point (a hole); a jump discontinuity is where the graph suddenly leaps to a different value; an infinite discontinuity is where the graph shoots off toward infinity.

Pick a discontinuity type and see its description

What does it mean informally for a function to be continuous at a point?

You could trace through a continuous point without lifting your pencil.

The chain rule

Differentiating a function nested inside another function.

What the chain rule handles

When one function is nested inside another, like (3x+1)⁵, the chain rule tells you how to differentiate the whole composite expression.

The rule itself

The derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) · g'(x) — differentiate the outer function (leaving the inside untouched), then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

A worked example

For (3x+1)⁵, the outer function is u⁵ with derivative 5u⁴, and the inner function is 3x+1 with derivative 3 — so the full derivative is 5(3x+1)⁴ · 3 = 15(3x+1)⁴.

Chain rule example: derivative of (ax+b)ⁿ at a given x is n·a·(ax+b)^(n-1)

a · b · n · x

What does the chain rule tell you to do with a composite function f(g(x))?

That multiplication accounts for how a change in x ripples through both layers of the composition.

Product & quotient rules

Differentiating functions that are multiplied or divided.

The product rule

The derivative of a product f(x)·g(x) isn't just f'·g' — it's f'g + fg': differentiate the first and keep the second, plus keep the first and differentiate the second.

The quotient rule

The derivative of a quotient f(x)/g(x) is (f'g - fg')/g² — often remembered with the phrase 'low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.'

Why you can't just differentiate each separately

A common mistake is assuming the derivative of a product equals the product of the derivatives — but that's not true, which is exactly why these dedicated rules are needed.

Pick a rule and see its formula

What is a common mistake the product rule prevents?

The derivative of a product isn't simply the product of each derivative — the correct rule involves both terms.

Implicit differentiation

Finding a derivative when y isn't isolated.

When you need it

Some equations, like x² + y² = 25, can't easily be solved for y alone — implicit differentiation lets you find dy/dx directly without isolating y first.

The process

Differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to x, treating y as a function of x (so applying the chain rule whenever you differentiate a y term), then solve algebraically for dy/dx.

Why it works

Since y depends on x, every derivative of a y-term must include a dy/dx factor from the chain rule — that's the key step people forget.

Pick an implicit differentiation fact to explore

What's the key extra step when differentiating a y term implicitly?

Since y is treated as a function of x, its derivative carries a dy/dx factor.

Optimization

Using derivatives to find maximums and minimums.

Critical points

A function's maximum or minimum (on a smooth curve) occurs where its derivative equals zero or is undefined — these are called critical points, and they're the candidates to check.

The second derivative test

At a critical point, if the second derivative is positive, the point is a local minimum (curve opens upward); if negative, it's a local maximum (curve opens downward).

Real-world optimization

Optimization problems appear constantly in practice: maximizing the area of a fenced enclosure with fixed fencing, minimizing a container's material cost for a fixed volume, or maximizing profit given cost and revenue functions.

Pick a second-derivative result and see the meaning

If the second derivative is negative at a critical point, what kind of point is it?

A negative second derivative means the curve is concave down there, forming a peak.

Related rates

How changing one quantity changes another connected to it.

The core idea

Related rates problems involve two or more quantities that change over time and are connected by an equation — knowing how fast one changes lets you calculate how fast another changes.

The general approach

Write an equation relating the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to time (using the chain rule), plug in the known values, and solve for the unknown rate.

A classic example

If a circular ripple's radius grows at a known rate, related rates lets you calculate how fast its area is growing at any given moment, using A = πr² and differentiating with respect to time.

Circle area growth rate (dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt)

Current radius · Radius growth rate (dr/dt)

What is the first step in solving a typical related rates problem?

That connecting equation is what lets you relate the different rates of change through differentiation.

The fundamental theorem of calculus

The deep link between derivatives and integrals.

What it says

The fundamental theorem of calculus links the two main operations of calculus: differentiation and integration are essentially inverse processes — one undoes the other.

Part one

If you integrate a function to build up an accumulated total (an area function), then differentiate that accumulated total, you get back the original function.

Part two

To evaluate a definite integral, find any antiderivative of the function, then subtract its value at the lower limit from its value at the upper limit — no need to actually add up infinitely many tiny pieces.

Pick a part of the theorem and see what it says

What does the fundamental theorem of calculus reveal about differentiation and integration?

One operation undoes the other, which is what makes calculating definite integrals possible via antiderivatives.

Integration by substitution

Simplifying an integral by swapping in a new variable.

The idea

Integration by substitution is the reverse of the chain rule — you replace a complicated inner expression with a single new variable u, turning a hard integral into a simpler one.

The steps

Choose u as an inner function whose derivative also appears in the integrand, rewrite the whole integral in terms of u (and du), integrate, then substitute back to the original variable.

When to use it

Whenever an integrand looks like a function of an expression multiplied by that expression's derivative — like x·cos(x²) — substitution is often the right move.

Pick an integral and see the substitution to try

Integration by substitution is essentially the reverse of which differentiation rule?

Substitution unwinds exactly the nesting that the chain rule creates when differentiating.

Integration by parts

Integrating a product of two different kinds of functions.

The formula

Integration by parts, derived from the product rule, states ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du — it trades one integral for (hopefully) a simpler one.

Choosing u and dv

A helpful guideline is LIATE: choose u by priority Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — whichever comes first in that list is usually best to pick as u.

A classic example

∫ x·eˣ dx works well by parts: let u = x (so du = dx) and dv = eˣ dx (so v = eˣ), giving x·eˣ - ∫ eˣ dx = x·eˣ - eˣ + C.

Pick a fact about integration by parts to explore

Integration by parts is derived by rearranging which differentiation rule?

Integrating the product rule and rearranging terms gives the integration by parts formula directly.

Areas between curves

Using integrals to measure the space between two graphs.

The idea

The area between two curves is found by integrating the difference between the upper function and the lower function over the interval where they enclose a region.

Finding the limits

The limits of integration are usually the x-values where the two curves intersect, found by setting the two functions equal and solving.

A caution about crossing curves

If the curves cross within the interval, the 'upper' and 'lower' function swap — so the area must be split into separate integrals at each crossing point to avoid canceling positive and negative regions.

Pick a fact about areas between curves to explore

What do you integrate to find the area between two curves?

Subtracting the lower function from the upper one leaves the vertical distance between them at each x, which is what accumulates as area.

Differential equations: an introduction

Equations that involve a function and its own rate of change.

What a differential equation is

A differential equation relates a function to one or more of its own derivatives — describing how a quantity changes in terms of its own current value.

Why they appear everywhere

Differential equations model an enormous range of real phenomena: population growth, radioactive decay, cooling coffee, spring oscillations, and the spread of disease.

A simple example

The equation dy/dt = ky says a quantity's growth rate is proportional to its current size — its solution, y = y₀eᵏᵗ, describes exponential growth (if k>0) or decay (if k<0).

Exponential growth/decay (y = y₀·e^(kt))

Initial amount · Rate constant k · Time

What does the differential equation dy/dt = ky describe?

That self-proportional growth is the signature of exponential growth or decay.

Standard deviation & variance

Measuring how spread out a set of values is.

What variance measures

Variance measures how far each value in a data set typically sits from the mean — found by averaging the squared differences between each value and the mean.

Standard deviation

Standard deviation is simply the square root of the variance — putting the measure of spread back into the same units as the original data, making it easier to interpret.

Interpreting it

A small standard deviation means values cluster tightly around the mean; a large one means values are spread widely — two data sets can share the exact same mean yet have very different standard deviations.

Enter a comma-separated list of numbers

What does a small standard deviation indicate?

A small standard deviation means the data points sit close to the average rather than scattering far from it.

The normal distribution

The bell curve that shows up throughout nature.

The bell curve shape

The normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve centered on the mean, where values near the mean are most common and extreme values become progressively rarer.

The 68-95-99.7 rule

In a normal distribution, roughly 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three.

Why it appears so often

Many natural measurements — heights, measurement errors, test scores — approximately follow a normal distribution, partly explained by the central limit theorem, which shows that sums of many independent effects tend toward a bell curve.

Pick a range and see the percentage of data it covers

Roughly what percentage of a normal distribution falls within one standard deviation of the mean?

The 68-95-99.7 rule puts about 68% of values within one standard deviation of the mean.

Probability distributions

Describing every possible outcome and how likely each one is.

What a probability distribution is

A probability distribution lists every possible outcome of a random process along with how likely each one is — the probabilities across all outcomes always add up to exactly 1.

Discrete vs continuous

A discrete distribution covers outcomes you can list (like rolling a die), while a continuous distribution covers outcomes that can take any value within a range (like a person's exact height).

Expected value

The expected value of a distribution is its long-run average outcome, found by multiplying each outcome by its probability and adding up the results.

Expected value of a fair six-sided die roll

Number of faces

What must the probabilities across all outcomes of a distribution add up to?

Something must happen, so the total probability across all possible outcomes is always exactly 1.

Permutations & combinations

Counting arrangements and selections.

Permutations

A permutation counts the number of ways to arrange items where order matters — arranging 3 different books on a shelf can be done in 3! = 6 different orders.

Combinations

A combination counts the number of ways to choose items where order doesn't matter — choosing 2 people from a group of 5 for a committee is the same regardless of who's listed first.

The formulas

Permutations of r items from n: nPr = n!/(n-r)!. Combinations: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) — a combination is just a permutation divided by r!, since order no longer matters.

Combinations calculator (nCr)

n (total items) · r (items chosen)

What's the key difference between a permutation and a combination?

Order matters for permutations (arrangements) but not for combinations (selections).

Conditional probability

How likely something is, given that something else already happened.

What it means

Conditional probability, written P(A|B), measures the probability of event A happening given that event B is already known to have happened.

The formula

P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B) — narrowing down the sample space to only cases where B occurred, then finding what fraction of those also include A.

Independent vs dependent events

If knowing B occurred doesn't change the probability of A at all, the events are independent; if it does, they're dependent, like drawing two cards from a deck without putting the first one back.

Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

P(A and B) · P(B)

What does P(A|B) represent?

The vertical bar means 'given that' — narrowing focus to only situations where B is already known to have occurred.

Bayes' theorem

Updating a probability when new evidence arrives.

What Bayes' theorem does

Bayes' theorem shows how to update the probability of a hypothesis in light of new evidence — flipping around a conditional probability to answer 'given this evidence, how likely is my hypothesis?'

The formula
