P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B) — the updated probability depends on how likely the evidence is if the hypothesis is true, weighted by how likely the hypothesis was to begin with.

The base rate lesson

Bayes' theorem famously shows that even a very accurate test can give mostly false positives when the condition being tested for is rare — ignoring the underlying base rate is a common and costly reasoning mistake.

Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B)

P(B|A) · P(A) · P(B)

Why can even a highly accurate test give mostly false positives for a rare condition?

When the condition is rare, even a small false-positive rate produces more false alarms than true cases among everyone tested.

Correlation & regression

Measuring and modeling relationships between two variables.

Correlation

Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together, from -1 (perfect negative relationship) through 0 (no linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive relationship).

Correlation is not causation

Two variables can be strongly correlated without one causing the other — a hidden third factor might drive both, or the link might be pure coincidence.

Linear regression

Linear regression finds the straight line that best fits a set of data points, letting you predict one variable from another — minimizing the total squared vertical distance between the data points and the line.

Pick a correlation value and see what it means

Does a strong correlation between two variables prove that one causes the other?

Correlation only shows two variables move together, not why — causation requires much stronger evidence.

Sampling methods

How to learn about a whole population from just part of it.

Why sample

Measuring an entire population is often too expensive or impractical, so statisticians study a smaller sample and use it to draw conclusions about the whole group.

Random sampling

In a simple random sample, every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen — the best protection against bias creeping into which individuals end up in the sample.

Bias and its causes

A biased sample systematically over- or under-represents part of the population — for instance, surveying only people who answer their phone during the day can skew results toward those who happen to be home.

Pick a sampling scenario and see whether it risks bias

What makes a simple random sample resistant to bias?

Equal selection probability prevents any part of the population from being systematically over- or under-represented.

Hypothesis testing

Deciding whether data is strong enough evidence against a claim.

The null hypothesis

A hypothesis test starts by assuming a 'null hypothesis' — typically that there's no effect or no difference — and then asks whether the observed data is unlikely enough under that assumption to reject it.

The p-value

The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what was actually observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true — a small p-value (commonly below 0.05) counts as evidence against the null.

What a p-value is not

A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that a result happened 'by chance' in a simple sense — it's specifically about how surprising the data is if the null hypothesis holds.

Pick a p-value and see the usual interpretation

What does a small p-value suggest?

A small p-value means the observed data is unlikely under the null hypothesis, counting as evidence against it.

Confidence intervals

A range of plausible values for an unknown quantity.

What a confidence interval is

A confidence interval gives a range of values likely to contain an unknown population quantity (like an average), calculated from a sample — such as a 95% confidence interval for a population mean.

Interpreting confidence level

A 95% confidence level means that if you repeated the sampling and interval-building process many times, about 95% of the intervals built would actually contain the true value.

Width and sample size

A confidence interval gets narrower (more precise) as the sample size increases, since bigger samples give more reliable estimates — quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the interval's width.

95% confidence interval half-width (1.96 × σ/√n)

Standard deviation σ · Sample size n

What happens to a confidence interval's width as the sample size increases?

Larger samples give more precise estimates, tightening the range of plausible values.

Set theory

Collections of objects, and how they overlap and combine.

What a set is

A set is a collection of distinct objects, called elements — written with curly braces, like {1, 2, 3}. Order doesn't matter, and repeats aren't counted.

Set operations

The union of two sets contains everything in either; the intersection contains only what's in both; the complement contains everything not in the set (within some larger universal set).

Venn diagrams

A Venn diagram uses overlapping circles to picture set relationships — the overlapping region shows the intersection, and the combined area of all circles shows the union.

Pick a set operation and see what it gives

What does the intersection of two sets contain?

The intersection is the overlap — just the elements the two sets have in common.

Logic & truth tables

The rules of valid reasoning, made precise.

Statements and connectives

A logical statement is either true or false. Connectives like AND, OR, and NOT combine statements into more complex ones, whose truth depends on the truth of the parts.

Truth tables

A truth table lists every possible combination of truth values for a compound statement's parts and shows the resulting truth value — a systematic way to check exactly when a statement is true.

Implication

The statement 'if P then Q' is only false in one case: when P is true but Q is false — if P is false, the implication counts as true regardless of Q (called vacuous truth).

Pick a logical operation and see when it's true

When is the statement 'P AND Q' true?

AND demands that every part be true for the whole statement to hold.

Proof techniques

How mathematicians establish that something is definitely true.

Direct proof

A direct proof starts from known facts or definitions and reasons step by step, using logic alone, to reach the statement you want to prove.

Proof by contradiction

To prove a statement by contradiction, assume it's false and show this leads to an impossible or self-contradictory result — meaning the original statement must be true after all.

Proof by induction

Induction proves a statement about all natural numbers by showing it holds for the first case (the base case), and that if it holds for any one case, it must hold for the next — like knocking over a whole line of dominoes.

Pick a proof technique and see how it works

How does proof by contradiction work?

Deriving an impossible result from the assumption that a statement is false forces the statement to be true.

Graph theory basics

Points, connections, and the maths of networks.

Vertices and edges

In graph theory, a graph is made of vertices (points) connected by edges (lines) — a simple but powerful way to model networks like roads, social connections, or computer networks.

Degree of a vertex

A vertex's degree is the number of edges connected to it — a useful measure of how 'connected' each point in the network is.

Paths and cycles

A path is a sequence of edges connecting vertices; a cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex — the famous Königsberg bridge problem, which asked whether all seven bridges could be crossed exactly once, launched the whole field.

Pick a graph theory term and see its meaning

In graph theory, what is a vertex's degree?

Degree simply counts how many edges touch a given vertex.

The binomial theorem

Expanding powers of a two-term expression.

What it does

The binomial theorem gives a formula for expanding (a+b)ⁿ into a sum of terms, without multiplying the expression out n times by hand.

Pascal's triangle

The coefficients in the expansion of (a+b)ⁿ match row n of Pascal's triangle, where each number is the sum of the two directly above it — 1, 2, 1 for (a+b)², or 1, 3, 3, 1 for (a+b)³.

The general term

The kth term in the expansion of (a+b)ⁿ involves the combination nCk multiplied by a^(n-k) and b^k — connecting the binomial theorem directly to counting combinations.

Binomial coefficient calculator (nCk)

n · k

Where can the coefficients of a binomial expansion be found quickly?

Pascal's triangle rows list exactly the binomial coefficients for each power.

Recursion

Defining something in terms of a smaller version of itself.

What recursion is

A recursive definition describes something in terms of a simpler version of itself, plus a base case that stops the process — like defining a number's factorial as n × (n-1)!, with 0! = 1 as the base case.

The Fibonacci sequence

The famous Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively: each term is the sum of the two before it, starting with 1 and 1 — giving 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and so on.

Why a base case matters

Without a base case, a recursive definition would never stop — it would keep referring to smaller and smaller versions forever without ever reaching a concrete answer.

Fibonacci number calculator (nth term)

n (term number)

Why does every recursive definition need a base case?

Without a base case, the recursion would never terminate.

Modular arithmetic

Arithmetic that wraps around, like a clock.

Clock arithmetic

Modular arithmetic works with remainders after division — on a 12-hour clock, 10 o'clock plus 5 hours is 3 o'clock, since 15 wraps around to 3.

The notation

'a mod n' means the remainder when a is divided by n — so 17 mod 5 = 2, since 17 = 3×5 + 2.

Why it matters

Modular arithmetic underlies many everyday systems: repeating schedules, ISBN and credit card check digits, and public-key cryptography that secures online transactions.

Modulo calculator (a mod n)

a · n

What is 17 mod 5?

Dividing 17 by 5 gives 3 with a remainder of 2, so 17 mod 5 = 2.

The pigeonhole principle

A surprisingly powerful idea from simple counting.

The principle

If you place more items than containers, at least one container must hold more than one item — if 10 pigeons occupy 9 holes, some hole must contain at least two pigeons.

A surprising consequence

Among any 13 people, at least two must share a birth month, since there are only 12 months — no need to know anyone's actual birthday to be certain.

Why it's useful

Despite sounding trivial, the pigeonhole principle proves surprisingly deep results in mathematics and computer science, especially in showing that some collision or repetition is unavoidable.

Pick a scenario and see the guaranteed outcome

What does the pigeonhole principle guarantee when you place more items than containers?

If items outnumber containers, some container must necessarily receive multiple items.

Vector operations

Adding, scaling, and combining vectors.

Vector addition and scaling

Vectors add by combining matching components — (1,2) + (3,4) = (4,6) — and scale by multiplying every component by the same number, stretching or shrinking the vector without changing its direction (unless the number is negative, which flips it).

The dot product

The dot product of two vectors multiplies matching components and adds the results — a single number that measures how much the two vectors point in the same direction.

Using the dot product

A dot product of zero means the two vectors are perpendicular; a large positive value means they point in similar directions; a negative value means they point in generally opposite directions.

Dot product calculator for 2D vectors (a·b = a1b1 + a2b2)

a1 · a2 · b1 · b2

What does a dot product of exactly zero tell you about two vectors?

A zero dot product means the vectors meet at a right angle, since no part of one points along the other.

Matrix multiplication

Combining two matrices into a new one.

How it works

Multiplying two matrices produces a new matrix where each entry is the dot product of a row from the first matrix and a column from the second — so the first matrix's column count must equal the second's row count.

Order matters

Unlike ordinary number multiplication, matrix multiplication isn't commutative — A×B generally doesn't equal B×A, and sometimes one order works while the other isn't even defined.

Why it's useful

Multiplying by a matrix can apply a transformation (like rotating or scaling a shape) to an entire set of points at once, making matrix multiplication the workhorse of computer graphics and many scientific computations.

Pick a matrix multiplication fact to explore

Is matrix multiplication generally commutative?

A×B generally doesn't equal B×A, unlike ordinary number multiplication.

Determinants

A single number that captures a matrix's key behavior.

The 2×2 determinant

For a 2×2 matrix with entries a, b (top row) and c, d (bottom row), the determinant is ad - bc — a single number computed from the four entries.

What the determinant tells you

A matrix has an inverse only if its determinant is not zero. Geometrically, the determinant of a 2×2 matrix gives the factor by which it scales areas when used as a transformation.

A zero determinant

When the determinant is zero, the matrix squashes space down into a lower dimension (like flattening a plane into a line), which is exactly why it can't be reversed — information has been lost.

2×2 determinant calculator (ad − bc)

a · b · c · d

What does a zero determinant mean for a matrix?

A zero determinant means the matrix collapses space, losing information — so it can't be undone by an inverse.

Solving systems with matrices

Turning a system of equations into a single matrix equation.

Matrix form

A system of linear equations can be written compactly as a single matrix equation, Ax = b, where A holds the coefficients, x holds the unknowns, and b holds the constants.

Solving with the inverse

If A has an inverse, multiplying both sides by it gives x = A⁻¹b — solving the entire system in one step, no matter how many equations and unknowns it has.

Gaussian elimination

In practice, large systems are usually solved by Gaussian elimination — systematically adding multiples of rows to other rows to reduce the system to a simple triangular form that can be solved from the bottom up.

Pick a fact about solving systems with matrices

What does the equation Ax = b represent?

Compactly bundling many linear equations into one matrix equation is exactly its purpose.

Eigenvalues & eigenvectors

Special directions a matrix only stretches, never turns.

The core idea

An eigenvector of a matrix is a special vector that, when the matrix acts on it, only gets stretched or shrunk — not rotated to a new direction. The stretch factor is called its eigenvalue.

The defining equation

Formally, Av = λv, where A is the matrix, v is the eigenvector, and λ is the eigenvalue — the matrix acting on v gives back just a scaled copy of v.

Where they appear

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors show up throughout science and engineering — in vibration analysis of structures, in quantum mechanics, and in algorithms like the one Google originally used to rank web pages.

Pick a term and see what it means

What happens to an eigenvector when its matrix acts on it?

That preserved direction is exactly what defines an eigenvector.

Vector spaces

The abstract setting where vectors live.

What a vector space is

A vector space is any collection of objects that can be added together and scaled by numbers, following a consistent set of rules — ordinary arrows in 2D or 3D are the most familiar example, but far more abstract collections qualify too.

Basis and dimension

A basis is a minimal set of vectors from which every other vector in the space can be built as a combination; the number of vectors in a basis is the space's dimension.

Why the abstraction matters

By focusing only on the rules of addition and scaling, vector space theory applies equally well to lists of numbers, polynomials, and even functions — the same techniques then work across wildly different areas.

Pick a vector space concept and see its meaning

What is the dimension of a vector space?

Dimension counts how many independent directions are needed to reach every vector in the space.

Simple & compound interest

How money grows over time.

Simple interest

Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount (the principal): I = P × r × t — so the interest earned stays the same each period.

Compound interest

Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus all previously earned interest, so the interest itself earns interest — the total grows according to A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt).

The power of compounding

Over long periods, compound interest grows dramatically faster than simple interest, which is why starting to save early makes such a large difference to long-term results.

Compound interest calculator (A = P(1+r/n)^(nt))

Principal · Annual rate (e.g. 0.05) · Compounds per year · Years

What is the key difference between simple and compound interest?

Compounding means each period's interest is added to the base, so future interest is calculated on a growing amount.

Loans & amortization

How borrowed money is repaid over time.

How loan payments work

A standard loan is repaid through regular equal payments, each covering both the interest owed that period and some of the original amount borrowed (the principal).

Amortization

Amortization describes how each payment's split changes over time — early payments go mostly toward interest, while later payments go increasingly toward reducing the principal.

Why the interest rate and term matter

A higher interest rate or a longer repayment term both increase the total interest paid over the life of the loan, even though a longer term lowers each individual payment.

Monthly loan payment calculator

Loan amount · Annual rate (e.g. 0.06) · Years

Why do early loan payments go mostly toward interest?

With a big outstanding balance early on, that period's interest charge is larger, taking up more of each payment.

Real-world mensuration

Applying area and volume formulas to practical problems.

What mensuration is

Mensuration is the branch of maths dealing with measuring lengths, areas, and volumes of shapes — turning geometric formulas into practical answers about the physical world.

Practical examples

Everyday uses include calculating how much paint a wall needs (area), how much water a tank holds (volume), or how much fencing encloses a garden (perimeter).

Units matter

Always check units: area is measured in square units and volume in cubic units — converting between units like meters and centimeters requires squaring or cubing the conversion factor, not just multiplying by it once.

Rectangular tank volume in litres (1 m³ = 1000 L)

Length (m) · Width (m) · Height (m)

Why must unit conversions for area or volume use a squared or cubed conversion factor?

Converting each dimension of length means the conversion factor multiplies once per dimension involved.

Expected value & games

The long-run average result of a chance-based situation.

What expected value measures

Expected value is the long-run average outcome of a chance-based situation, found by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and summing them all.

Fair and unfair games

A game is fair if its expected value to a player is zero — meaning that over many plays, they'd neither win nor lose money on average. Most casino games are deliberately designed with a negative expected value for the player.

Using expected value to decide

Expected value helps compare risky options rationally — such as deciding whether a raffle ticket, insurance policy, or investment is worth its cost on average.

Expected value of a bet (win amount × P(win) − loss amount × P(lose))

Win amount · Probability of winning · Loss amount

What does a negative expected value mean for a player of a game?

A negative expected value means the long-run average result is a loss, even if individual plays can still win.

Cryptography basics

Using maths to keep information private.

The goal of encryption

Encryption scrambles a message so only someone with the right key can read it — modern encryption relies on mathematical problems that are easy to do in one direction but extremely hard to reverse without a secret.

Public-key cryptography

In public-key systems, each person has a public key anyone can use to encrypt messages to them, and a private key only they hold to decrypt — no need to secretly share a key beforehand.

The role of prime numbers

Many public-key systems rely on the fact that multiplying two large primes together is easy, but factoring the resulting huge number back into those primes is extraordinarily hard for a computer.

Pick a cryptography concept and see its meaning

What makes public-key cryptography so useful?

The public/private split removes the need to arrange a secret key exchange in advance.

Fractals

Shapes with endless detail at every scale.

What a fractal is

A fractal is a shape that shows similar structure at every level of magnification — zoom in on part of it, and you find a smaller copy of the whole (or something very like it).

Famous examples

The Mandelbrot set, the Sierpinski triangle, and the Koch snowflake are classic fractals, each built by repeating a simple rule over and over.

Fractals in nature

Coastlines, ferns, lightning, and blood vessel networks all show fractal-like branching or roughness, which is why fractal maths is useful for modeling complex natural shapes.

Pick a fractal fact to explore

What defines a fractal?

That repeating detail across scales is the essence of a fractal.

Game theory basics

The maths of strategic decisions.

What game theory studies

Game theory analyzes situations where the best choice for one participant depends on what the others choose — from economics to biology to everyday negotiations.

The prisoner's dilemma

In the famous prisoner's dilemma, two people each do better by betraying the other regardless of what the other does — yet if both betray, both end up worse off than if both had cooperated.

Nash equilibrium

A Nash equilibrium is a set of choices where no player can improve their own outcome by changing their choice alone, given what everyone else is doing — a central concept for predicting strategic outcomes.

Pick a game theory concept and see its meaning

What defines a Nash equilibrium?

At equilibrium, each player's choice is already the best given everyone else's choices.

Maths of music

Frequency ratios behind harmony.

Octaves as a 2:1 ratio

Two notes an octave apart have frequencies in a simple 2:1 ratio — doubling a note's frequency raises it exactly one octave, which is why the two notes sound so similar.

Simple ratios and harmony

Notes whose frequencies form simple whole-number ratios, like 3:2 (a perfect fifth) or 4:3 (a perfect fourth), sound especially pleasant together, since their sound waves line up regularly.

Equal temperament

Modern pianos use equal temperament, dividing the octave into 12 equal steps, each raising frequency by the same factor of the 12th root of 2 (about 1.0595) — a compromise letting music sound acceptable in every key.

Note frequency n semitones above A440

Semitones above A440

What is the frequency ratio between two notes exactly one octave apart?

Doubling a note's frequency raises it exactly one octave.

The golden ratio & Fibonacci

A famous ratio connecting a famous sequence.

The golden ratio

The golden ratio, φ ≈ 1.618, is the number where the ratio of a whole to its larger part equals the ratio of the larger part to the smaller part — an irrational number with a surprisingly rich mathematical role.

Link to Fibonacci

Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers (1/1, 2/1, 3/2, 5/3, 8/5...) get closer and closer to the golden ratio as the sequence continues.

Appearances and myths

The golden ratio genuinely appears in some plant growth patterns and pentagon geometry, but many popular claims about it appearing everywhere in art and architecture are exaggerated or unsupported.

Ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers F(n+1)/F(n)

n

What happens to the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers as the sequence goes on?

The ratios settle closer and closer to φ, a remarkable link between the sequence and the constant.

Non-Euclidean geometry

Geometry where parallel lines behave differently.

Euclid's fifth postulate

For over two thousand years, mathematicians tried to prove Euclid's parallel postulate — that through a point not on a line, exactly one parallel line can be drawn — from his other axioms, and failed.

Curved geometries

In the 1800s, mathematicians showed that consistent geometries exist where this postulate fails: spherical geometry (no parallel lines at all) and hyperbolic geometry (infinitely many parallel lines through a point).

Real-world relevance

Non-Euclidean geometry isn't just an abstract curiosity — on the curved surface of the Earth, spherical geometry describes real flight paths, and Einstein's general relativity uses curved, non-Euclidean geometry to describe gravity.

Pick a geometry and see how parallel lines behave

In spherical geometry, how many lines through a point are parallel to a given line?

On a sphere, any two great circles must eventually intersect, so no true parallel lines exist.

Topology: an introduction

The geometry of stretching without tearing.

Rubber-sheet geometry

Topology studies properties of shapes that stay the same when you stretch, bend, or squish them — as long as you don't tear or glue anything together.

The classic joke

A topologist famously can't tell a coffee mug from a donut: both have exactly one hole, so one can be smoothly deformed into the other.

Why it matters

Topology's ideas — connectedness, holes, and continuous deformation — turn out to underlie far more than shapes, including data analysis, network structure, and modern physics.

Pick a pair of shapes and see if they're topologically equivalent

Why is a coffee mug considered topologically the same as a donut?

Topology only cares about features like the number of holes that survive smooth stretching and bending.

History of mathematics

How maths grew from counting to calculus and beyond.

Ancient foundations

Early civilizations, including the Babylonians and Egyptians, developed arithmetic and geometry for practical needs like trade, land measurement, and calendars.

Greek and Islamic contributions

Ancient Greek mathematicians introduced formal proof and geometry, while scholars in the medieval Islamic world advanced algebra — the word itself comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr' — and helped spread the Hindu-Arabic number system.

The birth of calculus

In the late 1600s, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz independently developed calculus, launching a mathematical revolution that made modern physics and engineering possible.

Pick a mathematical milestone and see its story

Who independently developed calculus in the late 1600s?

Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz each developed calculus around the same time, sparking a famous priority dispute.

Famous unsolved problems

Open questions that still resist proof.

What 'unsolved' means

Despite centuries of progress, many simply stated mathematical questions remain open — nobody has managed to prove them true or false.

The Millennium Prize Problems

In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute named seven problems, each with a $1 million prize; only one, the Poincaré conjecture, has been solved so far.

Examples

The Riemann hypothesis (about the distribution of prime numbers) and the P versus NP problem (about whether every quickly checkable problem is also quickly solvable) are two of the most famous still-open questions.

Pick an unsolved problem and see what it asks

How many of the seven Millennium Prize Problems have been solved so far?

Only the Poincaré conjecture, proved by Grigori Perelman, has been solved.

Mathematical modeling

Turning real-world situations into equations.

What modeling is

Mathematical modeling translates a real-world situation into equations or other mathematical structures, so its behavior can be analyzed, predicted, and tested.

The modeling cycle

A typical cycle: identify the question, make simplifying assumptions, build the model, solve it, compare the results with reality, and refine the model if they don't match well enough.

Every model is imperfect

Since models simplify reality, they're always approximations — a good model is useful for its purpose, and knowing where its assumptions break down is just as important as knowing what it predicts.

Pick a modeling step and see what it involves

Why is comparing model results with reality an essential step?

A mismatch between predictions and observations signals that the assumptions or structure need revisiting.

Numerical methods: Newton's method

Homing in on solutions by repeated improvement.

Why numerical methods

Many equations can't be solved exactly with a neat formula, so numerical methods find increasingly accurate approximate solutions by repeating a calculation.

Newton's method

Newton's method finds a root of a function by starting with a guess, then improving it with x_new = x - f(x)/f'(x) — repeating until the guesses settle down to the root.

Speed and caution

When it works, Newton's method converges extremely quickly, roughly doubling the number of correct digits each step — but a poor starting guess can send it wandering or even failing to converge.

One Newton step for f(x) = x² − 2 (converging to √2)

Current guess x

What does Newton's method do with each repeated step?

Each iteration uses the function and its slope to refine the guess toward an actual root.

The mathematics of infinity

Some infinities are bigger than others.

Countable infinity

The counting numbers 1, 2, 3... go on forever, but this kind of infinity is called countable — and, surprisingly, so are the integers and the rationals, since they can be listed in a sequence.

Cantor's diagonal argument

Georg Cantor proved that the real numbers can't be listed in any sequence: for any supposed complete list, you can construct a new real number that differs from every entry, showing there are more real numbers than counting numbers.

A hierarchy of infinities

Cantor's work showed that infinities come in different sizes — the infinity of the real numbers is strictly larger than the infinity of the counting numbers, and there are even larger infinities beyond that.

Pick a set and see its size of infinity

What did Cantor's diagonal argument show about the real numbers?

Any supposed complete list of real numbers can be used to construct a real number missing from it.

Chemical bonding

Why atoms bond, and the three main ways they do it.

Why atoms bond

Atoms bond because on their own, most of them are unstable — their outer electron shell isn't full. By sharing, gaining, or losing electrons, atoms reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement, often ending up with 8 electrons in their outer shell. This drive toward stability is what holds nearly all matter together.

Ionic bonding

Ionic bonds form when one atom gives up an electron and another accepts it. The atom that loses an electron becomes a positively charged ion; the one that gains it becomes negatively charged. Opposite charges attract, holding the ions together in a rigid lattice.

Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl

This usually happens between a metal and a nonmetal. Ionic compounds tend to have high melting points and conduct electricity once dissolved in water.

Covalent bonding

Covalent bonds form when atoms share electron pairs instead of transferring them, usually between two nonmetals. Sharing one pair makes a single bond, two pairs a double bond, three pairs a triple bond — more shared pairs mean a shorter, stronger bond.

Water forms when an oxygen atom shares one electron pair with each of two hydrogen atoms. Covalent compounds generally melt at lower temperatures than ionic ones and don't conduct electricity as solids.

Metallic bonding

In a metal, atoms don't hold their outermost electrons tightly. Instead, those electrons move freely through the whole structure, forming a "sea of electrons" around fixed positive metal ions. That free movement is why metals conduct electricity and heat so well, and why they bend rather than shatter.

Electronegativity and polarity

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself. When two bonded atoms differ a lot in electronegativity, the electrons sit closer to one of them, giving a polar covalent bond with a slightly negative and slightly positive end. When the difference is large enough, the pull becomes one-sided enough to count as ionic. When two identical atoms bond, they pull equally, giving a nonpolar covalent bond.

Pick two elements and see what kind of bond they'd form

Which pair is most likely to form an ionic bond?

Sodium (a metal) readily gives up an electron, and chlorine (a nonmetal) readily accepts one — a large electronegativity gap, which is what drives ionic bonding.

In water, how are the electrons held between oxygen and hydrogen?

Oxygen and hydrogen are both nonmetals, so they share electron pairs rather than transferring them — but oxygen pulls harder, making the bond polar.

What lets metals conduct electricity so well?

That "sea of electrons" isn't bound to any one atom, so it can carry a current through the whole piece of metal.

Atomic structure

What atoms are made of, and how their electrons are arranged.

The three subatomic particles
ParticleChargeMassLocation
Proton+11 unitNucleus
Neutron01 unitNucleus
Electron−1~0Shells around nucleus

Protons and neutrons together make up the tiny, dense nucleus. Electrons occupy the much larger space around it.

Atomic number, mass number, isotopes

The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom, and it defines which element it is — every atom with 6 protons is carbon, no matter what else changes. The mass number is protons plus neutrons combined.

Atoms of the same element can carry different numbers of neutrons; these variants are called isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but carbon-14 has two extra neutrons, making it slightly heavier and radioactive.

Electron shells

Electrons fill defined energy levels called shells, starting from the one closest to the nucleus. For the first 18 elements, the pattern is simple: up to 2 electrons in the first shell, up to 8 in the second, and up to 8 in the third.

An atom's outermost shell, called the valence shell, largely determines how it reacts and bonds with other atoms.

What determines which element an atom is?

Protons fix the identity of an element. Neutrons and electrons can vary (as isotopes or ions) without changing what element it is.

Two atoms both have 6 protons — one has 6 neutrons, the other has 8. What are they?

Same proton count means same element — carbon, in this case. Different neutron counts just make them isotopes of it.

How many electrons can the second shell hold at most?

The first shell holds up to 2, the second up to 8 — the pattern used in the atom builder above.

Reactions & equations

How substances change into new ones, and how to describe it in symbols.

What counts as a chemical reaction

A chemical reaction happens when reactants transform into different products with new properties. Signs that one has happened include a color change, gas bubbles forming, a solid appearing out of solution, or a change in temperature — different from a physical change like melting ice, where the substance itself doesn't change.

Writing and balancing equations

A chemical equation shows reactants turning into products, like a recipe. Because matter can't be created or destroyed, the same number of each type of atom must appear on both sides — the law of conservation of mass.

Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ (unbalanced)
4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ (balanced)

Balancing means adjusting the coefficients in front of each formula until the atom counts match, without changing the formulas themselves.

Types of reactions
  • Combination — two substances combine into one.
    2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
  • Decomposition — one substance breaks into simpler ones.
    2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
  • Displacement — one element replaces another in a compound.
    Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
  • Double displacement — two compounds swap partners.
    AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃
  • Combustion — a substance reacts fast with oxygen, releasing heat and light.
    CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Exothermic and endothermic reactions

Exothermic reactions release energy, usually as heat, so the surroundings warm up — combustion is a good example. Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings, which cool down as a result, like the reaction inside an instant cold pack.

What type of reaction is this?

Why must a chemical equation be balanced?

Balancing reflects the law of conservation of mass — every atom present in the reactants has to show up somewhere in the products.

States of matter

Solids, liquids, gases, and what changes between them.

The three common states

In a solid, particles are packed tightly in a fixed arrangement — they vibrate in place but don't move around, which is why solids hold their shape. In a liquid, particles stay close together but can slide past each other, so a liquid takes the shape of its container. In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely and quickly, so a gas expands to fill whatever space it's in.

There's a fourth state, plasma, made of charged particles at very high energy — it's what stars and lightning are made of, though it's far less common in everyday life.

Changes of state
ChangeName
Solid → liquidMelting
Liquid → solidFreezing
Liquid → gasBoiling / evaporation
Gas → liquidCondensation
Solid → gasSublimation
Gas → solidDeposition

These changes are physical, not chemical — the substance is still made of the same molecules, just arranged and moving differently. Adding heat energy generally pushes a substance toward gas; removing it pushes toward solid.

Pick a substance and a temperature to see its state

25°C

What happens to the particles in a solid as it melts into a liquid?

Melting adds enough energy for particles to break out of their fixed positions, while still staying close together — that's what makes it a liquid instead of a gas.

What's it called when a gas turns directly into a solid, skipping the liquid stage?

Sublimation goes solid → gas; deposition is the reverse, gas → solid, like frost forming directly from water vapor.

Acids, bases & salts

The pH scale, neutralization, and everyday examples.

What makes something acidic or basic

Acids release hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water — the more they release, the stronger the acid. Bases do the opposite: they release hydroxide ions (OH⁻) or otherwise accept H⁺ ions. The pH scale measures this from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic (alkaline), and exactly 7 is neutral, like pure water.

Indicators

Indicators are dyes that change color depending on pH, which makes them useful for testing a solution without special equipment. Litmus paper turns red in acid and blue in base. Universal indicator goes further, shifting through a whole range of colors to show roughly how strong the acid or base is.

Neutralization and salts

When an acid and a base react, they cancel each other out in a neutralization reaction, producing a salt and water.

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

Despite the name, a "salt" here means any ionic compound formed this way, not just table salt — different acid-base pairs produce different salts.

Common acids and bases
SubstanceApprox. pH
Stomach acid1.5–3.5
Lemon juice~2
Black coffee~5
Pure water7
Baking soda solution~9
Ammonia~11
Drain cleaner~13.5

Drag the slider to explore the pH scale

pH 7
0714

A solution has a pH of 3. What is it?

Anything below pH 7 is acidic — the lower the number, the stronger the acid.

What two things does neutralizing an acid with a base always produce?

Acid + base → salt + water, no matter which specific acid and base you start with.

Moles & stoichiometry

Counting atoms and molecules using Avogadro's number.

Why chemists count in moles

Atoms and molecules are far too small and numerous to count one by one, so chemists count them in bulk using a unit called the mole. One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles — a number known as Avogadro's number. It's just a very large counting unit, the same idea as a "dozen" meaning 12, just scaled up enormously.

Molar mass

The molar mass of a substance is the mass of one mole of it, in grams, found by adding up the atomic masses of all the atoms in its formula. Water (H₂O) has a molar mass of about 18 grams per mole: roughly 2×1 for the hydrogens plus 16 for the oxygen.

Moles, mass, and particles
moles = mass ÷ molar mass
particles = moles × 6.022 × 10²³

These two relationships let you convert between how much of something you have by mass and how many actual atoms or molecules that represents.

Using moles in reactions

A balanced equation's coefficients also describe mole ratios. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to make 2 moles of water — so knowing the moles of one substance lets you calculate the moles of any other substance in the same reaction.

Try the mole calculator

grams of the selected compound

Roughly how many particles are in one mole of any substance?

That's Avogadro's number — a mole is just a fixed, enormous counting unit, the same for atoms, molecules, or anything else.

Chemical equilibrium

Reversible reactions and Le Chatelier's principle.

Reversible reactions

Some reactions don't just run one way to completion — they run forward and backward at the same time. When the forward and backward reactions happen at the same rate, the amounts of reactants and products stop changing overall, even though both reactions are still happening. This balanced state is called dynamic equilibrium.

The equilibrium constant

The equilibrium constant, K, compares how much product is present versus how much reactant is present once a reaction settles into equilibrium. A large K means the reaction favors products at equilibrium; a small K means it favors reactants. K stays the same at a given temperature, no matter how much of each substance you start with.

Le Chatelier's principle

If you disturb a system at equilibrium — by changing concentration, temperature, or pressure — the system shifts to partly counteract that change and settle into a new equilibrium. Adding more of a reactant pushes the reaction to make more product; removing product pulls the reaction to make more of it; raising the temperature favors whichever direction absorbs heat.

The Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (releases heat). Which way does it shift?

Organic chemistry

Carbon compounds, hydrocarbons, and functional groups.

Why carbon is special

Carbon can form four strong bonds at once and readily bonds to other carbon atoms, building long chains, branches, and rings. This ability, called catenation, is why carbon forms far more known compounds than any other element — organic chemistry, the study of carbon compounds, covers everything from fuels to plastics to the molecules of life itself.

Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. They're grouped by the bonds between their carbon atoms:

  • Alkanes — only single bonds, named with an -ane ending (methane, ethane, propane).
  • Alkenes — contain at least one C=C double bond, named with an -ene ending (ethene, propene).
  • Alkynes — contain at least one C≡C triple bond, named with a -yne ending (ethyne, propyne).
Functional groups

A functional group is a specific cluster of atoms attached to a carbon chain that gives a molecule its characteristic chemical behavior, no matter how long the rest of the chain is.

GroupEndingExample
−OHAlcohol (-ol)Ethanol
−COOHCarboxylic acidAcetic acid
C=O (chain end)Aldehyde (-al)Formaldehyde
C=O (mid-chain)Ketone (-one)Propanone
−NH₂AmineMethylamine

What type of compound is this?

What special ability of carbon explains why there are so many organic compounds?

Catenation — carbon's ability to bond to more carbon atoms — is what lets it build the huge variety of chains, branches, and rings found in organic molecules.

Electrochemistry

Oxidation, reduction, and turning reactions into electricity.

Oxidation and reduction

Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons — often remembered as "OIL RIG" (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). These always happen together in a redox reaction: whatever one substance loses, another substance gains.

Electrochemical cells

A galvanic (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to generate electricity, which is how batteries work. Electrons flow from the electrode where oxidation happens (the anode) through a wire to the electrode where reduction happens (the cathode), producing a usable current along the way.

Electrolysis

Electrolysis runs the idea in reverse: it uses an outside source of electricity to force a non-spontaneous reaction to happen. Passing an electric current through water, for example, splits it into hydrogen and oxygen gas — a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own.

2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂

Which species is oxidized (loses electrons)?

In a battery (galvanic cell), where does reduction take place?

Oxidation happens at the anode, reduction happens at the cathode — electrons flow from one to the other through the external circuit.

Water

What makes it unusual, hardness, and the water cycle.

Why water is unusual

A water molecule is bent, with oxygen pulling harder on the shared electrons than hydrogen does — that makes it polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end and slightly positive hydrogen ends. Neighboring water molecules attract each other through this polarity, forming hydrogen bonds that are individually weak but collectively powerful.

Those hydrogen bonds are why water has an unusually high boiling point for such a small molecule, why it can dissolve so many other substances (earning it the nickname "universal solvent"), and why ice floats — it's actually less dense than liquid water.

Hard and soft water

Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, usually picked up as water passes through rock like limestone. It's not harmful to drink, but it reacts with soap to leave a scummy residue instead of lathering well, and it can build up as scale inside kettles and pipes over time. Soft water lacks these ions, either naturally or because it's been treated to remove them.

The water cycle

Water constantly moves between the oceans, atmosphere, and land in a cycle driven by the sun's energy: it evaporates from oceans and lakes, condenses into clouds, falls back down as precipitation, and eventually collects again in rivers, lakes, and oceans to start over.

Purifying water

Drinking water is treated to remove particles, microbes, and harmful chemicals before it reaches taps. Common methods include filtration (straining out solid particles), chlorination (killing bacteria and other microbes), and distillation (boiling water and condensing the steam, leaving dissolved impurities behind).

Why does water dissolve so many different substances?

Water's slightly negative and positive ends can surround and pull apart ions and polar molecules, which is why it dissolves so many substances.

What causes water to be "hard"?

Those minerals, picked up from rock, are what leave scale in kettles and stop soap from lathering well.

Chemical kinetics

What speeds up or slows down a reaction.

Reaction rate

Reaction rate is how quickly reactants turn into products — usually measured as the change in concentration of a substance over time. Some reactions, like an explosion, finish in a fraction of a second; others, like rusting, take years.

Collision theory

For a reaction to happen, particles have to collide with each other with enough energy — called the activation energy — and in the right orientation. Anything that increases how often effective collisions happen will speed up the reaction; anything that reduces them will slow it down.

Catalysts

A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It isn't used up in the reaction — the same catalyst can keep working on new batches of reactants. Enzymes are biological catalysts that make reactions in the body happen fast enough to sustain life.

Pick a change and see what happens to the rate

What does a catalyst do to a reaction's activation energy?

A catalyst opens up an alternative reaction pathway that needs less energy to get going, without being used up itself.

Why does crushing a solid into powder usually speed up its reaction?

More exposed surface means more particles are available to collide and react at once.

Thermochemistry

Where the energy in a reaction comes from and goes.

Energy and bonds

Breaking a chemical bond always requires energy input, while forming a new bond always releases energy. Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall depends on the balance between those two: if forming the new bonds releases more energy than was needed to break the old ones, the reaction is exothermic; if breaking the old bonds needs more energy than forming the new ones releases, it's endothermic.

Enthalpy change (ΔH)

Chemists track this energy balance with enthalpy change, ΔH. A negative ΔH means the reaction released energy overall — exothermic. A positive ΔH means it absorbed energy overall — endothermic. Combustion and neutralization are typically exothermic; photosynthesis and thermal decomposition are typically endothermic.

Measuring heat: calorimetry

Calorimetry measures the heat given off or absorbed by a reaction, often by tracking the temperature change of water surrounding the reaction vessel. That heat can be calculated with q = mcΔT, where m is the mass of the water, c is its specific heat capacity, and ΔT is the temperature change.

Enter the energy involved to see if a reaction is exothermic or endothermic

energy to break bonds (kJ) · energy released forming bonds (kJ)

In an exothermic reaction, is energy overall released or absorbed?

Exothermic reactions release more energy forming new bonds than they used breaking old ones, so the surroundings warm up.

Which best describes an exothermic reaction at the bond level?

That extra released energy is what escapes into the surroundings as heat.

Metals & non-metals

Properties, reactivity, and where metalloids fit.

Physical properties

Metals are typically malleable (can be hammered into sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), lustrous, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are typically brittle if solid, dull, and poor conductors — with graphite being a notable exception that conducts electricity well.

Chemical properties

Metals tend to lose electrons to form positive ions (cations), react with acids to release hydrogen gas, and form basic oxides. Non-metals tend to gain electrons to form negative ions (anions) and typically form acidic oxides.

The reactivity series

Metals can be ranked by how readily they react — the reactivity series. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one from a compound; for example, iron placed in a copper sulfate solution displaces the copper, since iron is more reactive.

Metalloids

Metalloids, like silicon and boron, sit along the "staircase" line on the periodic table and share properties of both metals and non-metals — often brittle like a non-metal but able to semi-conduct electricity, which is exactly why silicon is the backbone of computer chips.

Is this element a metal, non-metal, or metalloid?

What type of oxide does a metal typically form?

Metal oxides are typically basic, while non-metal oxides are typically acidic.

What happens when a more reactive metal is added to a solution containing a less reactive metal's salt?

This displacement reaction is a direct way of comparing where two metals sit in the reactivity series.

Nuclear chemistry

Radioactivity, half-life, fission and fusion.

Radioactivity

Some atomic nuclei are unstable and spontaneously emit radiation to become more stable — a process called radioactive decay. This happens at the nucleus, so it's unaffected by the atom's chemical bonds or surroundings.

Types of radiation
TypeWhat it isStopped by
Alpha (α)2 protons + 2 neutrons (helium nucleus)A sheet of paper
Beta (β)A high-speed electronA few mm of aluminum
Gamma (γ)High-energy electromagnetic radiationThick lead or concrete
Half-life

Half-life is the time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay. It's constant for a given isotope no matter how much material you start with, which makes it useful for things like carbon dating fossils or timing radiotherapy doses in medicine.

Fission and fusion

Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (like uranium) into smaller ones, releasing energy — this is how nuclear power plants generate electricity. Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei (like hydrogen) into a heavier one, releasing even more energy — this is what powers the sun and other stars, though sustaining it on Earth for power remains a major engineering challenge.

Drag to see how much of a 100g sample remains after each half-life

0 half-lives elapsed

What is emitted when an unstable nucleus undergoes radioactive decay?

The nucleus releases radiation to shed energy and move toward a more stable configuration.

Which type of radiation is stopped by just a sheet of paper?

Alpha particles are relatively large and slow, so they're stopped very easily — even by skin or a sheet of paper.

Triads & diagonal relationship

Döbereiner's triads and why some diagonal neighbors act alike.

Döbereiner's triads

In 1817, long before the periodic table existed, Johann Döbereiner noticed that certain sets of three chemically similar elements — which he called triads — showed a striking numerical pattern: the atomic mass of the middle element was roughly the average of the atomic masses of the other two.

For example, in the triad lithium, sodium, potassium, sodium's atomic mass sits almost exactly between lithium's and potassium's. The same pattern showed up in calcium, strontium, barium, and in chlorine, bromine, iodine.

Why triads eventually fell short

Döbereiner's rule only worked for a handful of triads — most groups of similar elements didn't fit neatly into threes at all, and it broke down badly for the transition metals. It was an important first clue that atomic mass and chemical behavior were connected, but it needed replacing. Newlands' law of octaves came next, and eventually Mendeleev arranged all known elements into a full repeating table by atomic mass, which became the ancestor of the modern periodic table.

Diagonal relationship

Some elements near the top of the periodic table resemble the element diagonally below and to the right of them — in the next period and the next group — more closely than they resemble other members of their own group. The three classic pairs are:

Period 2Period 3 diagonal partner
Lithium (Li)Magnesium (Mg)
Beryllium (Be)Aluminium (Al)
Boron (B)Silicon (Si)
Why it happens

Two trends are pulling in opposite directions here. Moving across a period, atomic size shrinks and charge density (and electronegativity) rises. Moving down a group, atomic size grows instead. Along a diagonal, these two effects partly cancel out, leaving the diagonal partners with a similar atomic size and charge density — and therefore similar chemical behavior — even though they sit in different groups.

That's why lithium, like magnesium, forms a nitride directly with nitrogen gas (unusual for an alkali metal) and has a carbonate that decomposes easily on heating. It's why beryllium, like aluminium, is amphoteric — reacting with both acids and bases — and forms mostly covalent chlorides. And it's why boron and silicon are both brittle metalloids that behave as semiconductors.

Check Döbereiner's rule against a real triad

What pattern did Döbereiner notice within a triad of similar elements?

It was one of the earliest signs that atomic mass and chemical behavior were connected, decades before the periodic table was built.

Which pair is a classic example of a diagonal relationship?

Lithium and sodium, or sodium and potassium, are in the same group — a diagonal relationship instead links elements in different groups and periods, like lithium (group 1, period 2) and magnesium (group 2, period 3).

Why does a diagonal relationship happen at all?

That cancellation leaves diagonal partners with a similar atomic size and charge density, which drives similar chemistry.

Metallurgy

How metals are pulled out of their ores.

Where metals are found

Very unreactive metals, like gold and platinum, are often found "native" — as the free element, needing little more than physical separation. Reactive metals are never found free; they occur combined with other elements in rocks called ores, most commonly as oxides, sulfides, or carbonates.

Steps in extraction

Getting a pure metal out of its ore usually takes a few stages: concentrating the ore (removing the unwanted rock, or gangue), converting it to an oxide if needed (roasting sulfide ores or heating, "calcining," carbonate ores), reducing the oxide to the free metal, and finally refining the crude metal to remove remaining impurities, often by electrolytic refining.

Reactivity decides the method

How hard a metal is to extract tracks directly with how reactive it is. Highly reactive metals, like sodium and aluminium, hold on to their compounds so tightly that only electrolysis supplies enough energy to free them. Moderately reactive metals, like iron and zinc, can be reduced with carbon or carbon monoxide instead — cheaper than electrolysis. The least reactive metals sometimes need nothing more than heat to decompose their compounds.

Pick a metal and see how it's typically extracted

Why is gold often found as a free element in nature?

Because gold barely reacts with anything, it doesn't combine into ores the way reactive metals do — it just stays as the metal itself.

Which extraction method suits a highly reactive metal like sodium or aluminium?

Only the energy from an electric current is enough to break apart the very stable compounds these reactive metals form.

Ammonia & hydrogen chloride

Two everyday gases, one basic and one acidic.

Ammonia (NH₃)

Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp, pungent smell. Industrially it's made by the Haber process — nitrogen and hydrogen combining over an iron catalyst under high pressure. It's extremely soluble in water, forming a weakly basic solution (ammonium hydroxide), which turns damp red litmus paper blue. Ammonia is used heavily in fertilizers, cleaning products, and as a starting material for making nitric acid.

Hydrogen chloride (HCl)

Hydrogen chloride is a colorless, fuming gas with a sharp smell, prepared in the lab by heating sodium chloride with concentrated sulfuric acid. It's extremely soluble in water, forming hydrochloric acid, a strong acid. Dilute hydrochloric acid is even found naturally in the stomach, helping digest food, and it's used industrially to clean metal surfaces (pickling).

A classic test: the white fumes

Ammonia is basic and hydrogen chloride is acidic — so when the two gases meet, they neutralize each other, forming a solid, ammonium chloride, that appears instantly as dense white fumes. This reaction is a standard laboratory test for the presence of either gas: bring a rod dipped in the other solution nearby, and white fumes confirm it.

Which gas is being described?

What effect does ammonia gas have on damp red litmus paper?

Ammonia dissolves in the moisture on the paper to form a basic solution, which is what turns red litmus blue.

Nitric & sulphuric acid

Two of industry's most important acids.

Nitric acid (HNO₃)

Nitric acid is a strong, highly corrosive acid. Concentrated nitric acid is also a powerful oxidizing agent — when it reacts with most metals, it releases nitrogen oxide gases instead of the hydrogen gas you'd expect from a typical acid-metal reaction. Its biggest use is manufacturing ammonium nitrate fertilizer; it's also used to make explosives and dyes.

Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)

Sulphuric acid is sometimes called the "king of chemicals" because more of it is manufactured worldwide than any other industrial chemical — it's used to make fertilizers, detergents, dyes, and car batteries. Concentrated sulphuric acid is also a powerful dehydrating agent: it can pull water (or hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio) directly out of other compounds, which is why it chars sugar and paper black on contact.

Diluting it safely

Concentrated sulphuric acid must always be added slowly to water, never the other way around. Mixing releases a large amount of heat; adding water to the acid can make that heat boil the water almost instantly, spitting droplets of concentrated acid outward.

Which acid is being described?

Why must concentrated sulphuric acid always be added to water, never the reverse?

The heat released when the two mix can flash-boil water added directly to concentrated acid, throwing droplets of acid out with it.

Environmental chemistry

Pollution, the greenhouse effect, and acid rain.

Air pollution

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particulates into the air. These harm respiratory health directly and contribute to smog — carbon monoxide is especially dangerous since it binds to blood far more strongly than oxygen does, even at fairly low concentrations.

The greenhouse effect

Certain gases — carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor among them — trap heat radiating from Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm enough to support life. This is a natural and necessary process, but rising levels of these gases from human activity are intensifying it, driving global warming beyond its natural balance.

Acid rain

Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with water vapor in the atmosphere to form sulfuric and nitric acid, which then fall back to Earth as acid rain — damaging buildings, forests, and aquatic ecosystems.

Ozone depletion

Chemicals like CFCs, once common in refrigerants and aerosol sprays, release chlorine atoms high in the atmosphere that break down ozone molecules. This thins the ozone layer that normally shields Earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Which pollutant causes this effect?

What do greenhouse gases do to Earth's temperature?

They let sunlight in but trap the heat radiating back out from the surface, which is what makes Earth's temperature stable enough for life.

Polymers

Natural and synthetic chains of repeating units.

What is a polymer

A polymer is a large molecule built from many small repeating units, called monomers, joined together into a long chain. The word literally means "many parts."

Natural vs synthetic polymers

Natural polymers are built by living organisms — starch and cellulose in plants, proteins in every living cell, and natural rubber from the sap of rubber trees. Synthetic polymers are human-made, like polyethylene, PVC, and nylon, engineered by chemists to link monomers together on purpose.

Addition vs condensation polymerization

In addition polymerization, monomers join together with no atoms left over — polyethylene forms this way from ethylene monomers. In condensation polymerization, monomers join while releasing a small molecule, usually water, with every new bond — nylon forms this way.

Plastics and waste

The same durability that makes synthetic polymers so useful — resisting decay, moisture, and chemicals — also makes them a major waste problem, since many common plastics can take centuries to break down naturally in the environment.

Is this a natural or synthetic polymer?

What is a polymer built from?

Those repeating monomer units, linked into long chains, are what give polymers their characteristic length and strength.

What's the key difference between addition and condensation polymerization?

Addition polymerization joins monomers with nothing left over; condensation polymerization loses a small molecule, usually water, at every joint.

Chemical formulae & valency

Working out chemical formulas from valencies.

What is valency

Valency is the combining power of an element — roughly, how many bonds one of its atoms typically forms, or how many electrons it gains, loses, or shares. Sodium has a valency of 1, oxygen has a valency of 2, and so on. Elements combine in ratios that balance out their valencies.

The criss-cross method

A quick way to write a formula: take the valency (or ionic charge) of each element and swap it down as the subscript of the other. Calcium (valency 2) and chlorine (valency 1) cross over to give CaCl₂ — calcium's 2 becomes chlorine's subscript, and chlorine's 1 becomes calcium's subscript (which is simply omitted, since 1 isn't written).

Polyatomic ions

Some ions are made of more than one atom bonded together but still act as a single charged unit — like sulfate (SO₄²⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻), and carbonate (CO₃²⁻). These combine with metals the same way single-element ions do, using the same criss-cross logic, and get wrapped in brackets if more than one is needed, like Al(NO₃)₃.

What's the correct formula?

What does an element's valency describe?

Valency is what determines the ratio in which two elements combine to form a compound.

Atomic models

From Dalton's solid sphere to the quantum model.

Dalton's solid sphere

In the early 1800s, John Dalton proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible spheres called atoms, and that atoms of a given element are all identical. This was the first real scientific atomic theory, though it had no idea yet that atoms had any internal structure.

Thomson's plum pudding model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 and proposed that atoms are a positively charged sphere with negative electrons scattered through it, like fruit in a pudding — the first model to admit atoms have smaller parts inside them.

Rutherford's nuclear model

Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil, expecting them to pass straight through. Most did — but a few bounced back sharply, which could only mean atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at their center, with mostly empty space around it. This overturned Thomson's model entirely.

Bohr and the quantum model

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels, or shells, rather than spiraling in freely — explaining why atoms don't just collapse. Later, the quantum mechanical model (built by Schrödinger and others) refined this further: electrons don't follow neat orbits at all, but exist in probability clouds, or orbitals, describing where they're likely to be found.

Pick a scientist and see their model

What did Rutherford's gold foil experiment reveal?

Only a small, dense, positive core could explain why a few alpha particles bounced straight back instead of passing through.

Periodic trends

How size, ionization energy, and electronegativity shift.

Atomic radius

Atomic radius shrinks across a period, left to right, because the nuclear charge grows while electrons are still being added to the same shell — the stronger pull pulls the whole electron cloud in tighter. Down a group, atomic radius grows instead, since each row adds a whole new electron shell farther from the nucleus.

Ionization energy

Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom. It generally increases across a period, since a stronger nuclear pull on a smaller atom makes its electrons harder to remove. It generally decreases down a group, since outer electrons sit farther away and are shielded by more inner shells.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond. It increases across a period for the same reason ionization energy does — rising nuclear charge — and decreases down a group, as increasing size and shielding weaken the nucleus's grip on shared electrons.

Pick a property and a direction to see the trend

What happens to atomic radius going down a group?

Each period down adds a whole new electron shell, pushing the outer electrons farther from the nucleus.

Gas laws

How pressure, volume, and temperature relate for gases.

Boyle's law

At constant temperature, a gas's pressure and volume are inversely related — squeeze a gas into a smaller volume and its pressure rises, expand it and pressure falls. This is written P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

Charles's law

At constant pressure, a gas's volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in kelvin) — heat a gas and it expands; cool it and it contracts. This is written V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.

The combined gas law

Boyle's and Charles's laws combine into a single relationship: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, useful whenever pressure, volume, and temperature all change together for a fixed amount of gas.

Boyle's law calculator

P₁ (kPa) · V₁ (L) · V₂ (L)

According to Boyle's law, what happens to a gas's pressure when its volume decreases (at constant temperature)?

Squeezing the same amount of gas into a smaller space makes its particles collide with the container walls more often, raising the pressure.

Solutions & solubility

Concentration, saturation, and what changes it.

Solutions and concentration

A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Concentration describes how much solute is packed into a given amount of solution — commonly expressed in grams per liter (g/L) or moles per liter (mol/L, also called molarity).

Saturated, unsaturated, and supersaturated

A solution is unsaturated if it can still dissolve more solute at that temperature, saturated once it holds the maximum amount possible, and supersaturated if it somehow holds more than that maximum — an unstable state that usually crystallizes out again with the slightest disturbance.

Solubility and temperature

For most solids, solubility in water rises with temperature — that's why warm water dissolves more sugar than cold water. Gases behave the opposite way: their solubility in water falls as temperature rises, which is why a warm fizzy drink loses its bubbles faster than a cold one.

Concentration calculator

mass of solute (g) · volume of solution (mL)

What generally happens to the solubility of a solid in water as temperature rises?

Most solids dissolve more readily in warmer water — gases are the exception, becoming less soluble as it warms.

Colloids & suspensions

Between a true solution and a settling mixture.

Three kinds of mixtures

Mixtures fall into three rough categories based on particle size. True solutions have particles dissolved at the molecular or ionic level — far too small to scatter light or ever settle out. Suspensions have large, visible particles that eventually settle and can be filtered out. Colloids sit in between: particles small enough to stay dispersed indefinitely, but large enough to scatter light.

The Tyndall effect

Shine a beam of light through a colloid and the path of the beam becomes visible, scattered by the dispersed particles — this is the Tyndall effect. It's why a car's headlight beam shows up in foggy air, but you can't see a beam of light passing through a glass of salt water.

Everyday colloids

Colloids are everywhere: milk (fat droplets in water), fog (water droplets in air), whipped cream (air in liquid), and even smoke (solid particles in air) are all colloids, each combining two different states of matter.

Is this a true solution, a colloid, or a suspension?

What causes the Tyndall effect?

Only particles in the colloid size range are large enough to scatter light like this, yet small enough to never settle out.

Alcohols, esters & soaps

Esterification, saponification, and how soap works.

Alcohols

Alcohols contain a hydroxyl (−OH) group attached to a carbon chain, named with an -ol ending — ethanol, the alcohol in drinks and hand sanitizer, is the most familiar example. Alcohols are generally soluble in water because the −OH group can form hydrogen bonds with it.

Esterification

When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, they form an ester and release water — a reaction called esterification. Esters are largely responsible for the fruity smells of many fruits and are used deliberately in perfumes and artificial flavorings.

Acid + Alcohol → Ester + Water
Saponification and soap

Soap is made by boiling a fat or oil with a strong base like sodium hydroxide, a reaction called saponification, which produces soap and glycerol. Soap molecules have a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and a grease-loving (hydrophobic) tail; in water, they cluster grease and oil into tiny spheres called micelles, which is how soap lifts dirt away and lets water rinse it off.

Pick an acid and alcohol to see the ester formed

What does saponification produce?

Boiling a fat or oil with a strong base breaks it apart into soap molecules and glycerol as a byproduct.

Corrosion & rusting

Why metals corrode and how to stop it.

What corrosion is

Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal through reaction with its environment, usually oxygen and moisture. Rusting is corrosion specific to iron: iron reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, the reddish-brown flaky substance known as rust.

What speeds up rusting

Rusting needs both oxygen and water to proceed — remove either one and it slows drastically. Dissolved salts speed it up further by making water a better electrical conductor, which accelerates the underlying electrochemical process.

Preventing corrosion

Common protection methods include painting or oiling a surface to keep out air and moisture, and galvanizing — coating iron with a layer of zinc. Since zinc is more reactive than iron, it corrodes first and protects the iron underneath even if the coating gets scratched, a strategy called sacrificial protection.

Pick a condition and see how fast rusting happens

Why does galvanizing protect iron even if the zinc coating gets scratched?

This is sacrificial protection — the more reactive metal takes the chemical hit so the less reactive one underneath doesn't have to.

Qualitative analysis

Identifying ions with flame tests and precipitates.

Flame tests

Many metal ions color a flame a distinctive way when heated, which makes flame tests a quick way to identify them without complex equipment — this is also why fireworks come in so many colors, using different metal salts on purpose.

Precipitate tests

Adding certain reagents to a solution can form an insoluble solid, or precipitate, that reveals which ion is present by its color and behavior. For example, adding sodium hydroxide solution to a metal salt often produces a colored hydroxide precipitate — the exact color depends on which metal ion is present.

Testing for anions

Anions have their own giveaway tests too: adding dilute acid to a carbonate produces fizzing carbon dioxide gas, and adding silver nitrate solution to a chloride solution produces a white precipitate of silver chloride.

Which ion gives this flame color?

What forms when silver nitrate solution is added to a chloride solution?

Silver chloride is insoluble in water, so it immediately appears as a white solid — a classic confirmatory test for chloride ions.

Fuels & combustion

Fossil fuels, calorific value, and complete vs incomplete burning.

What makes something a good fuel

A fuel is a substance that releases useful energy when it burns. A good fuel has a high calorific value (a lot of energy released per unit mass), ignites and burns easily and safely, and leaves behind minimal harmful residue or pollution.

Types of fuels

Fossil fuels — coal, petroleum, and natural gas — formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms, and remain the world's dominant energy source despite being non-renewable. Biofuels, like ethanol from crops, are renewable alternatives made from recently living material.

Complete vs incomplete combustion

With plenty of oxygen, a fuel undergoes complete combustion, producing carbon dioxide and water and releasing the maximum possible energy. With limited oxygen, incomplete combustion occurs instead, producing carbon monoxide and/or soot (unburned carbon) along with water — releasing less energy and, in the case of carbon monoxide, creating a serious health hazard.

Pick an oxygen supply and see what kind of combustion happens

Why is incomplete combustion dangerous indoors?

Carbon monoxide binds to blood far more strongly than oxygen does, making it dangerous even in small amounts — a real risk from fuel-burning appliances in poorly ventilated spaces.

Biomolecules

Carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids.

Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, usually in a 1:2:1 ratio. Simple sugars like glucose provide quick energy, while larger polysaccharides like starch and cellulose serve as energy storage or structural material in plants.

Proteins

Proteins are long chains of amino acids folded into specific 3D shapes. They do most of the work in living cells — as structural material (like keratin), transporters (like hemoglobin), and enzymes that drive biochemical reactions.

Lipids

Lipids, including fats, oils, and cholesterol, are mostly hydrocarbon chains and are insoluble in water. They store energy far more densely than carbohydrates and form the core of every cell membrane.

Is this a carbohydrate, protein, or lipid?

What are proteins built from?

Long chains of amino acids fold up into the specific shapes that give each protein its function.

Enzymes

Biological catalysts and what changes their activity.

What enzymes do

Enzymes are biological catalysts — proteins that speed up reactions in living cells without being used up, letting reactions happen fast enough to sustain life at body temperature.

The active site

Each enzyme has an active site shaped to fit a specific substrate molecule, like a lock and key. Binding there lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction to proceed.

What affects enzyme activity

Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH. Too much heat or too extreme a pH denatures the enzyme — permanently distorting its active site so the substrate can no longer bind.

Pick a condition and see its effect on enzyme activity

What happens to an enzyme when it's heated past its optimum temperature?

Excess heat distorts the enzyme's shape, ruining the active site's fit with its substrate.

Nucleic acids

DNA, RNA, and how base pairing works.

DNA's structure

DNA is a double helix made of two strands of nucleotides, each built from a sugar, a phosphate, and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). It carries the genetic instructions for building and running a living organism.

Base pairing

The two DNA strands are held together by bases pairing in a fixed way: adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine always pairs with cytosine. This strict pairing is what lets DNA be copied accurately.

RNA vs DNA
