RNA is usually single-stranded and uses uracil in place of thymine. It carries out DNA's instructions, most directly by copying genetic code and helping build proteins.

Pick a DNA base and see its pair

Which base does RNA use in place of thymine?

RNA swaps thymine for uracil, one of the key differences between the two nucleic acids.

Titration

Finding an unknown concentration by neutralization.

What titration measures

Titration finds the unknown concentration of an acid or base by carefully adding a solution of known concentration until the reaction is exactly complete — the endpoint, often spotted with an indicator's color change.

The calculation

For a simple 1:1 acid-base reaction, the concentrations and volumes at the endpoint satisfy M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where M is molarity and V is volume — letting you solve for whichever concentration is unknown.

Choosing an indicator

The right indicator changes color right at the endpoint's pH — phenolphthalein for a strong acid–strong base titration, for example, since it changes color right around neutral pH.

Titration calculator (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂)

acid molarity (M) · acid volume (mL) · base volume used (mL)

What does the endpoint of a titration mark?

An indicator's color change signals that just enough of the known solution has been added to react completely with the unknown.

Buffer solutions

Why some solutions resist pH change.

What a buffer is

A buffer is a solution, usually a weak acid and its conjugate base together, that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

How it works

The weak acid component neutralizes any added base, while the conjugate base component neutralizes any added acid — so the pH barely shifts either way, unlike in pure water.

Why buffers matter

Blood is buffered to stay very close to pH 7.4; even small deviations from that range can be dangerous, which is why the body's buffer systems are so tightly regulated.

Pick a scenario and see what happens to pH

Why does adding a little acid barely change a buffer's pH?

That built-in reserve of base is exactly what soaks up small additions of acid without a big pH swing.

Chromatography

Separating mixtures and calculating Rf values.

How it separates mixtures

In paper chromatography, a solvent travels up a strip of paper, carrying different dissolved substances at different speeds depending on how strongly each clings to the paper versus the solvent — separating a mixture into distinct spots.

The Rf value

The retention factor, Rf, is the distance a substance travels divided by the distance the solvent front travels. It's a fixed value for a substance in a given solvent, useful for identifying unknown spots by comparison.

Uses

Chromatography separates ink components, tests for food dye purity, and in more advanced forms (like gas chromatography) even identifies trace substances in blood or forensic samples.

Rf calculator

distance spot traveled (cm) · distance solvent traveled (cm)

What does an Rf value help you do?

Since Rf is consistent for a substance in a given solvent, matching an unknown spot's Rf to a known one helps identify it.

Crystallization & purification

Picking the right technique for a mixture.

Crystallization

Crystallization recovers a dissolved solid by evaporating its solvent until the solution becomes saturated and the solid forms pure crystals — useful when the goal is a solid product rather than the liquid it was dissolved in.

Filtration and distillation

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through a barrier that traps the solid. Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points by heating, then condensing the vapor.

Sublimation and chromatography

Sublimation separates a solid that turns directly to vapor (like iodine) from one that doesn't. Chromatography separates dissolved substances that travel at different speeds through a medium.

Which technique best separates this mixture?

What property does distillation rely on to separate two liquids?

Heating the mixture boils off the lower-boiling liquid first, which is then condensed and collected separately.

Isomerism

Same formula, different structure.

What isomers are

Isomers are compounds that share the exact same molecular formula but have their atoms arranged differently — which often gives them very different physical and chemical properties.

Chain and position isomerism

Chain isomerism comes from different arrangements of the carbon skeleton itself — straight versus branched, like butane and isobutane. Position isomerism keeps the same functional group but places it at a different point on the chain.

Functional group isomerism

Functional group isomers share a formula but belong to entirely different families of compounds — ethanol (an alcohol) and dimethyl ether (an ether) both have the formula C₂H₆O, yet behave completely differently.

Which type of isomerism is this?

What do all isomers of a compound share?

It's the arrangement of atoms that differs between isomers, not the formula's atom count.

Aromatic compounds

Benzene and its delocalized ring of electrons.

Benzene's structure

Benzene (C₆H₆) is a ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen. Its extra electrons aren't locked into fixed double bonds but are delocalized — spread evenly around the whole ring — which makes benzene far more stable than a typical alkene.

Why aromatic compounds resist addition reactions

Because that delocalized ring is so stable, benzene tends to undergo substitution reactions (swapping a hydrogen for another atom or group) rather than the addition reactions typical alkenes undergo, which would break up its stable ring.

Common aromatic compounds

Toluene (used in solvents and fuel), phenol (used in antiseptics and some plastics), and aspirin all contain a benzene ring as their core structure.

Why is benzene unusually stable compared to a typical alkene?

Spreading those electrons evenly around the ring, rather than locking them into fixed double bonds, lowers the molecule's overall energy.

What type of reaction does benzene typically undergo instead of addition?

Substitution swaps out one hydrogen for another group without disturbing benzene's stable delocalized ring.

Plastics & rubber

Thermoplastics, thermosets, and elastomers.

Thermoplastics

Thermoplastics, like polyethylene and PVC, soften when heated and harden again on cooling, and can be remolded repeatedly — their polymer chains aren't chemically linked to each other, just tangled together.

Thermosets

Thermosets, like Bakelite and melamine, form permanent cross-links between their chains when first molded. Once set, reheating chars or burns them rather than melting them, which makes them heat-resistant but impossible to reshape.

Elastomers

Elastomers, like natural and synthetic rubber, have coiled polymer chains loosely cross-linked just enough to let the material stretch significantly and snap back to its original shape once released.

Is this a thermoplastic, thermoset, or elastomer?

Why can't a thermoset plastic be remolded after it first sets?

Those permanent cross-links mean heating just breaks the material down instead of letting it flow and reshape.

Photochemistry

Light-driven reactions and photosynthesis.

Light-driven reactions

Photochemical reactions are triggered or driven by light energy rather than heat. Photographic film, for example, relies on light decomposing light-sensitive silver compounds to form an image.

Photosynthesis

Plants use light energy to drive photosynthesis, converting carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. It's the reverse, in a sense, of the combustion and respiration reactions that release that same energy back out.

What limits the rate

Photosynthesis speeds up with more light, more CO₂, and warmer temperatures — but only up to a point. Once any one of these becomes scarce, it becomes the limiting factor, and the rate levels off no matter how much of the others are available.

Pick a light level and see the effect on photosynthesis

What does photosynthesis produce from carbon dioxide and water?

Light energy drives the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen as a byproduct.

Lab safety

Hazard symbols and safe lab practice.

Why hazard symbols matter

Standardized hazard symbols let anyone recognize a chemical's main danger at a glance, no matter what language they read, which is essential for safe handling, storage, and transport.

Handling acids and bases safely

Always add concentrated acid to water, never the reverse, and wear eye protection whenever handling corrosive substances. Spills should be neutralized or diluted according to the specific chemical, not just wiped up.

Safe heating and general practice

Point test tubes away from yourself and others when heating, never look directly down into one being heated, and always know the location of safety equipment like eyewash stations and fire extinguishers before starting any experiment.

Which hazard does this symbol description warn about?

What's the correct way to dilute concentrated acid?

Adding water to concentrated acid can flash-boil the water and spit acid outward — always the reverse instead.

History of the periodic table

How Mendeleev predicted elements before they were found.

Mendeleev's arrangement

In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by increasing atomic mass into rows and columns, grouping elements with similar properties together — the first periodic table that actually worked as a predictive tool.

Leaving gaps on purpose

Where an element didn't fit the pattern, Mendeleev boldly left a gap instead of forcing a fit, and used the surrounding elements to predict the missing element's properties in detail — a striking act of confidence in the underlying pattern.

From atomic mass to atomic number

Mendeleev's table had a few awkward exceptions when ordered strictly by mass. Decades later, Henry Moseley showed that ordering elements by atomic number instead — not mass — resolved these exceptions completely, giving the modern periodic law used today.

Pick an element Mendeleev predicted before it was found

What does the modern periodic law arrange elements by?

Moseley's work showed atomic number, not mass, is what truly determines an element's place in the pattern.

Electrochemical series

Ranking metals by how easily they oxidize.

What the series shows

The electrochemical (reactivity) series ranks metals by how readily they lose electrons — the most reactive metals, like potassium and sodium, sit at the top; the least reactive, like gold, sit at the bottom.

Predicting displacement

A metal higher in the series will displace a metal lower in the series from a solution of its salt — this is the same idea used to predict which metal ends up as the free element in a displacement reaction.

Applications

The series also predicts corrosion tendencies (why zinc protects iron sacrificially) and helps explain how much voltage a battery made from two given metals can produce — the farther apart two metals sit, the bigger the voltage.

Pick two metals to see which displaces which

A metal high in the electrochemical series is placed in a solution of a lower metal's salt. What happens?

A more reactive metal gives up its electrons more readily, letting it push the less reactive metal out of its compound.

Hydrogen & its compounds

Isotopes, preparation, and hydrogen as a fuel.

Hydrogen's properties

Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe — a colorless, odorless gas that burns explosively in oxygen to form water, releasing a large amount of energy.

Hydrogen's isotopes

Hydrogen has three natural isotopes: protium (no neutrons, the common form), deuterium (one neutron, used in heavy water), and tritium (two neutrons, radioactive).

Hydrogen as a fuel

Because burning hydrogen produces only water, it's an appealing clean fuel — the challenge is producing, storing, and transporting it safely and efficiently at scale.

Pick a neutron count to identify the isotope

What does burning hydrogen in oxygen produce?

Hydrogen and oxygen combine directly to form water — no carbon involved, which is why hydrogen burns so cleanly.

Carbon & its allotropes

Diamond, graphite, fullerenes, and graphene.

What allotropes are

Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element. Carbon has several strikingly different allotropes, all made of nothing but carbon atoms arranged differently.

Diamond and graphite

In diamond, each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid 3D network, making it extremely hard with no free electrons to conduct electricity. In graphite, carbon atoms form flat, hexagonal layers that slide over each other easily, with delocalized electrons free to conduct.

Fullerenes and graphene

Fullerenes are hollow, cage-like carbon molecules, like the soccer-ball-shaped C₆₀. Graphene is a single layer of graphite's structure, just one atom thick — remarkably strong and an excellent conductor.

Which allotrope of carbon is being described?

Why can graphite conduct electricity while diamond can't?

Diamond locks every electron into a fixed bond, while graphite's layered structure leaves electrons free to flow.

Sulphur & its compounds

Allotropes, sulfur dioxide, and the Contact process.

Sulfur's allotropes

Sulfur exists in a few structural forms, most commonly rhombic and monoclinic sulfur, both built from rings of eight sulfur atoms arranged slightly differently.

Sulfur dioxide

Burning sulfur, or sulfur-containing fuels, produces sulfur dioxide, a pungent gas that's a major contributor to acid rain when it reacts with atmospheric water vapor.

The Contact process

Sulfuric acid is manufactured industrially through the Contact process: sulfur is burned to sulfur dioxide, which is converted to sulfur trioxide over a catalyst, then dissolved to eventually form sulfuric acid.

Pick a sulfur compound to see its role

What environmental problem is sulfur dioxide a major contributor to?

Sulfur dioxide reacts with water vapor in the atmosphere to form sulfuric acid, which falls back down as acid rain.

Halogens

Group 17's reactivity and displacement reactions.

Group 17 trends

The halogens — fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine — get less reactive going down the group, the opposite trend from metals, since it gets harder for a larger atom to attract one more electron to complete its outer shell.

Physical states

Their physical state at room temperature shifts down the group too: fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid — reflecting the increasing strength of intermolecular forces as the molecules get larger.

Displacement and uses

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from a solution of its salt — chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide, for instance. Chlorine is used to disinfect drinking water, and iodine is a common antiseptic.

Pick two halogens to see which displaces which

How does halogen reactivity change going down group 17?

Larger halogen atoms hold their nucleus's pull less tightly on an incoming electron, making them less reactive lower in the group.

Noble gases

Why group 18 barely reacts, and what that's used for.

Why they're inert

Noble gases have a completely full outer electron shell already, so they have almost no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons — making them the least reactive elements on the periodic table.

Physical properties

Noble gases are all colorless, odorless gases at room temperature with very low boiling points, since only weak forces hold their individual atoms together.

Uses that rely on inertness

Their unreactivity is exactly what makes them useful: helium in balloons (lighter than air, non-flammable), argon shielding welding arcs and filling light bulbs, and neon glowing in signs.

Pick a noble gas and see its main use

Why are noble gases so unreactive?

A full outer shell means there's little drive to gain, lose, or share electrons with anything else.

Fertilizers

NPK nutrients and the cost of overusing them.

The big three nutrients

Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) in the largest amounts. Nitrogen drives leafy green growth, phosphorus supports strong root development, and potassium supports overall plant health and disease resistance.

Common fertilizers

Ammonium nitrate and urea are common nitrogen fertilizers; superphosphate supplies phosphorus; potassium chloride (potash) supplies potassium. Many commercial fertilizers blend all three in a labeled NPK ratio.

Eutrophication

Excess fertilizer washed into rivers and lakes can trigger explosive algae growth, called eutrophication. When the algae die and decompose, the process consumes so much dissolved oxygen that fish and other aquatic life can suffocate.

Pick a fertilizer to see what nutrient it supplies

What is eutrophication?

The algae bloom and die-off that follows consumes so much dissolved oxygen that fish and other aquatic life can suffocate.

Intermolecular forces

Van der Waals, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.

Van der Waals (London dispersion) forces

Even nonpolar molecules experience brief, random shifts in their electron clouds, creating momentary attractions to neighboring molecules. These forces are weak individually but present in every substance, and grow stronger with larger electron clouds.

Dipole-dipole forces

Polar molecules have a permanent slightly positive end and slightly negative end. Neighboring molecules line up so opposite charges attract, giving a stronger pull than van der Waals forces alone.

Hydrogen bonding

When hydrogen is bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, the resulting dipole-dipole attraction is unusually strong — strong enough to be given its own name, hydrogen bonding. It's responsible for water's high boiling point and for holding DNA's two strands together.

Pick a substance and see its dominant intermolecular force

Why does water have an unusually high boiling point for such a small molecule?

Those hydrogen bonds take a lot of extra energy to break, which is why water boils at a much higher temperature than similarly sized nonpolar molecules.

Alkali & alkaline earth metals

Group 1 and group 2 reactivity trends.

Group 1: alkali metals

Alkali metals have just one outer electron, making them extremely reactive — so reactive they're stored under oil to keep them from reacting with air and moisture. They react vigorously with water, releasing hydrogen gas and forming a strongly basic hydroxide solution.

Group 2: alkaline earth metals

Alkaline earth metals have two outer electrons, making them reactive but noticeably less so than their group 1 neighbors. They're also harder and denser, and react with water less vigorously, though reactivity still increases going down the group.

Why reactivity increases down each group

Farther down a group, the outer electrons sit in shells farther from the nucleus and are more shielded by inner electrons, so they're held less tightly and lost more easily — the root cause of increasing reactivity down both groups.

Is this a group 1 or group 2 metal?

Why must alkali metals be stored under oil?

Their single outer electron makes them so reactive that even moisture in the air can set off a reaction.

Transition metals

Variable oxidation states, color, and catalysis.

Variable oxidation states

Unlike most main-group metals, transition metals commonly form more than one stable ion — iron can exist as Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺, for example — because their d-electrons are close enough in energy to be lost in different numbers.

Colored compounds

Many transition metal compounds are vividly colored, since their partially filled d-orbitals absorb specific wavelengths of visible light and reflect the rest. Copper sulfate's blue and potassium permanganate's deep purple are classic examples.

Catalytic activity

Transition metals frequently act as catalysts — iron in the Haber process, platinum in catalytic converters — because they can temporarily bond with reacting molecules, offering an alternative, lower-energy pathway for the reaction.

Pick a transition metal ion and see its typical color

Why do many transition metal compounds have vivid colors?

Absorbing certain wavelengths and reflecting the rest is exactly what gives these compounds their characteristic colors.

Entropy & spontaneity

Why some reactions happen on their own.

What entropy is

Entropy (S) measures disorder or randomness in a system. Nature tends toward states of higher entropy — gases spreading to fill a container, ice melting into more disordered liquid water.

Gibbs free energy

Whether a reaction happens spontaneously depends on both energy change (ΔH) and entropy change (ΔS), combined in Gibbs free energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A reaction is spontaneous whenever ΔG works out negative.

Endothermic reactions can still be spontaneous

A reaction can happen on its own even if it absorbs energy, as long as it increases disorder enough — especially at higher temperature, where the TΔS term carries more weight in the equation.

Pick the signs of ΔH and ΔS to see if a reaction is spontaneous

What does a negative Gibbs free energy (ΔG) indicate about a reaction?

A negative ΔG means the reaction can proceed on its own without continuous outside energy input.

Organic nomenclature

The IUPAC rules for naming carbon compounds.

Finding the root name

Start by finding the longest continuous carbon chain — its length sets the root name: meth- (1 carbon), eth- (2), prop- (3), but- (4), pent- (5), and onward.

Adding the suffix

The ending shows the main functional group: -ane for all single bonds, -ene for a double bond, -yne for a triple bond, -ol for an alcohol, -oic acid for a carboxylic acid.

Numbering and substituents

The chain is numbered to give the functional group (or double/triple bond) the lowest possible position number, and any branches are named and listed alphabetically with their own position numbers.

What's the correct IUPAC name?

What does the suffix '-oic acid' indicate in an IUPAC name?

The '-oic acid' ending always marks a carboxylic acid functional group.

Green chemistry

Designing safer, cleaner chemical processes.

What green chemistry means

Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances from the start, rather than cleaning up pollution after the fact.

Guiding principles

Broad principles include preventing waste rather than treating it, favoring renewable feedstocks, designing energy-efficient processes, and using catalysts instead of reagents used up in large excess.

Real examples

Replacing toxic organic solvents with water or supercritical CO₂, using enzymes as catalysts instead of harsh chemical ones, and designing plastics that biodegrade safely are all everyday applications of green chemistry.

Is this a green chemistry practice?

Why does green chemistry favor catalysts over reagents used in large excess?

Since a catalyst isn't used up, far less material needs to be produced, handled, and disposed of.

Water treatment

How raw water becomes safe to drink.

Municipal treatment steps

Raw water typically passes through sedimentation (letting heavy particles settle), coagulation and flocculation (chemicals clumping fine particles together), filtration (removing remaining solids), and disinfection (chlorination or UV light to kill pathogens).

Desalination

Desalination removes dissolved salts from seawater, mainly through reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane that blocks salt ions) or distillation (evaporating and recondensing pure water, leaving the salt behind).

Wastewater treatment

Sewage goes through similar physical stages plus biological treatment, where microorganisms break down organic waste before the treated water is safely released or reused.

Pick a treatment stage and see what it does

What does reverse osmosis rely on to remove salt from seawater?

The membrane's tiny pores let water molecules through while blocking the larger, charged salt ions.

Radioactivity in use

Dating, medicine, and everyday applications.

Carbon dating

Living organisms constantly exchange carbon-14 with their environment. Once they die, that exchange stops, and the carbon-14 decays at a known, steady half-life of about 5,730 years — measuring how much remains estimates how long ago the organism died.

Medical uses

Radioactive tracers, like iodine-131, are absorbed by specific tissues (the thyroid, in this case), letting doctors diagnose or treat conditions there directly. Radiotherapy uses carefully targeted radiation to destroy cancer cells.

Everyday and industrial uses

Smoke detectors use a tiny americium-241 source; industrial radiography uses gamma rays to check welds and castings for hidden cracks, since gamma rays pass through metal and reveal internal flaws on film.

Pick an application and see how it uses radioactivity

What makes carbon-14 useful for dating ancient remains?

Comparing the remaining carbon-14 to its known half-life gives a reliable estimate of time since death.

Hybridization

How atomic orbitals mix to form new shapes.

What hybridization is

Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals (like s and p) into new, equivalent orbitals that better explain a molecule's observed shape and bonding.

sp³, sp², and sp

An sp³ carbon (like in methane) has four equivalent orbitals arranged tetrahedrally. An sp² carbon (like in ethene) has three orbitals in a plane plus one leftover p orbital forming a double bond. An sp carbon (like in ethyne) has two orbitals in a line plus two leftover p orbitals forming a triple bond.

Why it matters

Hybridization predicts bond angles and molecular shape well before you ever see the molecule — sp³ gives roughly 109.5°, sp² gives 120°, and sp gives 180°.

Pick a molecule and see its carbon hybridization

What bond angle does an sp³ hybridized carbon typically have?

Four equally spaced orbitals around a central atom naturally spread out to about 109.5°, the tetrahedral angle.

VSEPR theory

Predicting molecular shape from electron pair repulsion.

The core idea

VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory says electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible, since they repel each other — this arrangement determines a molecule's shape.

Lone pairs matter too

Lone (non-bonding) electron pairs take up more space than bonding pairs, so they push bonding pairs closer together — this is why water's bond angle (104.5°) is smaller than a perfect tetrahedral angle.

Common shapes

Two electron groups give a linear shape, three give trigonal planar, and four give tetrahedral — with lone pairs bending these into shapes like bent or pyramidal.

Pick a molecule and see its shape

Why is water's bond angle smaller than a perfect tetrahedral angle?

Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the H-O-H angle down from 109.5° to about 104.5°.

Coordination compounds

Metal ions surrounded by bonded ligands.

What a coordination compound is

A coordination compound has a central metal ion surrounded by molecules or ions, called ligands, that donate electron pairs to form bonds with the metal.

Coordination number

The coordination number is how many donor atoms are bonded to the central metal — commonly 4 or 6, giving tetrahedral, square planar, or octahedral shapes.

Uses

Coordination compounds show up in hemoglobin (iron bonded to a porphyrin ring), chlorophyll (magnesium at its center), and industrial catalysts.

Pick a coordination compound and see its role

What is a ligand?

Ligands are the electron-pair donors that surround and bond to the central metal ion.

Acid-base theories

Arrhenius, Brønsted-Lowry, and Lewis definitions.

Arrhenius theory

The earliest definition: an acid produces H⁺ ions in water, a base produces OH⁻ ions. It works well for water-based reactions but doesn't explain acid-base behavior without water.

Brønsted-Lowry theory

A broader definition: an acid donates a proton (H⁺), a base accepts one — this covers reactions that don't even involve water.

Lewis theory

The broadest definition: an acid accepts an electron pair, a base donates one — this covers reactions with no protons involved at all, like many metal-ligand bonds.

Pick a theory and see what it defines as an acid

Which acid-base theory is broad enough to cover reactions with no proton transfer at all?

Lewis theory defines an acid purely by its ability to accept an electron pair, which doesn't require a proton to be involved.

Amphoteric oxides

Oxides that can act as both an acid and a base.

What amphoteric means

An amphoteric substance can react as either an acid or a base, depending on what it's reacting with.

Amphoteric oxides

Metal oxides are usually basic and non-metal oxides are usually acidic, but a few oxides — like aluminium oxide and zinc oxide — sit right at the metal/non-metal boundary and react both ways.

Why this happens

These elements have intermediate electronegativity, so their oxides can either donate or accept electron pairs (or protons) depending on the other reactant.

Pick an oxide and see how it behaves

What does it mean for an oxide to be amphoteric?

An amphoteric oxide sits at the boundary between typical basic metal oxides and acidic non-metal oxides.

Lattice energy & the Born-Haber cycle

The energy that holds an ionic crystal together.

What lattice energy is

Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of a solid ionic compound — a measure of how strongly the ions attract each other in the crystal.

What affects it

Lattice energy is larger for smaller ions and for ions with greater charge, since both increase the electrostatic attraction between them.

The Born-Haber cycle

Since lattice energy can't be measured directly, chemists calculate it indirectly by adding up a cycle of other measurable energy changes — sublimation, ionization, bond breaking, electron affinity — that should sum to the same overall energy change as forming the compound directly.

Pick a compound and see its relative lattice energy

Which factor increases lattice energy?

Smaller, more highly charged ions attract each other more strongly, releasing more energy as the lattice forms.

Real vs ideal gases

Where the simple gas laws start to break down.

The ideal gas assumption

The ideal gas law assumes gas particles have no volume and no attraction to each other — a useful simplification that works well under normal conditions.

Where real gases deviate

At high pressure, gas particles are squeezed close enough that their own volume and their attractions to each other start to matter, causing real gases to deviate from ideal behavior.

When the assumption holds best

Real gases behave most like ideal gases at low pressure and high temperature, where particles are far apart and moving fast enough that weak attractions barely matter.

Pick a condition and see how closely a gas follows ideal behavior

Under what conditions do real gases behave most like ideal gases?

Spread-out, fast-moving particles barely interact, which is exactly what the ideal gas model assumes.

Kinetic theory of gases

How particle motion explains gas behavior.

The core assumptions

Kinetic theory pictures gas particles as tiny points in constant, random motion, colliding elastically with each other and their container's walls without losing energy overall.

Temperature and speed

Temperature is directly related to the average kinetic energy of gas particles — heating a gas makes its particles move faster on average.

Explaining pressure

Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the container walls. More frequent or more energetic collisions — from higher concentration or higher temperature — mean higher pressure.

Pick a change and see its effect on particle behavior

What does temperature directly relate to, according to kinetic theory?

A gas's temperature is a direct measure of how fast its particles are moving on average.

Osmosis & osmotic pressure

Why water moves across a membrane on its own.

What osmosis is

Osmosis is the movement of solvent (usually water) across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of lower solute concentration to one of higher solute concentration, without any energy input.

Why it happens

Water moves to balance out concentration on both sides of the membrane — diluting the more concentrated side until, ideally, both sides reach equilibrium.

Osmotic pressure

Osmotic pressure is the pressure that would need to be applied to stop osmosis entirely — it's why cells placed in very salty water shrivel, and cells in pure water can swell and even burst.

Pick a scenario and see what happens to the cell

Which direction does water move during osmosis?

Water moves to dilute the more concentrated side, evening out solute concentration across the membrane.

Colligative properties

Properties that depend on how many particles are dissolved, not what they are.

What makes a property colligative

Colligative properties depend only on the number of dissolved particles in a solution, not on what those particles actually are.

Boiling point elevation and freezing point depression

Dissolving a solute raises a solvent's boiling point and lowers its freezing point — which is exactly why salt is spread on icy roads, lowering the freezing point of water on the surface.

Vapor pressure lowering

Dissolved solute particles also lower a solvent's vapor pressure, since they take up space at the surface where evaporation would otherwise happen.

Pick a scenario and see the colligative effect

What determines the size of a colligative property's effect?

Colligative properties care only about how many particles are dissolved, regardless of what they are.

Phase diagrams

Mapping which state of matter exists at a given temperature and pressure.

What a phase diagram shows

A phase diagram maps out which state of matter — solid, liquid, or gas — is stable at every combination of temperature and pressure.

Phase boundaries

Lines on the diagram mark conditions where two states coexist in equilibrium — crossing a line means the substance changes state.

The triple point and critical point

The triple point is the unique temperature and pressure where solid, liquid, and gas all coexist at once. The critical point marks where the distinction between liquid and gas disappears entirely.

Pick a special point on a phase diagram

What happens at a substance's triple point?

The triple point is the unique condition where all three phases are simultaneously stable.

Hess's law

Adding up reaction steps to find an overall energy change.

What Hess's law says

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same, whether it happens in one step or through a series of steps — energy change only depends on the start and end points, not the path taken.

Why it's useful

Some reactions are hard or dangerous to measure directly. Hess's law lets chemists calculate their enthalpy change indirectly, by combining the enthalpy changes of other reactions that add up to the same overall transformation.

The rule for combining equations

When combining equations to build the target reaction, if an equation is reversed, its enthalpy change flips sign; if it's multiplied by a factor, its enthalpy change is multiplied by the same factor.

Pick an action and see how it affects an equation's enthalpy value

According to Hess's law, what determines a reaction's overall enthalpy change?

Whether a reaction happens directly or through several intermediate steps, the total energy change comes out the same.

Bond enthalpy calculations

Estimating a reaction's energy change from its bonds.

What bond enthalpy is

Bond enthalpy is the average energy needed to break one mole of a specific type of bond in the gas phase — a fixed, tabulated value for common bonds.

Estimating reaction enthalpy

A reaction's overall enthalpy change can be estimated as the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants, minus the total energy released forming all bonds in the products.

Why it's only an estimate

Because bond enthalpies are averages taken across many different molecules, calculations using them give a good estimate rather than an exact value.

Bond enthalpy calculator (kJ/mol)

energy to break reactant bonds · energy released forming product bonds

What does bond enthalpy measure?

It's a tabulated average energy value used to estimate reaction enthalpies from the bonds involved.

Rate laws & reaction order

How concentration mathematically controls reaction speed.

What a rate law is

A rate law is an equation showing how a reaction's rate depends on the concentration of its reactants, found experimentally rather than just read off the balanced equation.

Reaction order

The order of reaction with respect to a substance is the power its concentration is raised to in the rate law — zero order means concentration has no effect, first order means rate is directly proportional, second order means rate depends on the square of concentration.

Determining order experimentally

Chemists find reaction order by measuring how rate changes as they vary one reactant's concentration at a time, holding the others constant.

Pick a reaction order and see what it means

If doubling a reactant's concentration doubles the reaction rate, what order is the reaction with respect to that reactant?

A direct, proportional relationship between concentration and rate is the hallmark of first order.

Homogeneous vs heterogeneous catalysis

Two ways catalysts speed up reactions.

Homogeneous catalysis

A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants — usually all dissolved together in solution — letting it interact freely and directly with reactant molecules.

Heterogeneous catalysis

A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants — commonly a solid catalyst speeding up a gas or liquid reaction — working by adsorbing reactants onto its surface.

Why heterogeneous catalysts are common industrially

Solid catalysts are easy to separate from liquid or gas products afterward, and often more durable, which is why they're used heavily in industrial processes like the Haber process (iron catalyst) and catalytic converters (platinum).

Pick a catalytic process and see its type

What phase is a heterogeneous catalyst usually in, relative to its reactants?

A solid catalyst speeding up a gas or liquid reaction is the classic example of heterogeneous catalysis.

Batteries & cells

Primary and secondary electrochemical cells.

Primary cells

Primary cells, like ordinary alkaline batteries, run a one-way chemical reaction to produce electricity and can't be recharged once their reactants are used up.

Secondary cells

Secondary cells, like rechargeable nickel-metal hydride or lead-acid batteries, use a reaction that can be reversed by applying an outside electric current, restoring the original reactants.

Why some batteries can't be recharged

In a primary cell, the chemical reaction often produces a different, more stable structure that resists being pushed backward — so the original reactants can't be easily reformed.

Pick a battery type and see if it's rechargeable

What's the key difference between primary and secondary cells?

A secondary cell's reaction can be pushed backward by an outside current, restoring the original reactants for reuse.

Fuel cells

Generating electricity directly from a fuel and oxygen.

How a fuel cell works

A fuel cell generates electricity directly from a continuous supply of fuel (often hydrogen) and an oxidizer (usually oxygen), reacting them electrochemically rather than by burning.

Why they're efficient and clean

Since a hydrogen fuel cell's only product is water, it avoids the pollutants of ordinary combustion, and converts chemical energy to electricity more directly and efficiently than burning fuel to drive a generator.

Where they're used

Fuel cells power some buses and cars, provide backup power for buildings, and have supplied electricity on spacecraft for decades.

Pick a fuel cell fact to explore

What is the only byproduct of a hydrogen fuel cell?

Since only hydrogen and oxygen react, water is the sole product — no carbon-based pollutants at all.

Chemistry of glass

How melted sand becomes a transparent solid.

What glass is made from

Ordinary glass is made mainly from silica (sand), soda ash, and limestone, melted together at high temperature and cooled quickly enough that it solidifies without forming an orderly crystal structure.

Why glass is transparent

Glass's disordered atomic structure has no regular boundaries to scatter visible light, letting most of it pass straight through.

Specialty glass

Adding different ingredients changes glass's properties: boron oxide gives heat-resistant borosilicate glass (used in lab equipment and ovenware), and lead oxide gives dense, sparkly lead crystal glass.

Pick a glass additive and see its effect

Why is glass transparent?

Without a repeating crystal structure to scatter light at internal boundaries, visible light passes through largely unimpeded.

Cement & concrete

The chemistry behind the world's most-used building material.

What cement is

Cement is made by heating limestone and clay to very high temperatures, producing a powder that reacts with water in a chemical process called hydration, hardening into a solid, rock-like binder.

Cement vs concrete

Cement is the binding powder; concrete is what you get when cement is mixed with water, sand, and gravel (aggregate), which fills out the mixture and gives it bulk strength.

Why concrete gets stronger over time

The hydration reaction that hardens cement continues slowly for weeks or even years, which is why fresh concrete keeps gaining strength long after it first sets.

Pick a term and see what it means

Why does concrete keep getting stronger for weeks after it's poured?

Cement's hardening reaction with water isn't instantaneous — it continues gradually, adding strength long after the initial set.

Alloys

Mixing metals to improve on their individual properties.

What an alloy is

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (often another metal), designed to have better properties than the pure metal alone.

Why alloying works

Mixing in atoms of a different size disrupts a pure metal's regular layered structure, making it harder for those layers to slide past each other — which is why alloys are typically harder and stronger than pure metals.

Common alloys

Steel (iron plus carbon) is much harder than pure iron; brass (copper plus zinc) resists corrosion better than pure copper; bronze (copper plus tin) was one of the earliest alloys ever used by humans.

Pick an alloy and see what it's made from

Why are alloys generally harder than the pure metals they're made from?

That disrupted structure is exactly what resists the sliding that makes pure metals soft and malleable.

Dyes & pigments

What gives color to fabric, paint, and ink.

Dyes vs pigments

Dyes are soluble colored compounds that chemically bond to a material (like fabric fibers), while pigments are insoluble colored particles mixed into a medium like paint or ink, sitting on the surface rather than bonding into it.

Why compounds appear colored

A compound appears colored when it absorbs certain wavelengths of visible light and reflects the rest — the reflected wavelengths are what we perceive as its color.

Natural vs synthetic

Early dyes came from natural sources like plants (indigo) and insects (cochineal red); modern synthetic dyes, first developed in the 1850s, offer far more colors, consistency, and affordability.

Pick a coloring agent and see its type

What's the main difference between a dye and a pigment?

That chemical bond is what makes dyes penetrate fabric, while pigments simply sit within their medium.

Petroleum refining

Turning crude oil into usable fuels and materials.

Fractional distillation

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths and boiling points. Fractional distillation heats crude oil and separates it into fractions — groups of similar-sized hydrocarbons — as vapors condense at different heights in a tall column.

What each fraction becomes

Lighter fractions, with shorter chains, become gases and petrol; heavier fractions, with longer chains, become diesel, lubricating oil, and bitumen for roads.

Cracking

Since demand for lighter fractions like petrol usually exceeds natural supply, cracking breaks longer, heavier hydrocarbon chains into shorter, more useful ones, often using heat and a catalyst.

Pick a fraction and see what it becomes

Why is cracking used in petroleum refining?

Cracking converts less useful heavy fractions into more valuable lighter fractions like petrol, matching supply to demand.

Food chemistry

The reactions that make cooking work.

The Maillard reaction

The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars, triggered by heat, that produces the browning and rich flavors of toasted bread, seared meat, and roasted coffee.

Emulsification

An emulsion mixes two liquids that normally separate, like oil and water, by using an emulsifier — a molecule with one water-loving and one oil-loving end — to keep tiny droplets of one dispersed evenly through the other, as in mayonnaise.

Why baking soda makes things rise

Baking soda releases carbon dioxide gas when it reacts with an acid (like buttermilk or vinegar) or with heat, and those trapped gas bubbles expand and lift a batter as it bakes.

Pick a cooking process and see the chemistry behind it

What triggers the Maillard reaction?

That heat-driven reaction between amino acids and sugars is exactly what produces browning and savory flavor.

Nanomaterials

Why matter behaves differently at the nanoscale.

What counts as a nanomaterial

Nanomaterials have at least one dimension between roughly 1 and 100 nanometers — small enough that a huge fraction of their atoms sit right at the surface.

Why properties change at this scale

With so many atoms exposed at the surface, nanomaterials can have very different chemical reactivity, strength, or color compared to the same substance in bulk form — gold nanoparticles, for instance, can appear red or purple instead of gold-colored.

Uses

Nanomaterials show up in sunscreen (nano zinc oxide, transparent yet UV-blocking), stronger and lighter composite materials, and targeted drug delivery in medicine.

Pick a nanomaterial use and see why it works

Why do nanomaterials often behave differently from the same bulk substance?

Surface atoms behave differently from atoms buried inside a bulk material, and nanomaterials are almost all surface.

Lithium-ion batteries

The chemistry behind rechargeable phone and EV batteries.

How they work

A lithium-ion battery moves lithium ions back and forth between two electrodes through an electrolyte — discharging as ions flow one way, generating current, and recharging as an outside current pushes them back.

Why lithium

Lithium is the lightest metal and readily loses an electron, letting lithium-ion batteries pack a lot of energy into a small, light package — ideal for phones, laptops, and electric vehicles.

Limitations

Lithium-ion batteries degrade gradually with repeated charge cycles, and can overheat or even catch fire if damaged or manufactured poorly, which is why battery management systems closely monitor their temperature and charge.

Pick a fact about lithium-ion batteries to explore

Why is lithium a good choice for these batteries?

Being light and readily giving up an electron lets lithium pack a lot of energy into very little weight.

Chirality & optical isomerism

Mirror-image molecules that can't be superimposed.

What chirality is

A chiral molecule has a mirror image that can't be superimposed onto itself, no matter how it's rotated — much like your left and right hands are mirror images that never quite match up.

Optical isomers

The two mirror-image forms of a chiral molecule are called optical isomers, or enantiomers. They share identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point) but rotate polarized light in opposite directions.

Why chirality matters in biology

Living systems are often extremely sensitive to which mirror-image form of a molecule is present — one enantiomer of a drug might work as intended, while its mirror image does nothing, or even causes harm.

Pick a fact about chirality to explore

What do the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule have in common?

They're mirror images with the same formula and connectivity — only their spatial arrangement differs.

Reaction mechanisms

The step-by-step story behind a chemical reaction.

What a mechanism describes

A reaction mechanism is the detailed, step-by-step sequence of bond-breaking and bond-forming events that get reactants to products — the overall equation only shows the start and end points.

Nucleophiles and electrophiles

A nucleophile is electron-rich and seeks out a positive or electron-poor center to bond with; an electrophile is electron-poor and seeks out electrons. Most organic reaction mechanisms are built from these two roles interacting.

Why mechanisms matter

Understanding a mechanism lets chemists predict how a reaction will behave under different conditions, and helps explain why some reactions happen fast while others, with a similar overall equation, happen slowly or not at all.

Pick a term and see what it means

What is a nucleophile attracted to?

Being electron-rich, a nucleophile seeks out a positive or electron-deficient center to bond with.

Vitamins & minerals

The small molecules your body can't make on its own.

What vitamins are

Vitamins are organic molecules the body needs in small amounts but usually can't produce itself, so they must come from food — each one supports specific biochemical processes.

Fat-soluble vs water-soluble

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fat and can be stored in the body's fatty tissue; water-soluble vitamins (like vitamin C and the B vitamins) dissolve in water and aren't stored as easily, so they need more regular replenishing.

Minerals

Minerals are inorganic elements — like calcium, iron, and potassium — needed for functions like building bone, carrying oxygen in blood, and conducting nerve signals.

Pick a vitamin or mineral and see its main role

Why are water-soluble vitamins generally needed more regularly than fat-soluble ones?

Since they don't accumulate in fatty tissue like fat-soluble vitamins do, water-soluble vitamins need more frequent replenishing.

History of chemistry

A quick timeline of the field's biggest turning points.

From alchemy to chemistry

Early alchemists, working mostly to transform base metals into gold, developed many lab techniques still in use today — chemistry emerged as a rigorous science once experiments began being measured and repeated systematically.

Lavoisier and conservation of mass

Antoine Lavoisier's careful measurements in the 1770s and 1780s established that mass is conserved in chemical reactions, helping transform chemistry from a qualitative craft into a quantitative science.

The 20th century and beyond

The 20th century brought quantum mechanical models of the atom, an explosion of organic and polymer chemistry, and the tools (like spectroscopy) that let chemists finally see molecular structure directly rather than infer it indirectly.

Pick a chemist and see their key contribution

What did Lavoisier's careful measurements establish about chemical reactions?

This conservation of mass was a foundational shift from qualitative alchemy toward quantitative chemistry.

Le Chatelier in industry

Using equilibrium shifts to maximize industrial yield.

Applying the principle industrially

Industrial chemists deliberately choose conditions — pressure, temperature, concentration — that shift a reversible reaction's equilibrium toward more product, using Le Chatelier's principle to boost yield and profitability.

The Haber process

Making ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) uses high pressure to favor the side with fewer gas molecules, and a compromise temperature — high enough for a fast rate, but not so high that it favors the reverse reaction too much.

The Contact process

Making sulfur trioxide for sulfuric acid (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃) similarly balances a moderate temperature and pressure to get both a good yield and an acceptably fast reaction rate.

Pick an industrial process and see its optimized conditions

Why don't industrial processes always use the absolute highest pressure and lowest temperature to maximize theoretical yield?

Real industrial conditions are always a compromise between maximum yield, an acceptable rate, and practical cost and safety.

Electrolysis: aqueous vs molten

Why water can complicate electrolysis.

Electrolysis of a molten compound

Electrolyzing a pure molten ionic compound is straightforward: only the compound's own ions are present, so they're the only ones that can be discharged at the electrodes.

Electrolysis of an aqueous solution

In water, both the dissolved compound's ions and water's own H⁺ and OH⁻ ions are present, competing to be discharged — which one actually gets discharged depends on their relative reactivity and concentration.

A practical example

Electrolyzing molten sodium chloride produces sodium metal and chlorine gas. Electrolyzing aqueous sodium chloride instead produces hydrogen and chlorine gas, because water is discharged in preference to the more reactive sodium ions.

Pick a scenario and see what's produced at the cathode

Why does electrolyzing aqueous sodium chloride produce hydrogen instead of sodium at the cathode?

Reactive metal ions like sodium are harder to reduce than water, so water gets discharged first.

Faraday's laws of electrolysis

Calculating exactly how much product electrolysis makes.

Faraday's first law

The mass of a substance produced at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the amount of electric charge passed through the solution.

Faraday's second law

When the same amount of charge is passed through different electrolytes, the mass of substances liberated is proportional to their chemical equivalent weight — that is, ions needing more electrons per particle need proportionally more charge to produce the same amount.

Why this matters

These laws let engineers calculate exactly how much metal or gas electrolysis will produce for a given current and time, which is essential in industrial processes like electroplating and metal extraction.

Pick a factor and see its effect on the amount of product

According to Faraday's first law, what is the mass of product directly proportional to?

More charge passed through the electrolyte always means proportionally more product discharged.

Spectroscopy basics

How light reveals a molecule's structure.

The core idea

Spectroscopy studies how matter absorbs or emits different wavelengths of light, and different types of bonds and structures absorb characteristic wavelengths — turning a spectrum into a kind of structural fingerprint.

Infrared (IR) spectroscopy

IR spectroscopy detects the vibration of specific bonds (like C=O or O-H) by which wavelengths of infrared light they absorb, helping identify which functional groups are present in a molecule.

UV-Visible spectroscopy

UV-Visible spectroscopy detects how molecules absorb visible or ultraviolet light, often revealing the presence of conjugated or aromatic systems, and is commonly used to measure concentration in solution.

Pick a spectroscopy type and see what it reveals

What does infrared spectroscopy mainly help identify in a molecule?

Different bonds vibrate at characteristic frequencies, which show up as absorption in the infrared spectrum.

Mass spectrometry

Weighing molecules atom by atom.

How it works

A mass spectrometer ionizes a sample, breaking it into charged fragments, then sorts those fragments by their mass-to-charge ratio using electric and magnetic fields, producing a spectrum of peaks.

Reading the spectrum

The heaviest peak (the molecular ion peak) usually shows the molecule's overall mass, while smaller peaks represent characteristic fragments, which together help piece together the molecule's structure.

Applications

Mass spectrometry identifies unknown compounds in forensic and environmental samples, determines the precise mass of isotopes, and helps sequence proteins in biochemistry.

Pick a fact about mass spectrometry to explore

What property does a mass spectrometer actually sort fragments by?

Electric and magnetic fields deflect ionized fragments based on this ratio, spreading them out to be measured.

Metallic bonding & properties

The electron sea model behind metal behavior.

The electron sea model

In a metal, outer electrons aren't tied to any one atom — they form a shared 'sea' of delocalized electrons flowing freely around a lattice of positive metal ions.

Why metals conduct electricity and heat

That sea of free-moving electrons carries electric current and thermal energy easily through the whole structure, which is why metals are such good conductors.

Why metals are malleable and ductile

Since the electron sea holds the positive ions together without fixed, directional bonds, layers of ions can slide past each other without breaking anything, letting metal be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires.

Pick a metallic property and see why it happens

What lets metal be hammered into a sheet without shattering?

The non-directional electron sea lets the metal's structure deform smoothly instead of fracturing.

Stable isotopes & applications

Non-radioactive isotopes with their own scientific uses.

What stable isotopes are

Stable isotopes are versions of an element with a different number of neutrons that don't undergo radioactive decay — unlike the isotopes used in nuclear chemistry, they stay exactly as they are indefinitely.

Isotope tracing

Because stable isotopes behave chemically almost identically to the more common isotope of the same element, they can be used as traceable labels in reactions, biological pathways, or environmental studies without introducing any radioactivity.

Isotope ratios as clues

The natural ratio of stable isotopes (like oxygen-18 to oxygen-16) in ice cores or fossils shifts slightly with temperature, letting scientists reconstruct past climates.

Pick a use of stable isotopes to explore

What makes stable isotopes different from the radioactive isotopes used in nuclear chemistry?

Stable isotopes stay unchanged indefinitely, which is exactly what makes them safe, long-lasting tracers.

Soil chemistry

What makes soil support (or fail to support) plant life.

Soil pH

Soil pH strongly affects which nutrients plants can actually absorb — most plants prefer slightly acidic to neutral soil, since extreme pH locks certain nutrients into forms roots can't take up.

Nutrient content

Healthy soil holds a reserve of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and trace minerals, either from natural mineral weathering, decomposing organic matter, or added fertilizer.

Cation exchange and organic matter

Clay particles and organic matter (humus) hold onto positively charged nutrient ions (cations) and release them gradually to plant roots — soil with more of both generally holds nutrients better than sandy soil.

Pick a soil factor and see its effect

Why does soil pH matter so much for plant growth?

Even if nutrients are physically present in the soil, the wrong pH can make them chemically unavailable to roots.

Atmospheric chemistry

The layered composition of the air above us.

Atmospheric composition

Earth's atmosphere is roughly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with the remaining 1% made up of argon, carbon dioxide, and trace gases — a mixture remarkably stable over recent geological history.

Layers of the atmosphere

The atmosphere is divided into layers by temperature behavior: the troposphere (where weather happens), the stratosphere (home to the ozone layer), the mesosphere, and the thermosphere, each with distinct chemistry.

The ozone layer's role

Ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, continuously forming and breaking down in a natural chemical cycle that shields life on Earth's surface.

Pick an atmospheric layer and see what happens there

What is the two most abundant gases in Earth's atmosphere?

Nitrogen makes up about 78% and oxygen about 21% of the atmosphere by volume.

Surface chemistry & adsorption

How substances stick to a surface without dissolving into it.

Adsorption vs absorption

Adsorption is when particles stick to the surface of a material, forming a thin layer, without penetrating inside it — different from absorption, where a substance is taken up throughout the whole material.

Why surface area matters

Since adsorption happens only at a surface, materials with a huge surface area relative to their size — like activated charcoal, full of tiny pores — can adsorb a remarkable amount of material.

Applications

Activated charcoal adsorbs toxins in water filters and some medical treatments; solid catalysts rely on adsorbing reactant molecules onto their surface as the first step in speeding up a reaction.

Pick a term and see what it means

Why does activated charcoal adsorb so much material?

All that exposed internal surface gives it vastly more area to adsorb particles onto than a solid block of the same size.

Chemiluminescence & bioluminescence

Light produced by a chemical reaction, not heat.

What chemiluminescence is

Chemiluminescence is light produced directly by a chemical reaction, as excited electrons drop back to a lower energy level and release that energy as light instead of heat — this is often called 'cold light.'

Glow sticks

A glow stick works by chemiluminescence: breaking the stick mixes two chemicals that react, exciting a dye molecule that then releases the energy as visible light.

Bioluminescence

Bioluminescence is chemiluminescence produced by living organisms — fireflies, some deep-sea fish, and certain fungi and bacteria all use a light-producing reaction (usually involving a molecule called luciferin and the enzyme luciferase) for signaling, hunting, or defense.

Pick an example and see how it produces light

Why is chemiluminescence sometimes called 'cold light'?

Unlike a light bulb's filament, chemiluminescent reactions convert most of their energy directly into light rather than heat.

Forensic chemistry

How chemistry helps solve crimes.

Trace evidence

Locard's exchange principle holds that every contact between two objects leaves some trace behind — fibers, paint chips, and glass fragments can all be matched to their source by comparing their chemical composition and physical properties under a microscope or with spectroscopy.

Fingerprint chemistry

Fingerprints are made visible by developing the sweat and oil residue left behind by ridges on the skin. Cyanoacrylate (superglue) fuming reacts with that residue to form a visible white print on hard surfaces, while ninhydrin spray reacts with amino acids in sweat to develop a purple print on porous surfaces like paper.

Toxicology & drug testing

Detecting drugs or poisons in blood or urine relies on the same separation and identification techniques used elsewhere in chemistry — gas chromatography paired with mass spectrometry can separate a complex mixture and identify trace substances with remarkable precision. A breathalyzer works by chemically oxidizing alcohol vapor, producing a measurable signal proportional to blood alcohol concentration.

Pick a piece of evidence and see how chemistry analyzes it

What does Locard's exchange principle state?

This principle is the foundation of trace evidence analysis — contact between objects or people almost always leaves something measurable behind.

Why does ninhydrin reveal fingerprints on paper?

Sweat contains trace amino acids, and ninhydrin's reaction with them produces a visible purple color that outlines the fingerprint ridges.
